modules.title: Python: Stage 0 · Layman
modules.summary: What it is, install it, run one line

lessons.title: The whole path on one page

blocks.text: Python is a programming language that reads almost like English. You type instructions in a text file, and a program called the **interpreter** carries them out line by line.

It is the main language of AI work and one of the most common languages for backend servers. That is why this track goes in one straight line: the language first, then servers, then AI on top of the server.
Each lesson has the same parts: the idea in plain words, how it maps to Swift or Dart, code you can run, a flow diagram, a real example, common mistakes and questions to test yourself.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A mobile app is the shop counter. The backend is the kitchen behind the wall. Python is one of the languages kitchens are written in.
Where a mobile developer already stands

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A grocery order goes: phone app, HTTP request, Python server (FastAPI), database, response. Later an AI feature is added, such as "suggest what I forgot to add". The same Python server calls a language model and streams the answer back to the phone. By the end of this track you can build each box in that chain.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why learn Python instead of only Swift or Dart for backend and AI?
blocks.text: Most AI libraries, model SDK examples and data tools are Python first, and frameworks like FastAPI make it a quick way to ship a backend. Swift and Dart have small server ecosystems by comparison.

blocks.title: What does the interpreter do?
blocks.text: It reads your source file, compiles it to bytecode and executes that bytecode one instruction at a time. There is no separate build step that you run yourself.

lessons.title: Install Python and make a project

blocks.text: Three tools are all you need at the start: the `python3` program, a **virtual environment** and a package installer.
A virtual environment is a private folder of libraries for one project. Without it every project shares one global set of libraries and they break each other.

`pip` is the installer that ships with Python. `uv` is a newer, much faster tool that does the same job and also creates the environment. Learn `pip` and `venv` first, because every tutorial and server uses them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A virtual environment is a separate toolbox per job. The plumber's wrench set never gets mixed with the electrician's.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `venv` plays the role of the per-project `Pods/` or `.dart_tool/` folder. `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml` is your `Podfile` / `pubspec.yaml`. A lock file is `Podfile.lock` / `pubspec.lock`.

blocks.code:
python3 --version              # 3.12 or newer is a good target
mkdir shop-api && cd shop-api
python3 -m venv .venv          # make the private toolbox
source .venv/bin/activate      # switch this terminal to it
pip install httpx              # installs into .venv only
pip freeze > requirements.txt  # write down exact versions
python main.py                 # run a file
deactivate                     # leave the environment
blocks.caption: Create and use a project

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A teammate clones your repository. They run `python3 -m venv .venv`, activate it and run `pip install -r requirements.txt`. They now have the same library versions you have, so "works on my machine" bugs mostly disappear. The `.venv` folder itself is never committed to git.
Pitfalls

items: Forgetting to activate the environment, then installing into the system Python. Check with `which python`: the path should contain `.venv`.
Committing `.venv` to git. Add it to `.gitignore`.
Naming your own file `random.py` or `json.py`. Python imports your file instead of the standard library one.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What problem does a virtual environment solve?
blocks.text: Two projects that need different versions of the same library. Each environment has its own site-packages folder, so they do not clash.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `pip install x` and `pip install -r requirements.txt`?
blocks.text: The first installs one named package. The second installs every package listed in a file, usually with pinned versions, so the setup is repeatable.

blocks.title: What is PyPI?
blocks.text: The public package index that pip downloads from. It is the Python equivalent of pub.dev or CocoaPods trunk.

When you run `python main.py`, Python does two things. First it translates your text into **bytecode**, a compact list of small instructions. Then a loop inside the interpreter runs those instructions one by one.

There is no compile step you wait for, and types are checked while the program runs. A typo in a line that never runs is never reported. That is why tests and type checkers matter more in Python than in Swift.
The **REPL** is Python's interactive prompt. Type `python3`, then type a line, and you get the answer straight away. Use it to try things.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Swift and Dart (release mode) compile ahead of time to machine code, and the compiler rejects type errors before the app runs. Python is closer to Dart in debug mode: code is loaded and run directly, and mistakes show up at run time.

blocks.code:
import dis

def total(price, qty):
    return price * qty

print(total(40, 3))
dis.dis(total)   # shows the bytecode the interpreter actually runs

blocks.text: What happens on `print(total(40, 3))`

rows: Python reads the file and defines the function `total`. Nothing inside it runs yet.
The call `total(40, 3)` starts. A new frame is pushed with its own local names.
`price * qty` is computed and returned. The frame is removed.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Expecting Python to catch a wrong type before running. `total("a", "b")` only fails when that line executes.
Thinking `.pyc` files in `__pycache__` are something to edit. They are cached bytecode. Ignore them and keep them out of git.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
blocks.text: Both in sequence. Source is compiled to bytecode, then the bytecode is interpreted by the CPython virtual machine. It is not compiled to machine code ahead of time.

blocks.title: What is CPython?
blocks.text: The standard implementation of Python, written in C. When people say Python they almost always mean CPython.

blocks.title: What is the REPL good for?
blocks.text: Trying a single expression or library call and seeing the result at once, without creating a file.
A variable is a name stuck on a value. You do not declare a type. The value carries its own type, and the name can be pointed at a different value later.
The basic types are `int` (whole number, any size), `float` (decimal), `str` (text), `bool` (`True` / `False`) and `None` (no value).

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A variable is a sticky note with a name on it. You stick it on a box. You can peel it off and stick it on another box. The box, not the note, knows what is inside.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: There is no `let` versus `var` and no `final`. Every name can be reassigned. `None` is `nil` / `null`. There are no optionals in the language itself. Type hints (a later lesson) give you `str | None`, which reads like `String?`.

blocks.code:
name = "Asha"            # str
items = 3                # int
price = 49.5             # float
is_member = True         # bool
coupon = None            # no value yet

total = items * price
print(f"{name} pays {total:.2f}")      # f-string: values inside { }
print(type(total), type(coupon))

items = "three"          # allowed: the name now points at a str
print(10 // 3, 10 % 3, 2 ** 10)        # floor divide, remainder, power

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Money should not be a `float`. `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Backends store prices as whole paise in an `int`, or use `decimal.Decimal`. An order total is computed in paise and formatted to rupees only when shown.
Pitfalls

items: Using `==` to compare with `None`. Write `if coupon is None`.
Storing money in floats.
Assuming `/` gives a whole number. `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Use `//` for whole division.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is dynamic typing?
blocks.text: The type belongs to the value, not to the variable name. A name can refer to an int now and a str later, and type errors appear at run time.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `is` and `==`?
blocks.text: `==` asks whether two values are equal. `is` asks whether two names point at the very same object. Use `is` for `None`, `True` and `False`.

blocks.title: How big can a Python int get?
blocks.text: As big as memory allows. There is no overflow at 64 bits.
How Python stores values and frees memory

Every value is an **object** on the heap with three things: an identity (its address, `id(x)`), a type and a reference count. A variable is only a name bound to an object. Assignment never copies. It binds another name to the same object.

Objects are either **immutable** (`int`, `float`, `str`, `tuple`, `frozenset`) or **mutable** (`list`, `dict`, `set`, most classes). "Changing" an immutable value builds a new object and rebinds the name. Changing a mutable one alters the object that every name sees.

Memory is freed by **reference counting**: when the last reference disappears the object is released at once. Counting cannot free two objects that point at each other, so a second mechanism, the **cyclic garbage collector**, runs periodically to find such groups.

blocks.code:
import gc, sys, weakref

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
print(id(a) == id(b), a is b, sys.getrefcount(a) - 1)     # same object, two references

n = 10
before = id(n)
n += 1                                 # int is immutable: a new object, the name is rebound
print(id(n) == before)

items = [1, 2]
same = id(items)
items += [3]                           # list is mutable: changed in place
print(id(items) == same)

t = ([1, 2], "x")                      # an immutable tuple can hold a mutable list
t[0].append(3)
print(t)

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.other = name, None

x, y = Node("x"), Node("y")
x.other, y.other = y, x                # a reference cycle
watch = weakref.ref(x)                 # a weak reference does not keep the object alive
del x, y                               # refcounts never reach zero because of the cycle
print("still alive:", watch() is not None)
gc.collect()                           # the cycle collector finds and frees them
print("after gc:", watch())

blocks.text: Reference counts on one list

rows: `a = [1, 2, 3]` creates a list and binds the name `a` to it.
`b = a` binds a second name. Nothing is copied.
`del a` removes one name. The object lives on.
`b = None` removes the last reference. The list is freed immediately.

blocks.text: Mutable or immutable

rows: Yes (hashes by identity unless you define `__eq__`)

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does Python manage memory?
blocks.text: Every object has a reference count and is freed as soon as it reaches zero. A generational cyclic garbage collector additionally finds groups of objects that reference each other and are otherwise unreachable.

blocks.title: What is the difference between mutable and immutable objects?
blocks.text: A mutable object can be changed in place, so every name bound to it sees the change. An immutable one cannot, so any "change" creates a new object.

blocks.title: Why does `a = 256; b = 256; a is b` print True but large numbers may not?
blocks.text: CPython pre-creates and reuses small integers from -5 to 256, so both names point at the same object. This is an implementation detail, which is why you compare values with `==`.

blocks.title: What is a weak reference?
blocks.text: A reference that does not increase the reference count. It is used for caches and observers so they do not keep objects alive.
A string is text. Strings cannot be changed in place: every operation returns a new string. Most backend work is reading, cleaning and building strings, so a few methods carry a lot of weight.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Slicing `s[0:3]` replaces Swift's index dance and Dart's `substring`. f-strings are string interpolation: `f"{x}"` is `"\(x)"` in Swift and `"$x"` in Dart.

blocks.code:
raw = "  Tomato, onion ,POTATO  "
clean = [part.strip().lower() for part in raw.split(",")]
print(clean)                         # ['tomato', 'onion', 'potato']
print(", ".join(clean).title())      # Tomato, Onion, Potato

order_id = "BB-2026-000184"
print(order_id[:2], order_id[-6:])   # first two, last six
print(order_id.startswith("BB"), "2026" in order_id)
print(order_id.replace("-", ""))
print(f"{'Total':<10}{1234.5:>10.2f}")   # padding and alignment

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A user types a pincode as " 560 103 ". The server strips spaces, checks it is six digits with `value.isdigit() and len(value) == 6`, and only then looks up delivery slots. Every text field coming from a phone gets this treatment.
Pitfalls

items: Building a long string with `+=` inside a loop. Collect parts in a list and call `"".join(parts)`.
Forgetting strings are immutable. `s.upper()` returns a new string, it does not change `s`.
Building SQL with f-strings. This allows SQL injection. Always pass parameters separately (database lesson).

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why are strings immutable?
blocks.text: So they can be shared safely and used as dictionary keys. Any change creates a new string object.

blocks.title: How do you reverse a string?
blocks.text: With a slice that steps backwards: `s[::-1]`.

blocks.title: What does `"a,b,,c".split(",")` return?
blocks.text: `['a', 'b', '', 'c']`. Empty pieces are kept when you pass a separator.
Python uses **indentation** to show which lines belong together. There are no curly braces. Four spaces is the standard.
`if / elif / else` chooses a path. `for` walks over a collection. `while` repeats until a condition turns false. `break` leaves a loop early and `continue` skips to the next round.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `for item in items` is the same as Swift's `for item in items` and Dart's `for (final item in items)`. There is no C-style `for (i = 0; ...)`. Use `range(n)` for counting and `enumerate(items)` when you need the index.
The loop, round by round

rows: Round 3: ghee, 540 × 1 = 540 is added. The list is finished, so the loop ends.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Mixing tabs and spaces. Set your editor to insert four spaces.
Changing a list while looping over it. Loop over a copy (`for x in items[:]`) or build a new list.
Writing `for i in range(len(items))` then `items[i]`. Loop over the items directly.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What values are treated as false in an `if`?
blocks.text: `False`, `None`, zero, and empty containers such as `""`, `[]`, `{}` and `set()`. Everything else is true.

blocks.title: What does `for ... else` do?
blocks.text: The `else` block runs only if the loop finished without hitting `break`. It is useful for "searched everything, found nothing".

blocks.title: What is the difference between `range(5)` and `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]`?
blocks.text: `range` produces numbers one at a time and stores only start, stop and step. The list holds all five numbers in memory.
A function is a named block of code that takes inputs and returns an output. In Python functions are ordinary values: you can store one in a variable, pass it to another function and return it.
Arguments can be passed by position or by name. A parameter can have a default. `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects extra named ones into a dict.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Python has no argument labels like Swift. Any parameter can be passed by name: `fee(total=300)`. A bare `*` in the parameter list forces everything after it to be named, which gives you Dart-style named parameters. `lambda x: x * 2` is a one-expression closure.

blocks.code:
def delivery_fee(total, *, member=False, surge=1.0):
    """Return the fee in rupees. Arguments after * must be named."""
    if member or total >= 500:
        return 0
    return round(20 * surge)

print(delivery_fee(300))
print(delivery_fee(300, surge=1.5))
print(delivery_fee(300, member=True))

def log(event, *args, **kwargs):
    print(event, args, kwargs)

log("order_placed", 184, "express", city="Bengaluru", items=7)

prices = [62, 45, 540]
print(sorted(prices, key=lambda p: -p))      # a function passed as a value
print(list(map(lambda p: p * 2, prices)))

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Every backend endpoint is a function: it receives the request data as arguments and returns the response. A framework such as FastAPI calls your function for you when a matching URL arrives. Keeping the business rule (`delivery_fee`) in a plain function, separate from the web layer, makes it trivial to test.
Pitfalls

items: A mutable default argument: `def add(item, cart=[])`. The list is created once and shared by every call. Use `cart=None` and create the list inside.
Forgetting `return`. The function then returns `None`.
Changing a list or dict that was passed in, when the caller did not expect it.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the mutable default argument bug?
blocks.text: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A default list or dict is shared between calls, so data leaks from one call to the next. Use `None` as the default and build the object inside the function.

blocks.title: What are `*args` and `**kwargs`?
blocks.text: `*args` gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple. `**kwargs` gathers extra keyword arguments into a dict. They let a function accept any call shape, which wrappers and decorators rely on.

blocks.title: Does Python pass arguments by value or by reference?
blocks.text: Neither exactly. It passes a reference to the object. Reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller, but mutating the object (appending to a list) does.

blocks.title: What is a closure?
blocks.text: A function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.
Scope, closures and the late-binding trap

When Python meets a name it searches four places in order, known as **LEGB**: the **L**ocal function, any **E**nclosing functions, the module's **G**lobals and the **B**uilt-ins. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local to that function unless you declare `nonlocal` or `global`.

A **closure** is an inner function that keeps access to variables of the enclosing function after that function has returned. Closures capture the **variable**, not its value at that moment. This causes the best-known Python trap: functions created in a loop all see the loop variable's final value.

blocks.code:
total = 100                       # global

def outer():
    total = 10                    # enclosing
    def inner():
        return total + 1          # found in the enclosing scope, not the global one
    return inner()
print(outer(), total)

def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count            # without this line: UnboundLocalError
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

next_id = make_counter()
print(next_id(), next_id(), next_id.__closure__[0].cell_contents)

handlers = [lambda: n * 10 for n in range(3)]
print([h() for h in handlers])            # [20, 20, 20]: all share one variable n

fixed = [lambda n=n: n * 10 for n in range(3)]   # a default argument captures the value now
print([h() for h in fixed])               # [0, 10, 20]

def broken():
    print(total)                  # looks global, but the assignment below makes it local
    total = 5
try:
    broken()
except UnboundLocalError as err:
    print("UnboundLocalError:", err)

blocks.text: Argument kinds in one signature

rows: Extra positional arguments as a tuple
Extra keyword arguments as a dict
At a call site: unpack a sequence or dict into arguments

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the LEGB rule?
blocks.text: The order in which Python resolves a name: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module), Built-in.

blocks.title: Why do closures created in a loop all return the same value?
blocks.text: They capture the variable, which is looked up when the function is called. By then the loop has finished and the variable holds its last value. Bind the current value with a default argument or `functools.partial`.

blocks.title: What does `nonlocal` do?
blocks.text: It tells Python that an assignment refers to a variable in an enclosing function's scope instead of creating a new local one.

blocks.title: What is a pure function and why prefer it?
blocks.text: A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing outside itself. It is easy to test, cache and run concurrently.

modules.title: Python: Stage 2 · Data
modules.summary: The four containers you use every day

blocks.text: A **list** is an ordered, changeable sequence. A **tuple** is an ordered sequence that cannot be changed after creation. Use a list for "many of the same kind of thing" and a tuple for "one record with fixed positions".
Slicing takes a piece: `items[start:stop:step]`. Unpacking splits a sequence into names in one line.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `list` is `Array` / `List`. A tuple is a Swift tuple or a Dart record. Negative indexes count from the end: `items[-1]` is `items.last`.

blocks.code:
slots = ["7-9", "9-11", "11-13", "17-19", "19-21"]
slots.append("21-23")
slots.insert(0, "6-7")
print(slots[0], slots[-1], slots[1:3], slots[::2])
print(len(slots), "9-11" in slots, slots.index("17-19"))

first, *middle, last = slots          # unpacking with a star
print(first, len(middle), last)

point = (12.97, 77.59)                # tuple: latitude, longitude
lat, lon = point

orders = [("A", 320), ("B", 90), ("C", 760)]
orders.sort(key=lambda o: o[1], reverse=True)
print(orders[0])
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # same list, two names
c = a.copy()     # a new list
b.append(4)
print(a, c)      # [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3]

blocks.text: Two names, one list

rows: `b = a` does not copy. Both names point at the same object.
`c = a.copy()` creates a second, independent list.
`b.append(4)` changes object 1. `a` sees it. `c` does not.

nodes.label: Need to add or remove items?

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: `b = a` copies the reference, not the list. This is the opposite of Swift arrays, which are value types.
`[[0] * 3] * 3` makes three references to the same inner list. Use `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`.
`list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. `sorted(list)` returns a new list.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: List versus tuple: when do you use each?
blocks.text: A list for a collection that grows or changes. A tuple for a fixed group of values, as a dictionary key, or to signal "do not modify". Tuples are hashable when their contents are.

blocks.title: What is the cost of `x in some_list`?
blocks.text: It scans the list, so it is O(n). A set or dict does the same check in O(1) on average.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
blocks.text: A shallow copy makes a new outer container that still points at the same inner objects. `copy.deepcopy` copies everything recursively.
A **dict** maps keys to values. It is the most used structure in backend Python because JSON objects become dicts. Lookup by key is fast no matter how large the dict is.
A **set** is a collection of unique values with fast membership tests and set maths (union, intersection, difference).

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `dict` is `Dictionary` / `Map`. `d.get("key")` returns `None` when the key is missing, like optional subscript access in Swift. `d["key"]` on a missing key raises `KeyError`, like a force unwrap.

diagram.title: How a dict finds a key

nodes.label: Number picks a slot in a table

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: "Group orders by city", "count how many times each product was bought" and "which of these 5,000 product ids are out of stock" are all one line with `defaultdict`, `Counter` and a set. Reaching for a nested loop instead turns a 10 millisecond job into a 10 second one.
Pitfalls

items: Using a list as a dict key. Keys must be hashable: use a tuple.
`d["missing"]` crashing a request. Use `.get()` with a default for optional fields.
Changing a dict while looping over it. Loop over `list(d.items())`.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is dict lookup O(1)?
blocks.text: The key is hashed to a number that points directly at a slot in a table, so no scan is needed. Collisions are handled internally and are rare on average.

blocks.title: What can be a dict key?
blocks.text: Any hashable value: str, int, float, tuple of hashables, frozenset. Lists, dicts and sets cannot, because they can change.

blocks.title: Do dicts keep order?
blocks.text: Yes. Since Python 3.7 a dict keeps keys in insertion order.

blocks.title: How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping order?
blocks.text: `list(dict.fromkeys(items))`. A set would remove duplicates but lose the order.
Inside the hash table

A dict is a **hash table**. To store a key Python calls `hash(key)`, uses part of that number to choose a slot and stores the key and value there. To look a key up it does the same calculation and goes straight to the slot. That is why lookup time does not grow with the size of the dict.

Two different keys can land on the same slot. This is a **collision**. Python then probes other slots in a fixed pattern until it finds a free one. When the table is about two thirds full it is resized to keep collisions rare, which costs a full copy now and then.

This design explains the rules you have met. A key must be **hashable**, meaning its hash never changes during its life. Objects that compare equal must have the same hash. And if every key hashed to the same number, the dict would degrade into a slow list.
Storing and finding a key

rows: `d["milk"] = 3`. Python computes `hash("milk")` and takes its low bits to pick a slot.
`d["eggs"] = 12` also hashes to slot 5, which is taken. A collision. Python probes the next slot in its sequence.
Lookup of `"eggs"`: slot 5 holds a different key, so the same probe sequence is followed to slot 6.
More keys arrive and the table passes two thirds full. Python allocates a bigger table and re-inserts everything.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How is a dict implemented?
blocks.text: As an open-addressing hash table. The key's hash selects a slot. Collisions are resolved by probing other slots, and the table grows when it gets too full.

blocks.title: What makes an object hashable?
blocks.text: It has a `__hash__` that returns the same value for its whole life and an `__eq__` consistent with it: equal objects have equal hashes.

blocks.title: What is the worst-case lookup time of a dict?
blocks.text: O(n), when many keys collide. With a good hash function the average is O(1).

blocks.title: What is the time complexity of common list operations?
blocks.text: Index and append are O(1). Insert or delete at the front and membership tests are O(n). Sorting is O(n log n).

A comprehension builds a list, dict or set from a loop in one expression. It reads as "give me this, for each item in that, if a condition holds". It is the idiomatic replacement for `map` and `filter`.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `[p.price for p in items if p.in_stock]` is `items.filter { $0.inStock }.map { $0.price }` in Swift and `items.where((p) => p.inStock).map((p) => p.price).toList()` in Dart. The filter is written last but applied first.

blocks.code:
cart = [
    {"name": "milk", "price": 62, "qty": 2, "in_stock": True},
    {"name": "ghee", "price": 540, "qty": 1, "in_stock": False},
    {"name": "bread", "price": 45, "qty": 1, "in_stock": True},
]
names = [item["name"] for item in cart]
available = [item for item in cart if item["in_stock"]]
price_by_name = {item["name"]: item["price"] for item in cart}
total = sum(item["price"] * item["qty"] for item in available)   # generator: no list built
print(names, price_by_name, total)
print(any(not item["in_stock"] for item in cart), all(item["qty"] > 0 for item in cart))

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Nesting three loops in one comprehension. If it does not fit on one readable line, write a normal loop.
Using a comprehension only for a side effect such as printing. Use a `for` loop.
Building a huge list just to sum it. Drop the square brackets to get a generator.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between `[x for x in data]` and `(x for x in data)`?
blocks.text: The first builds the whole list in memory. The second is a generator that produces one value at a time when asked.

blocks.title: When should you not use a comprehension?
blocks.text: When the logic needs several statements, error handling or side effects. Readability wins over brevity.
A **module** is one `.py` file. A **package** is a folder of modules. `import` runs the module once, caches it and gives you a name to reach what is inside.
Code at the top level of a file runs at import time. The line `if __name__ == "__main__":` means "only do this when the file is run directly, not when it is imported".

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A module is a Swift file or a Dart library, except nothing is visible until you import it by name. There is no `private` keyword. A leading underscore (`_helper`) is a convention meaning "internal, do not use from outside".

blocks.code:
shop-api/
  pyproject.toml
  app/
    __init__.py
    main.py          # creates the web app
    config.py        # settings from environment variables
    routes/orders.py # URL handlers
    services/pricing.py   # business rules, no web code
    db/models.py     # tables
  tests/test_pricing.py
blocks.caption: A typical backend layout

blocks.code:
# app/services/pricing.py
GST_RATE = 0.05

def with_tax(amount: int) -> int:
    return round(amount * (1 + GST_RATE))

if __name__ == "__main__":      # python -m app.services.pricing
    print(with_tax(200))

# app/routes/orders.py would then say:
# from app.services.pricing import with_tax

nodes.label: Run the file top to bottom

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Layers keep a backend changeable: routes know about HTTP, services know the business rules, the db layer knows SQL. A pricing rule change touches one file in `services/` and its test, and no web code.
Pitfalls

items: Circular imports: `a.py` imports `b.py` which imports `a.py`. Move the shared piece into a third module.
Doing slow work (database connections, network calls) at import time. Imports should only define things.
`from module import *`. It hides where names come from.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` do?
blocks.text: `__name__` is `"__main__"` only in the file that was started directly. The guard lets a file be both an importable module and a runnable script.

blocks.title: How does Python find a module?
blocks.text: It checks the cache `sys.modules`, then searches each folder in `sys.path`: the script's folder, installed packages in site-packages and the standard library.

blocks.title: What is the difference between absolute and relative imports?
blocks.text: `from app.services import pricing` is absolute, from the project root. `from . import pricing` is relative to the current package. Absolute imports are clearer and preferred.
When something goes wrong Python **raises** an exception. It travels up through the calling functions until some `try / except` catches it. If nothing does, the program stops and prints a traceback.
`try` wraps the risky code, `except` handles a specific error type, `else` runs when there was no error, and `finally` always runs, which makes it the place for cleanup.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `raise` is `throw`. `try / except` is `do / catch` in Swift and `try / on ... catch` in Dart. Functions are not marked `throws`: any call can raise, so you decide where it makes sense to catch.

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: In a web server you rarely catch errors inside each function. Business code raises a specific exception such as `OutOfStock`. One central handler turns it into an HTTP 409 with a clear message. Anything unexpected becomes a 500, is logged with its traceback and never leaks internals to the phone.
Pitfalls

items: A bare `except:` or `except Exception: pass` that swallows every error. The bug is still there, now it is invisible.
Catching too high up and losing the context needed to fix the problem.
Using exceptions for normal control flow in a hot loop.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between `except Exception` and a bare `except`?
blocks.text: A bare `except` also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, which you almost never want to swallow. `except Exception` leaves those alone.

blocks.title: When does `finally` run?
blocks.text: Always: after success, after a handled error, after an unhandled error and even after a `return` inside the `try`.

blocks.title: What does `raise ... from err` do?
blocks.text: It raises a new exception while keeping the original as its cause, so the traceback shows both.

blocks.title: What is EAFP?
blocks.text: "Easier to ask forgiveness than permission": try the operation and handle the failure, instead of checking every condition first. It is the common Python style.
The exception tree, chaining, groups and reading a traceback

Exceptions form a class tree. `except SomeError` also catches every subclass of it, so the order of your `except` clauses matters: put the most specific first. Your own errors should share one base class per application, with a subclass per situation. A central handler can then map any of them to an HTTP response.
**Chaining** keeps the original error when you raise a more meaningful one: `raise AppError(...) from err` stores the low-level error as `__cause__`, and the traceback shows both.

An **exception group** carries several unrelated errors at once, for example every failed validation or every failed task in a `TaskGroup`. `except*` handles the members of one type and lets the rest continue upward.

Read a **traceback** from the bottom. The last line is the error type and message. The lines above it are the call chain, most recent call last. The frame nearest the bottom that is in your own code is usually where to look.
The part of the built-in tree you meet most

rows: Root. Includes `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, which you should not catch
Root of everything you normally handle
Right type but bad value / wrong type
Missing dict key / list index out of range
Attribute does not exist, often on `None`
A task was cancelled. Derives from `BaseException`

blocks.text: Reading a traceback bottom-up

rows: Start at the last line: the exception type and message.
a dict had no such key
Go up one frame: the exact line that raised.
Keep going up until you leave library code and reach your own.
If you see "The above exception was the direct cause of", there are two errors. Read the first one too.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why order `except` clauses from specific to general?
blocks.text: The first matching clause wins, and a parent class matches all its subclasses. A general clause placed first would hide the specific ones.

blocks.title: What is exception chaining?
blocks.text: Raising a new exception while attaching the original as its cause with `raise New(...) from original`. Both appear in the traceback.

blocks.title: What is an ExceptionGroup?
blocks.text: An exception that bundles several exceptions. `except*` handles the members matching a type and re-raises the rest. Task groups raise them when several tasks fail.

blocks.title: What does `logging.exception` do?
blocks.text: It logs at error level and appends the current exception's traceback. Call it inside an `except` block.

blocks.title: Why should you not catch `BaseException`?
blocks.text: It includes `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and task cancellation, which must propagate so the program can stop or cancel cleanly.
`pathlib.Path` represents a file or folder. `open()` gives a file object, and wrapping it in `with` guarantees the file is closed even if an error happens.
JSON is the format phones and servers use to talk. `json.loads` turns JSON text into dicts and lists, and `json.dumps` turns them back into text.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `json.loads` is `JSONSerialization` / `jsonDecode`: you get loose dicts, not typed objects. The typed `Codable` / `fromJson` experience comes from Pydantic in the backend stage.

blocks.code:
import csv, json, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
orders_file = folder / "orders.json"

orders = [{"id": 184, "city": "blr", "total": 709}, {"id": 185, "city": "del", "total": 90}]
orders_file.write_text(json.dumps(orders, indent=2))

loaded = json.loads(orders_file.read_text())
print(loaded[0]["city"], orders_file.suffix, orders_file.exists())

report = folder / "report.csv"
with report.open("w", newline="") as handle:          # closed automatically
    writer = csv.DictWriter(handle, fieldnames=["id", "city", "total"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(loaded)

with report.open() as handle:
    for line in handle:               # one line at a time: fine for huge files
        print(line.strip())

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A nightly job reads a 4 GB export of orders. Reading it with `read_text()` would load all 4 GB into memory. Looping over the file object reads one line at a time and keeps memory flat. The same idea, streaming, comes back in the HTTP and AI lessons.
Pitfalls

items: Opening a file without `with` and forgetting to close it.
Building paths with string `+`. Use `Path(...) / "name"`.
Assuming JSON keeps types Python has but JSON does not: tuples become lists, `datetime` is not supported, dict keys become strings.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use `with open(...)`?
blocks.text: The file is closed when the block ends, even when an exception is raised inside it.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `json.load` and `json.loads`?
blocks.text: `load` reads from a file object. `loads` reads from a string. The same pairing exists for `dump` and `dumps`.

blocks.title: How do you read a file too big for memory?
blocks.text: Iterate over the file object line by line, or read fixed-size chunks, so only a small piece is in memory at a time.
A class bundles data with the functions that work on it. `__init__` sets up a new object and `self` is the object itself, written explicitly as the first parameter of every method.
For classes that mostly hold data, `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: All Python classes are reference types, like Swift `class`. There is no `struct`. A `@dataclass(frozen=True)` is the closest thing to an immutable Swift struct or a Dart class with `final` fields. `self` is `this` or Swift's `self`, but you must write it in the parameter list.

blocks.caption: Inheritance and duck typing

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Forgetting `self` in a method signature or when reading a field.
A class attribute that is a list (`items = []` at class level) is shared by every instance. Use `field(default_factory=list)`.
Deep inheritance trees. Prefer small classes passed into each other (composition).

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What does `@dataclass` generate?
blocks.text: `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the annotated fields. With `frozen=True` it also blocks assignment and makes instances hashable.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a class method, a static method and an instance method?
blocks.text: An instance method receives the object (`self`). A class method receives the class (`cls`) and is often an alternative constructor. A static method receives neither and is just a function placed in the class.

blocks.title: What is duck typing?
blocks.text: Code cares that an object has the needed method, not what class it is. `Protocol` lets a type checker verify that without inheritance.

blocks.title: What is `@property` for?
blocks.text: It makes a method read like a field, so a computed value such as `total` is accessed without parentheses.
Inheritance, `super()` and how attributes are found

A class can inherit from another and override its methods. `super()` calls the next class in line. With multiple inheritance "next in line" is defined by the **method resolution order (MRO)**, a single flat list Python computes for every class. You can print it with `ClassName.__mro__`.

An **abstract base class** declares methods that subclasses must provide, and refuses to be instantiated until they do. `__slots__` removes the per-instance dictionary, which saves memory when you create millions of small objects.
Attribute lookup follows a fixed order: the instance's own dictionary first, then each class along the MRO. That is why an instance attribute hides a class attribute of the same name.

nodes.label: In each parent along the MRO?

blocks.text: `AuditedCard("Asha").charge(10000)`

rows: Python searches the MRO for `charge`: AuditedCard has none, Audited does.
`Audited.charge` calls `super().charge`. `super()` means "next after Audited in this object's MRO", which is Card.
`Card.charge` calls `self.total`. Not on Card, found on PaymentMethod. `self.fee_percent` resolves to Card's 1.8.
The strings are joined on the way back up.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the MRO?
blocks.text: The method resolution order: the linear order of classes Python searches for an attribute, computed with the C3 algorithm. `super()` follows it.

blocks.title: What does `super()` do in multiple inheritance?
blocks.text: It delegates to the next class in the instance's MRO, which is not necessarily the parent of the class where it is written.

blocks.title: Class attribute versus instance attribute?
blocks.text: A class attribute lives on the class and is shared. An instance attribute lives in the instance's `__dict__` and hides a class attribute of the same name.

blocks.title: When would you use `__slots__`?
blocks.text: When creating very many instances of a small class: it removes the per-instance dict to save memory and speed up attribute access.

blocks.title: Composition versus inheritance?
blocks.text: Inheritance says "is a" and couples the child to the parent's implementation. Composition says "has a" and passes collaborators in. Prefer composition unless there is a true is-a relationship.

Methods with double underscores, such as `__len__` or `__eq__`, are hooks that Python calls for you. `len(x)` calls `x.__len__()`, `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)` and `for i in x` calls `x.__iter__()`. Implementing them makes your own classes behave like built-in ones.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: This is operator overloading plus protocol conformance. `__repr__` is `CustomStringConvertible` / `toString()`, `__eq__` and `__hash__` are `Equatable` and `Hashable`, `__iter__` is `Sequence` / `Iterable`, `__getitem__` is `subscript` / `operator []`.
The ones worth knowing
Pitfalls

items: Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__`. The class becomes unhashable and cannot be a dict key or set member.
Overloading operators for things that are not obviously arithmetic. It surprises readers.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between `__repr__` and `__str__`?
blocks.text: `__repr__` is for developers and should be unambiguous. `__str__` is for end users. If only `__repr__` exists, `print` uses it.

blocks.title: Why must equal objects have equal hashes?
blocks.text: Dicts and sets find an item by hash first, then compare with `==`. Two equal objects with different hashes would be treated as different keys.

Type hints are notes that say what type a value should be. Python itself ignores them at run time. Tools read them: your editor for autocomplete, a checker such as `mypy` or `pyright` to find bugs before running, and frameworks such as FastAPI and Pydantic to validate data.
In backend code, write hints on every function signature. They are how a large Python codebase stays understandable.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: With hints and a checker turned on, Python feels much closer to Swift or Dart. `str | None` is `String?`. `list[int]` is `[Int]` / `List<int>`. The difference: nothing stops the program from running with a wrong type unless a tool checks it.

blocks.code:
from typing import Literal, TypedDict

Status = Literal["placed", "packed", "shipped", "delivered"]

class OrderRow(TypedDict):
    id: int
    status: Status
    coupon: str | None

def next_status(current: Status) -> Status | None:
    flow: list[Status] = ["placed", "packed", "shipped", "delivered"]
    position = flow.index(current)
    return flow[position + 1] if position + 1 < len(flow) else None

def discount(order: OrderRow, table: dict[str, int]) -> int:
    code = order["coupon"]
    if code is None:          # the checker now knows code is str below
        return 0
    return table.get(code, 0)

row: OrderRow = {"id": 184, "status": "packed", "coupon": "FIRST50"}
print(next_status(row["status"]), discount(row, {"FIRST50": 50}))

nodes.label: mypy / pyright in CI: fail the build on a mismatch
Pydantic / FastAPI: validate real data at run time

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Believing hints are enforced. `def f(x: int)` happily accepts a string unless a checker or Pydantic is involved.
Sprinkling `Any` everywhere, which turns checking off.
Not handling the `None` branch of an optional value.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Are type hints enforced at run time?
blocks.text: No. They are metadata. Static checkers enforce them before running, and libraries such as Pydantic choose to enforce them on data.

blocks.title: What is `Optional[str]`?
blocks.text: The same as `str | None`: the value is either a string or `None`.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `TypedDict`, `dataclass` and a Pydantic model?
blocks.text: `TypedDict` only describes the shape of a plain dict for the checker. A dataclass is a real class with typed fields and no validation. A Pydantic model validates and converts data when it is created.
Generics, protocols and types that catch real bugs
Hints become powerful when they describe relationships, not just single values.

A **generic** function keeps the link between what goes in and what comes out: "a list of T in, a T out". A **Protocol** describes what an object must be able to do, without requiring inheritance. `NewType` creates distinct types for values that are all integers underneath, so passing a user id where an order id is expected becomes an error. A union of small classes with a literal `kind` field, handled with `match` and `assert_never`, makes the checker prove you covered every case.
The sample below is checked by `mypy --strict` every time this page is built, and it also runs.

blocks.caption: Checked with `mypy --strict`

blocks.text: Tools in this sample

rows: Functions that work for any type and preserve it
"Anything that has these methods", no base class needed
Ids and units that must not be mixed up
A fixed set of allowed strings or numbers
Results with different shapes, exhaustively handled
Decorators that preserve the wrapped signature
Methods that return their own instance, for chaining

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a generic function?
blocks.text: A function with a type parameter, so one definition works for many types while the checker tracks which type each call uses.

blocks.title: Protocol versus abstract base class?
blocks.text: A Protocol is satisfied by any class with the right members, checked structurally. An ABC requires explicit inheritance and can also provide shared code and block instantiation.

blocks.title: What is `NewType` for?
blocks.text: Creating a distinct type for the checker over an existing one, at no run-time cost, to prevent mixing values such as user ids and order ids.

blocks.title: How do you get exhaustiveness checking in Python?
blocks.text: Use a union of types or a `Literal`, handle each case, and call `assert_never` on the remainder. The checker reports an error if a case is missing.

blocks.title: What does `mypy --strict` add?
blocks.text: It disallows untyped functions and implicit `Any`, among other checks, so the whole module is actually verified.

modules.title: Python: Stage 4 · Advanced
modules.summary: The parts that separate seniors from juniors

blocks.text: An **iterator** hands out values one at a time when asked. A **generator** is the easy way to write one: a function that uses `yield`. Each `yield` pauses the function and hands a value to the caller. The function resumes from that line when the next value is requested.
The benefit is memory. A generator never holds the whole result, so it can work through a file or a database table far bigger than RAM.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A list is a printed book: all pages exist at once. A generator is a storyteller: the next sentence exists only when you ask for it.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `yield` in a `def` is Dart's `sync*` function with `yield`, and Swift's `AsyncStream` idea without the async part. A lazy Swift `sequence` is the same concept.
A generator pauses and resumes

rows: `gen = read_orders(lines)` creates the generator. No line of the body has run.
The loop asks for a value. The body runs to the first `yield` and pauses there.
The loop asks again. The body resumes after the `yield`, loops and pauses at the next one.
When the body ends, Python raises `StopIteration` and the `for` loop ends quietly.

nodes.label: for loop pulls one batch at a time

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Exporting two million orders to CSV: a generator reads 1,000 rows from the database, yields them, and the web framework streams them to the client. Memory stays at 1,000 rows instead of two million. The same shape streams tokens from a language model later in this track.
Pitfalls

items: Looping over a generator twice. It is used up after the first pass.
Calling `len()` on a generator. It has no length. Convert with `list()` only if it is small.
Forgetting that nothing runs until something consumes it.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between `return` and `yield`?
blocks.text: `return` ends the function and gives back one value. `yield` pauses it, gives back a value and keeps local state so it can continue later.

blocks.title: What is the difference between an iterable and an iterator?
blocks.text: An iterable can produce an iterator (`__iter__`). An iterator produces the values (`__next__`) and remembers its position. A list is iterable, a generator is an iterator.

blocks.title: Why use generators?
blocks.text: Constant memory for large or endless data, and work is done only for values that are actually consumed.
The iterator protocol, `yield from` and `itertools`

A `for` loop is built on two methods. It calls `iter(x)` to get an iterator, then calls `next()` on it until `StopIteration` is raised. Any object that implements `__iter__` and `__next__` works in a loop. A generator is Python writing those two methods for you.

`yield from other` hands control to another generator until it is exhausted, which lets you split one generator into several. `itertools` is a toolbox of fast, lazy building blocks: slice, chain, group and batch a stream without loading it.
An **async generator** (`async def` with `yield`) is the same idea for data that arrives over time, consumed with `async for`. You used one for server-sent events.

blocks.code:
import itertools, sys

class Countdown:                         # the protocol written by hand
    def __init__(self, start): self.current = start
    def __iter__(self): return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.current <= 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.current -= 1
        return self.current + 1

print(list(Countdown(3)))
it = iter([10, 20])
print(next(it), next(it), next(it, "empty"))

def pages(total_pages):
    for page in range(1, total_pages + 1):
        yield [f"order-{page}-{i}" for i in range(2)]      # one API page at a time

def all_orders(total_pages):
    for page in pages(total_pages):
        yield from page                                    # flatten without a nested loop

print(list(itertools.islice(all_orders(1000), 5)))         # only 3 pages are ever fetched

squares_list = [n * n for n in range(100_000)]
squares_gen = (n * n for n in range(100_000))
print(sys.getsizeof(squares_list), "bytes vs", sys.getsizeof(squares_gen), "bytes")

orders = [("blr", 300), ("blr", 760), ("del", 90), ("mum", 410), ("mum", 50)]
for city, group in itertools.groupby(orders, key=lambda o: o[0]):   # input must be sorted by key
    print(city, sum(amount for _, amount in group))
print(list(itertools.batched(range(7), 3)), list(itertools.chain([1, 2], [3])))

blocks.text: Lazy tools worth knowing

rows: First n items of any iterator
Consecutive items with the same key
Stop at the first decisive item

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the iterator protocol?
blocks.text: An object is iterable if `__iter__` returns an iterator. An iterator has `__next__`, which returns the next value or raises `StopIteration`.

blocks.title: What does `yield from` do?
blocks.text: It delegates to another iterable or generator, yielding each of its values, and returns that generator's return value.

blocks.title: Can you reuse a generator?
blocks.text: No. Once exhausted it stays empty. Create a new one, or store the values in a list if you need several passes.

blocks.title: What is an async generator?
blocks.text: A function defined with `async def` that contains `yield`. It can await between values and is consumed with `async for`.

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that wraps it. The `@name` line above a `def` applies it. It lets you add behaviour around many functions (timing, logging, retries, permission checks, caching) without editing each one.
Web frameworks are built on this. `@app.get("/orders")` is a decorator that registers your function as the handler for a URL.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Gift wrapping. The gift is unchanged, and the wrapper adds something before you reach it and after.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Swift property wrappers and Dart annotations look similar, but a Python decorator is plain code that runs at definition time and replaces the function. Think "higher-order function with special syntax".
What `@retry(times=3)` does at definition time

rows: Python defines the original function, then calls `decorator(original)`.
`decorator` returns `wrapper`, and the name is rebound to it.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Leaving out `functools.wraps`. The wrapped function loses its name and docstring, which breaks debugging and framework introspection.
Retrying operations that are not safe to repeat, such as charging a card without an idempotency key.
Caching a function whose result depends on something other than its arguments.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a decorator?
blocks.text: A callable that receives a function and returns a replacement, usually a wrapper that runs extra code before or after calling the original. `@d` above `def f` means `f = d(f)`.

blocks.title: Why are there three nested functions in a decorator with arguments?
blocks.text: The outer one takes the settings, the middle one takes the function and the inner one is the wrapper that takes the call's arguments.

blocks.title: What does `functools.wraps` do?
blocks.text: It copies the name, docstring and other metadata from the original function onto the wrapper.
Stacking order, class-based decorators and built-in ones

When several decorators are stacked, they are **applied bottom to top** and **run top to bottom**. `@a` above `@b` above `def f` means `f = a(b(f))`. A call enters `a`'s wrapper first, then `b`'s, then the function.

A decorator does not have to be a function. Any callable works, so a class with `__call__` can be a decorator that keeps state, such as a rate limiter. Python also ships decorators you will use constantly: `@property`, `@staticmethod`, `@classmethod`, `@dataclass`, `@functools.cache` and `@functools.wraps`.
A call through two stacked decorators

rows: `refund(user, 184)` is called. The name `refund` is bound to `log`'s wrapper.
The log wrapper calls what it wrapped, which is `require_role`'s wrapper. It checks the role.
The role is present, so the original function runs.
The value returns outward through both wrappers.
log: calling refund, log: refund returned refunded 184

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: In what order do stacked decorators apply?
blocks.text: The one closest to the function is applied first. At call time the outermost wrapper runs first. `@a @b def f` equals `f = a(b(f))`.

blocks.title: How do you write a decorator that takes arguments?
blocks.text: Write a function that accepts the arguments and returns a decorator, which in turn returns the wrapper. Or use a class whose `__init__` takes the arguments and whose `__call__` takes the function.

blocks.title: Name real uses of decorators in a backend.
blocks.text: Route registration, authentication and permission checks, caching, retries, timing and metrics, transactions and input validation.

A context manager is a setup and cleanup pair tied to a `with` block. The setup runs on entering the block and the cleanup runs on leaving it, **even if an exception is raised**. Files, database transactions, locks and timers are the classic uses.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `with` is Swift's `defer` with a name and reuse, or `try / finally` in Dart packaged as an object.

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Placing an order writes three rows: the order, its items and the stock change. Wrapping the three writes in one transaction context manager means either all three are saved or none are. A crash halfway cannot leave an order with no items.
Pitfalls

items: Returning `True` from `__exit__` by accident, which silently swallows the exception.
Doing the cleanup after `yield` without `try / finally`. It is skipped when the body raises.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What guarantees does `with` give?
blocks.text: The cleanup in `__exit__` runs however the block ends: normally, by exception, or by `return`.

blocks.title: How do you write a context manager without a class?
blocks.text: Decorate a generator with `@contextlib.contextmanager`. Code before `yield` is the setup, code after it (in `finally`) is the cleanup.
Several resources at once, and async context managers
Three situations go beyond a single `with`.

When the **number of resources is not known in advance**, such as "open every file in this list", `contextlib.ExitStack` collects them and closes all of them in reverse order, even if opening the fifth one fails.

When setup or cleanup must **await**, you need an async context manager: `__aenter__` / `__aexit__`, or `@asynccontextmanager`, used with `async with`. Database connections, HTTP clients and locks in async code all work this way.
Cleanup order is always **last opened, first closed**, like a stack of plates. That matters when one resource depends on another: the transaction must end before its connection is returned.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, contextlib, io

class Resource:
    def __init__(self, name, log, fail_on_open=False):
        self.name, self.log, self.fail = name, log, fail_on_open
    def __enter__(self):
        if self.fail:
            raise OSError(f"cannot open {self.name}")
        self.log.append(f"open {self.name}")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.log.append(f"close {self.name}")
        return False

log: list[str] = []
with Resource("connection", log), Resource("transaction", log):
    log.append("work")
print(log)                                             # closed in reverse order

log = []
try:
    with contextlib.ExitStack() as stack:              # a dynamic number of resources
        for name in ("a.csv", "b.csv", "c.csv"):
            stack.enter_context(Resource(name, log, fail_on_open=(name == "c.csv")))
except OSError as err:
    print("failed:", err, "| cleaned up:", log)

@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def db_connection(pool: list[str]):
    conn = pool.pop()                                  # setup may await in real code
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        await asyncio.sleep(0)                         # cleanup may await too
        pool.append(conn)

async def main() -> None:
    pool = ["conn-1", "conn-2"]
    lock = asyncio.Lock()
    async with db_connection(pool) as conn, lock:      # async with: for awaitable setup and cleanup
        print("using", conn, "| free in pool:", len(pool))
    print("returned | free in pool:", len(pool))

asyncio.run(main())

buffer = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):               # ready-made managers in the standard library
    print("captured, not shown")
print("captured text:", buffer.getvalue().strip())

blocks.text: Opening three files when the third fails

rows: `ExitStack` is entered. Its list of cleanups is empty.
a.csv opens. Its close is registered.
c.csv fails to open and raises. The stack runs its cleanups in reverse order.
The error continues to the caller. Nothing was left open.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: In what order are multiple context managers exited?
blocks.text: In reverse order of entry: the last one entered is exited first.

blocks.title: What is `ExitStack` for?
blocks.text: Managing a number of context managers decided at run time, with guaranteed cleanup of all those already entered if a later one fails.

blocks.title: `with` versus `async with`?
blocks.text: `async with` calls `__aenter__` and `__aexit__` and awaits them, so setup and cleanup can perform async I/O. It may only be used inside `async def`.

blocks.title: What do the three arguments of `__exit__` contain?
blocks.text: The exception type, the exception instance and the traceback if the block raised, otherwise three `None` values.
There are two kinds of slow work. **I/O-bound** work spends its time waiting: for a database, a network call, a disk. **CPU-bound** work spends its time computing: resizing images, crunching numbers.

Standard Python has a lock called the **GIL** (global interpreter lock). Only one thread can run Python code at a time. Threads still help with waiting, because a waiting thread releases the lock. Threads do not help with computing. For that you use several **processes**, each with its own interpreter and its own GIL.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: One kitchen, one knife. Many cooks can wait for ovens at the same time, but only the cook holding the knife can chop. More cooks do not make chopping faster. A second kitchen (a second process) does.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Swift's GCD and Dart isolates are the comparison. Python threads are like GCD threads that can never actually run Swift code in parallel. Python processes are like Dart isolates: no shared memory, messages are copied between them.

blocks.code:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

def fetch_price(sku: str) -> str:        # I/O-bound: mostly waiting
    time.sleep(0.2)
    return f"{sku}:ok"

def crunch(n: int) -> int:               # CPU-bound: mostly computing
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    skus = [f"sku{i}" for i in range(10)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(fetch_price, skus))
    print(f"10 waits with threads: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s (not 2.0s)")

    start = time.perf_counter()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        totals = list(pool.map(crunch, [300_000] * 4))
    print(f"4 crunches with processes: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

blocks.text: Two threads sharing the GIL

rows: Thread A holds the GIL and runs Python code. Thread B is ready but must wait.
Thread A starts a network call. It releases the GIL while it waits.
Thread B takes the GIL and runs. The waits overlap, which is where the speed-up comes from.
Thread A's response arrives. It queues for the GIL again.

nodes.label: Processes, or a library that releases the GIL (NumPy)

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A product page needs price, stock and reviews from three internal services at 100 ms each. Called one after another the page takes 300 ms. Called together with threads or async it takes about 100 ms. Generating 5,000 invoice PDFs is CPU work: it goes to worker processes, not threads.
Pitfalls

items: Expecting threads to speed up pure Python number crunching.
Sharing a mutable object between threads without a lock. `x += 1` is not atomic.
Forgetting the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard with process pools on macOS and Windows.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the GIL?
blocks.text: A lock in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. It keeps the interpreter's memory management simple and safe, at the cost of no parallel Python code within one process.

blocks.title: If there is a GIL, why use threads at all?
blocks.text: A thread releases the GIL while it waits on I/O. So many network or disk waits can overlap, which is the common case in a backend.

blocks.title: Threading versus multiprocessing versus asyncio?
blocks.text: Threads: I/O-bound work with blocking libraries. Multiprocessing: CPU-bound work, real parallelism, higher memory and copying cost. Asyncio: very many I/O-bound tasks in one thread with async libraries.

blocks.title: Is the GIL going away?
blocks.text: Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build without the GIL, and work continues on it. The default build that most servers run still has the GIL, so the guidance above still applies.
Why the GIL exists, and a race you can run

The GIL exists because of reference counting. Every assignment changes an object's reference count. If two threads changed the same count at the same instant without protection, counts would be wrong and memory would be corrupted or leaked. One big lock made the interpreter simple and fast for single-threaded code, and made C extensions easy to write.

A running thread gives up the GIL in two situations: when it starts blocking I/O, and after a time slice of about 5 milliseconds (the **switch interval**) so another thread gets a turn. Because that switch can land between any two bytecode instructions, the GIL does **not** make your own code thread-safe. `counter += 1` is three steps: read, add, store. A switch between them loses an update.
Heavy C libraries such as NumPy, compression and hashing release the GIL while they work, so threads can run those in true parallel.

blocks.code:
import sys, threading, time

counter = 0
safe_counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def unsafe_add(times):
    global counter
    for _ in range(times):
        current = counter           # read
        time.sleep(0)               # invite a thread switch at the worst moment
        counter = current + 1       # store: may overwrite another thread's update

def safe_add(times):
    global safe_counter
    for _ in range(times):
        with lock:                  # only one thread at a time in this block
            current = safe_counter
            time.sleep(0)
            safe_counter = current + 1

for target in (unsafe_add, safe_add):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=target, args=(2000,)) for _ in range(4)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

print("expected 8000 | without lock:", counter, "| with lock:", safe_counter)
print("switch interval:", sys.getswitchinterval(), "seconds")
print("free-threaded build:", not getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)())

blocks.text: A lost update between two threads

rows: Both threads want to add 1 to a counter that holds 5. Thread A reads it.
The interpreter switches threads before A stores its result. B reads the same value.
A resumes and stores 5 + 1. B's update is overwritten. Two increments, one result.

blocks.text: What releases the GIL
Check yourself

blocks.title: Why does CPython have a GIL?
blocks.text: To protect reference counts and interpreter state without fine-grained locks. It keeps single-threaded code fast and C extensions simple.

blocks.title: Does the GIL make my code thread-safe?
blocks.text: No. It protects the interpreter, not your data. A thread switch can occur between the steps of a compound operation, so shared state still needs locks.

blocks.title: What is a race condition?
blocks.text: A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads or tasks, typically a read-modify-write on shared data without synchronisation.

blocks.title: What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?
blocks.text: Two threads each hold a lock the other needs, so both wait forever. Avoid it by always acquiring locks in the same order, holding them briefly and using timeouts.

blocks.title: What is free-threaded Python?
blocks.text: An optional build, available from Python 3.13, that removes the GIL so threads can run Python code in parallel. It is not yet the default, and libraries must support it.

lessons.title: async, await and the event loop

blocks.text: `asyncio` runs many tasks in **one thread**. A task runs until it reaches an `await` on something slow. At that point it steps aside and the **event loop** runs another task. When the slow thing finishes, the loop resumes the first task from the line where it stopped.

Nothing runs in parallel. Tasks take turns, and the turns change only at `await`. That makes it cheap to hold thousands of open connections, which is exactly what a busy API or a streaming AI endpoint needs.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: One waiter, many tables. The waiter takes an order, hands it to the kitchen and serves another table instead of standing at the pass. A blocking call is the waiter standing still at the pass, and every table waits.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The syntax matches Swift and Dart. A coroutine is a `Future` / async function result. `asyncio.gather` is `Future.wait` in Dart and `async let` or a task group in Swift. The event loop is the Dart event loop. The big difference from Swift: there is no thread pool behind it, so one blocking call freezes everything.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, time

async def fetch(name: str, seconds: float) -> str:
    print(f"start {name}")
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)          # stands in for a network call
    print(f"done  {name}")
    return name

async def product_page() -> None:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    price, stock, reviews = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("price", 0.3), fetch("stock", 0.2), fetch("reviews", 0.3)
    )
    print(f"all three in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

    try:                                   # never wait forever on another service
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.1):
            await fetch("slow-recommendations", 1.0)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("recommendations skipped")

    limit = asyncio.Semaphore(2)           # at most two at a time
    async def limited(i: int) -> str:
        async with limit:
            return await fetch(f"job{i}", 0.05)
    await asyncio.gather(*(limited(i) for i in range(4)))

asyncio.run(product_page())

blocks.text: The event loop with three tasks

rows: `gather` schedules three tasks. The loop picks the first.
`price` reaches `await sleep` and steps aside. The loop starts `stock`, then `reviews`.
All three are waiting. The loop sleeps until a timer fires. Total waiting overlaps.
After 0.2 s the `stock` timer fires. The loop resumes it from its `await` line.
After 0.3 s the other two are ready. They resume one after the other. `gather` returns all three results.

diagram.title: One request in an async server

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Calling a blocking function inside `async def`: `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, a sync database driver. It freezes every request on that worker. Use the async version or `await asyncio.to_thread(func)`.
Forgetting `await`. You get a coroutine object and a "never awaited" warning, and the work does not happen.
Awaiting calls one by one when they could run together with `gather`.
Launching 10,000 tasks at once against one service. Limit with a semaphore.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does asyncio differ from threads?
blocks.text: Asyncio runs tasks in one thread and switches only at `await`, so switches are explicit and cheap. Threads are switched by the operating system at any moment and cost more memory each.

blocks.title: What happens if you call blocking code in a coroutine?
blocks.text: The event loop cannot switch away, so every other task waits. Run the blocking call in a thread with `asyncio.to_thread` or use an async library.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a coroutine and a task?
blocks.text: Calling an `async def` returns a coroutine, which does nothing until awaited. A task wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the loop so it runs in the background.

blocks.title: When is async the wrong choice?
blocks.text: For CPU-heavy work, and when the libraries you need have no async support. Async gives no speed-up to computation.
Tasks, cancellation, structured concurrency and blocking code

Calling an `async def` function does not run it. It returns a **coroutine object**. Something has to drive it: `await` runs it now and waits, while `asyncio.create_task` schedules it on the loop to run in the background and returns a **task** you can await or cancel later.

A `TaskGroup` starts several tasks and guarantees that when the block ends, every task has finished or been cancelled. If one fails, the others are cancelled and the error is raised. This is **structured concurrency**: no task outlives the block that started it.

**Cancellation** arrives as a `CancelledError` raised at the task's current `await`. Clean up in `finally` and let it propagate. For a blocking library with no async version, `asyncio.to_thread` runs it in a worker thread so the loop stays free.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, time

async def fetch(name, seconds, fail=False):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
        if fail:
            raise ConnectionError(f"{name} is down")
        return name
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"  {name} cancelled, cleaning up")
        raise                                  # always re-raise cancellation

def legacy_blocking_lookup(pincode):           # a sync library call
    time.sleep(0.2)
    return f"zone-{pincode[:3]}"

async def main():
    coro = fetch("never-awaited", 0)
    print(type(coro).__name__)                 # coroutine: nothing has run
    coro.close()

    task = asyncio.create_task(fetch("background", 0.05))      # starts running now
    print("task done yet?", task.done())
    print(await task)

    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:               # all succeed or all are cancelled
            group.create_task(fetch("price", 0.3))
            group.create_task(fetch("stock", 0.1, fail=True))
    except* ConnectionError as errors:
        print("group failed:", [str(e) for e in errors.exceptions])

    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a", 0.05), fetch("b", 0.05, fail=True), return_exceptions=True)
    print([r if isinstance(r, str) else type(r).__name__ for r in results])

    start = time.perf_counter()
    zone, _ = await asyncio.gather(asyncio.to_thread(legacy_blocking_lookup, "560103"), asyncio.sleep(0.2))
    print(zone, f"in {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s (loop was never blocked)")

    slow = asyncio.create_task(fetch("slow", 5))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    slow.cancel()
    try:
        await slow
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("caller saw the cancellation")

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: What the event loop really does

rows: The loop keeps a queue of callbacks that are ready, and asks the operating system which sockets and timers have become ready.
Task A runs until it awaits a database reply. The loop registers its socket with the OS and moves on.
Task B runs until `await asyncio.sleep(0.1)`. A timer is recorded. The ready queue is now empty.
With nothing ready, the loop sleeps inside one OS call until a socket has data or the nearest timer is due. No CPU is used.
The database replies. The OS wakes the loop, and task A goes back on the ready queue to continue after its `await`.

blocks.text: Ways to run several things

rows: Steps that depend on each other
Raises the first error, others keep running
Cancels the rest, raises an exception group

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Coroutine versus task versus future?
blocks.text: A coroutine is the object returned by calling an `async def` function and does nothing until driven. A task wraps a coroutine and runs it on the event loop. A future is a low-level placeholder for a result, and a task is a kind of future.

blocks.title: How does cancellation work in asyncio?
blocks.text: `task.cancel()` causes `CancelledError` to be raised inside the task at its current await point. The task should clean up in `finally` and re-raise.

blocks.title: What is structured concurrency?
blocks.text: Tasks are started inside a block that does not exit until all of them have finished, so no task leaks and errors are not lost. `asyncio.TaskGroup` provides it.

blocks.title: How do you call blocking code from async code?
blocks.text: `await asyncio.to_thread(func, args)` runs it in a thread pool so the event loop is not blocked. Prefer a native async library when one exists.

blocks.title: How does the event loop know a socket is ready?
blocks.text: It registers sockets with the operating system's readiness API (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) through the `selectors` module and waits in one system call.
