modules.summary: From a function to a deployed API

blocks.text: HTTP is the conversation between a client and a server. The client sends a **request**: a method (`GET`, `POST`, ...), a path, headers and sometimes a body. The server sends back a **response**: a status code, headers and a body, usually JSON.

You have been the client for years. As a backend developer you sit on the other side, and your server is also a client of other servers: payment gateways, inventory, AI models. `httpx` is the standard library for those outgoing calls.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `httpx.Client` is your `URLSession` / Dio instance: create one, reuse it, set a base URL, default headers and a timeout. `raise_for_status()` is the check you write by hand on `HTTPURLResponse.statusCode`.
Status codes you will return every day

rows: Server bug / bad gateway / unavailable / timeout

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Checkout calls the payment gateway. The gateway is slow today and takes 30 seconds. Without a timeout, every worker on your server ends up stuck waiting, and the whole API goes down because of someone else's outage. With `timeout=2.0`, a retry with backoff for safe requests, and a clear error to the user, your API stays up.
Pitfalls

items: No timeout on outgoing calls. This is the most common cause of cascading outages.
Retrying a `POST` that is not idempotent, which can charge a customer twice. Send an idempotency key.
Creating a new client per request. Reuse one client so connections are pooled.
Using blocking `requests` or `httpx.Client` inside `async def`. Use `httpx.AsyncClient` there.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
blocks.text: PUT replaces the whole resource with the body you send. PATCH changes only the fields you send.

blocks.title: What does idempotent mean?
blocks.text: Doing the request twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent. POST usually is not, which is why retries need an idempotency key.

blocks.title: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
blocks.text: 401 means the server does not know who you are. 403 means it knows and you are not allowed.

blocks.title: Why reuse an HTTP client?
blocks.text: It keeps a pool of open connections, so later requests skip the TCP and TLS handshakes.

FastAPI turns a Python function into an HTTP endpoint. A decorator gives the method and path. The function's parameters describe what the endpoint needs: values in the path, the query string or the JSON body. FastAPI reads the type hints, validates the incoming data and sends a 422 error by itself when it is wrong.
It also writes interactive documentation for you at `/docs`.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: FastAPI is the receptionist. It checks the visitor's form is filled in correctly, routes them to the right desk (your function) and hands back the reply in the right envelope.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: You have called endpoints like `POST /orders` from Dio. This is the other side of that call. The Pydantic model for the body is the same thing as your `Codable` request struct, used for decoding instead of encoding.

blocks.code:
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
fastapi dev main.py            # reloads on save, docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs
blocks.caption: Run it for real

blocks.text: Life of `POST /orders`

rows: The server (uvicorn) receives raw bytes and parses the HTTP request.
FastAPI matches method and path to `create_order`.
The body is validated against `OrderIn`. If `qty` is 0 the request stops here with a 422.
Your function runs with a typed, trusted object.
The return value is filtered through `OrderOut` and turned into JSON.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Keeping state in a module-level dict in production. Each worker process has its own copy and it is lost on restart. Use a database.
Returning database objects directly and leaking internal fields. Always set a `response_model`.
Writing `async def` handlers that call blocking libraries. Use plain `def` (FastAPI runs it in a thread pool) or use async libraries.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does FastAPI know where a parameter comes from?
blocks.text: A name that appears in the path is a path parameter. A simple type not in the path is a query parameter. A Pydantic model is the JSON body.

blocks.title: What is ASGI?
blocks.text: The standard interface between async Python web apps and servers. Uvicorn is an ASGI server and FastAPI is an ASGI application. WSGI is the older, synchronous equivalent used by Flask and Django.

blocks.title: When do you use `def` and when `async def` for an endpoint?
blocks.text: `async def` when everything inside is awaited async I/O. Plain `def` when you call blocking code, because FastAPI then runs it in a worker thread.

blocks.title: FastAPI versus Flask versus Django?
blocks.text: FastAPI: async, typed, validation and docs built in, the usual pick for APIs and AI services. Flask: minimal and synchronous, you add everything. Django: a full framework with ORM, admin and auth, best for large database-driven products.
Dependencies with cleanup, middleware, lifespan and background tasks
Four features carry most real FastAPI apps.
A **dependency with `yield`** gives a resource to the handler and cleans it up afterwards, like a context manager. This is how each request gets its own database session that is always closed.
**Middleware** wraps every request: it runs code before the handler and after it. Use it for request ids, timing and logging.
**Lifespan** runs once when the server starts and once when it stops. Open shared resources there: the database pool, an HTTP client, a model client.
A **background task** runs after the response has been sent. It is fine for small follow-up work. Anything that must not be lost belongs in a real queue.

blocks.code:
import time, uuid
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, Depends, FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

events: list[str] = []

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.pool = "db-pool"                 # open pools and clients once
    events.append("startup")
    yield
    events.append("shutdown")                  # close them on the way out

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

@app.middleware("http")
async def request_context(request: Request, call_next):
    request.state.request_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    events.append("middleware before")
    response = await call_next(request)        # everything below runs inside this call
    events.append("middleware after")
    response.headers["x-request-id"] = request.state.request_id
    response.headers["x-duration-ms"] = f"{(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f}"
    return response

def get_session(request: Request):
    events.append("session open")
    try:
        yield {"pool": request.app.state.pool}  # the handler runs while we are paused here
    finally:
        events.append("session closed")         # runs even if the handler raised

def current_user(request: Request) -> dict:
    return {"id": int(request.headers.get("x-user-id", 0))}

def send_receipt(order_id: int) -> None:
    events.append(f"receipt sent for {order_id}")

@app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
def create_order(tasks: BackgroundTasks, session: dict = Depends(get_session), user: dict = Depends(current_user)):
    events.append(f"handler ran for user {user['id']} using {session['pool']}")
    tasks.add_task(send_receipt, 184)           # runs after the response is sent
    return {"id": 184}

with TestClient(app) as client:                 # the with block triggers lifespan
    response = client.post("/orders", headers={"x-user-id": "7"})
    print(response.status_code, response.json(), "request id length:", len(response.headers["x-request-id"]))
print(events)

blocks.text: Order of execution for one request

rows: Server start: lifespan code before `yield` runs once.
A request arrives. Middleware code before `call_next` runs.
Dependencies are resolved. `get_session` runs up to its `yield`.
The handler runs with its dependencies and returns.
Middleware code after `call_next` adds headers, and the response goes out.
The background task runs. The client already has its response.

The dependency resumes after its `yield` and cleans up. This is the order the sample prints on the installed FastAPI version; it has changed between versions, so never use the request's session inside a background task.

blocks.text: `def` or `async def`

rows: FastAPI runs it in a thread pool (about 40 threads)
Neither: send to a worker or queue
It would block a thread or the loop

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a dependency with `yield` used for?
blocks.text: Setup and teardown around a request, typically a database session: code before `yield` provides the resource and code after it releases it, even on errors.

blocks.title: What is the difference between middleware and a dependency?
blocks.text: Middleware wraps every request and works with the raw request and response. A dependency is declared per route, can return a value to the handler and can depend on other dependencies.

blocks.title: When are background tasks not enough?
blocks.text: When the work must survive a crash or restart, needs retries or is heavy. They run in the same process after the response, so use a queue and worker for those.

blocks.title: What happens if a blocking call is made in an `async def` endpoint?
blocks.text: It blocks the event loop, so every other request on that worker waits. Use a plain `def` endpoint or `asyncio.to_thread`.

Never trust data from outside: a phone, another service, a file or a language model. Pydantic models describe the shape you expect. Creating a model from raw data **validates and converts** it. You either get a correct typed object or a precise list of what was wrong.
This one library sits at every boundary of a Python backend: request bodies, responses, settings and the structured output of AI models.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: It is `Codable` / `json_serializable` with rules attached: lengths, ranges, patterns and custom checks, plus automatic conversion such as `"7"` to `7` and an ISO string to `datetime`.

nodes.label: Business code can assume it is correct

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A phone on an old app version sends `qty` as the string "2" and leaves out a new field. Pydantic converts the string and applies the default for the missing field, so old and new app versions both work against one server. That is the backward compatibility problem you know from the client side, solved at the server.
Pitfalls

items: Validating by hand with `if` chains scattered across the handler.
Using one model for the request, the database row and the response. Keep them separate so internal fields never leak.
Forgetting that validation costs CPU. Do it once at the boundary, not again in every function.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What happens when validation fails in FastAPI?
blocks.text: Pydantic raises `ValidationError`, and FastAPI converts it into a 422 response listing each field and the reason.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `model_dump()` and `model_dump_json()`?
blocks.text: The first returns a Python dict. The second returns a JSON string.

blocks.title: Why keep request and response models separate?
blocks.text: They change for different reasons. The request model protects you from bad input, and the response model stops internal fields such as password hashes from leaving the server.
Cross-field rules, unions by a tag, strict mode and settings
Real request bodies need more than per-field checks.

A **model validator** checks several fields together, for example "wallet amount cannot exceed the order total". A **discriminated union** picks the right model from a tag field such as `method`, the same idea as an enum with associated values. A **computed field** is derived from others and included in the output.

`extra="forbid"` rejects unknown fields, which blocks clients from sneaking in something like `isAdmin`. An **alias generator** lets your Python code use `snake_case` while the JSON uses `camelCase`. **Strict mode** turns off the friendly conversions, so the string `"709"` is no longer accepted for an integer.
`pydantic-settings` applies the same validation to environment variables, which gives you typed, validated configuration at startup.

rows: Unknown fields are an error instead of being ignored
Instances cannot be changed and are hashable

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Field validator versus model validator?
blocks.text: A field validator checks or transforms one field. A model validator runs on the whole model and is used for rules that involve several fields.

blocks.title: What is a discriminated union?
blocks.text: A union of models that share a literal tag field. Pydantic reads the tag and validates against exactly that model, which gives clear errors and good performance.

blocks.title: Why set `extra="forbid"` on request models?
blocks.text: To reject unexpected fields. It catches client mistakes early and prevents mass-assignment style attacks.

blocks.title: What is strict mode?
blocks.text: Validation without type coercion. Values must already have the declared type.

blocks.title: How do you manage configuration with Pydantic?
blocks.text: Declare a `BaseSettings` class from `pydantic-settings`. It reads environment variables, converts and validates them, and fails at startup if something is missing.

A relational database (PostgreSQL in most Python backends) stores rows in tables and links tables with keys. **SQL** is the language for asking it questions. An **ORM** such as SQLAlchemy lets you work with Python classes and writes the SQL for you.
Learn enough SQL to read what the ORM produces. When a page is slow, the cause is almost always a query.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: This is Core Data or `sqflite` / Drift, on a server shared by every user at once. That sharing is why **transactions** (all or nothing), **indexes** (fast lookup) and **connection pools** (reuse of connections) matter far more than on a phone.

blocks.caption: The SQL underneath

blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, func, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column, relationship

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    city: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(default="placed")
    items: Mapped[list["OrderItem"]] = relationship(back_populates="order", cascade="all, delete-orphan")

class OrderItem(Base):
    __tablename__ = "order_items"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    order_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("orders.id"))
    sku: Mapped[str]
    price: Mapped[int]
    order: Mapped[Order] = relationship(back_populates="items")

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")          # in memory; production: postgresql+psycopg://...
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)

with Session(engine) as session, session.begin():      # one transaction: all or nothing
    session.add(Order(city="blr", items=[OrderItem(sku="milk", price=6200), OrderItem(sku="bread", price=4500)]))
    session.add(Order(city="del", items=[OrderItem(sku="ghee", price=54000)]))

with Session(engine) as session:
    blr = session.scalars(select(Order).where(Order.city == "blr")).all()
    print([(o.id, o.status, len(o.items)) for o in blr])
    revenue = session.execute(
        select(Order.city, func.sum(OrderItem.price)).join(OrderItem).group_by(Order.city)
    ).all()
    print([tuple(row) for row in revenue])

rows: BEGIN. Nothing is visible to other users yet.
UPDATE stock fails: not enough milk. An exception is raised.
order 186, item milk, item bread, !stock update failed
ROLLBACK. Every pending change is thrown away. No half-order exists.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: The **N+1 query**: load 50 orders, then touch `order.items` in a loop and fire 50 more queries. Load them together with `selectinload` or a join.
Building SQL with string formatting. Always pass parameters, which the ORM does for you.
No index on a column used in `WHERE` or `JOIN`. Fine with 1,000 rows, a 5 second query with 10 million.
Changing tables by hand in production. Use a migration tool (Alembic) so every change is a reviewed, versioned file.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is an index and what does it cost?
blocks.text: A sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. It makes reads faster and writes slightly slower, and it uses disk space.

blocks.title: What is the N+1 problem?
blocks.text: One query fetches N parent rows, then one more query runs per parent to fetch its children. Fix it by eager loading the children in one or two queries.

blocks.title: What does ACID mean?
blocks.text: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules always hold), Isolated (concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work), Durable (committed data survives a crash).

blocks.title: ORM versus raw SQL?
blocks.text: The ORM is faster to write and safer for ordinary create, read, update and delete. Raw SQL is better for complex reports and tuned queries. Most teams use both.

blocks.title: What is a connection pool?
blocks.text: A set of open database connections that requests borrow and return, because opening a connection per request is slow and the database allows only a limited number.
N+1 measured, isolation levels and how an index works

An index is usually a **B-tree**: a sorted, shallow tree. Finding one row among ten million takes three or four page reads instead of reading the whole table. The cost is that every insert and update must also update the tree, and a query can only use an index whose leading columns appear in its filter.

**Isolation level** decides what a transaction may see of other transactions running at the same moment. The PostgreSQL default, *read committed*, never shows uncommitted data, but two reads inside one transaction can return different results. For "check, then update" logic that is not enough: lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or put the check into the `UPDATE` itself.
The N+1 problem is easy to describe and easy to miss. Count the queries, as below.

blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, event, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column, relationship, selectinload

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    city: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(index=True)
    items: Mapped[list["Item"]] = relationship()

class Item(Base):
    __tablename__ = "items"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    order_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("orders.id"), index=True)
    sku: Mapped[str]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as session, session.begin():
    session.add_all(Order(city="blr", items=[Item(sku="milk"), Item(sku="bread")]) for _ in range(50))

queries = []
@event.listens_for(engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def count(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    queries.append(statement.split()[0])

with Session(engine) as session:
    orders = session.scalars(select(Order)).all()
    total = sum(len(o.items) for o in orders)            # each access fires one more SELECT
    print(f"lazy loading:  {len(queries)} queries for {len(orders)} orders, {total} items")

queries.clear()
with Session(engine) as session:
    orders = session.scalars(select(Order).options(selectinload(Order.items))).all()
    total = sum(len(o.items) for o in orders)
    print(f"selectinload:  {len(queries)} queries for {len(orders)} orders, {total} items")

with engine.connect() as conn:
    plan = conn.exec_driver_sql("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE city = 'blr'").all()
    print("plan:", plan[0][-1])                          # shows the index being used

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does a B-tree index speed up a query?
blocks.text: It keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree, so the database descends a few levels to the matching entries instead of scanning every row. It also serves range queries and ordering on the indexed columns.

blocks.title: When will the database not use your index?
blocks.text: When the filter does not use the index's leading column, when a function is applied to the column, when the types do not match, or when the planner estimates that most rows match and a scan is cheaper.

blocks.title: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL and what does it allow?
blocks.text: Read committed. A transaction never sees uncommitted data, but repeated reads may return different committed values.

blocks.title: How do you prevent two requests from both taking the last item?
blocks.text: Use one atomic conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE available >= n` and check the affected row count, or lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction.

blocks.title: How do you detect N+1 queries?
blocks.text: Count or log the SQL executed per request in tests or development. A count that grows with the number of rows returned signals N+1.

blocks.title: What is a composite index and does column order matter?
blocks.text: An index on several columns. Order matters: an index on `(user_id, created_at)` serves filters on `user_id` alone or on both, but not on `created_at` alone.

**Authentication** answers "who are you". **Authorisation** answers "are you allowed to do this". A login checks a password or an OTP, then gives the client a token. The client sends the token with every request and the server verifies it.
A **JWT** is a token that carries its own data (user id, expiry) and a signature. The server can verify it with a secret key and no database lookup.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: You already store and send this token from the app (Keychain, an `Authorization: Bearer` header in an interceptor) and handle the 401 by refreshing. Here you write the part that issues the token and rejects a bad one.

nodes.label: Issues access token (15 min) + refresh token (30 days)
Phone calls GET /orders with Bearer token
Does this order belong to this user?

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: `GET /orders/184` must check that order 184 belongs to the user in the token. Skipping that check lets any logged-in user read anyone's order by changing the number in the URL. This bug (broken object level authorisation) is the most common serious API vulnerability, and no framework prevents it for you.
Pitfalls

items: Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash like SHA-256. Use a slow, salted algorithm: scrypt, bcrypt or argon2.
Putting secrets in code or in git. Load them from environment variables or a secret manager.
Putting sensitive data inside a JWT. The payload is only encoded, anyone can read it.
Long-lived access tokens with no way to revoke them.
Checking that the user is logged in but not that the resource is theirs.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is inside a JWT?
blocks.text: Three base64 parts: a header (algorithm), a payload (claims such as `sub` and `exp`) and a signature over the first two. The signature proves it was not changed. The payload is readable by anyone.

blocks.title: Why hash passwords with a slow algorithm?
blocks.text: If the database leaks, an attacker must guess passwords. A slow hash with a per-user salt makes each guess expensive and stops precomputed tables.

blocks.title: Access token versus refresh token?
blocks.text: The access token is short-lived and sent on every request. The refresh token is long-lived, sent only to the token endpoint to get a new access token, and can be revoked on the server.

blocks.title: What is CORS?
blocks.text: A browser rule: a web page from one origin may call your API only if the API's response headers allow that origin. It protects browser users and does not apply to native mobile apps.

blocks.title: How do you prevent SQL injection?
blocks.text: Never build SQL by joining strings with user input. Use parameterised queries or an ORM, which send the values separately from the SQL text.
OAuth, refresh rotation, roles and rate limits

**OAuth 2.0** lets a user allow your app to act for them at another provider without sharing their password. "Sign in with Google" adds **OpenID Connect** on top, which returns an identity token describing the user. Mobile apps use the *authorization code flow with PKCE*.

**Refresh token rotation** makes stolen refresh tokens detectable. Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is ever presented again, someone has a copy, so the server revokes the whole chain and forces a new login.

Once you know who the user is, **authorisation** decides what they may do. Role-based access control (RBAC) attaches permissions to roles. Ownership checks ("is this order yours") are separate and always needed.

Opens the provider's login page with the hash
Provider redirects back with a one-time code
App sends code + verifier to the token endpoint
Access token + ID token + refresh token

blocks.text: Refresh rotation catching a thief

rows: The user logs in and receives refresh token R1.
An attacker copies R1 from a compromised device.
The user's app refreshes. R1 is spent and R2 is issued.
The attacker presents R1. The server sees a spent token being reused.
The server revokes the whole family, including R2. Both must log in again, and only the real user can.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: OAuth 2.0 versus OpenID Connect?
blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 is for authorisation: granting an app limited access to resources. OpenID Connect is a layer on top for authentication that adds an ID token describing who the user is.

blocks.title: What is PKCE and why do mobile apps need it?
blocks.text: A proof step where the app sends a hash of a secret at the start and the secret itself when exchanging the code. It stops an attacker who intercepts the redirect code from using it, since a mobile app cannot keep a client secret.

blocks.title: What is refresh token rotation?
blocks.text: Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the previous one. Reuse of an old token signals theft, and the server revokes the session.

blocks.title: Authentication versus authorisation?
blocks.text: Authentication establishes who the caller is. Authorisation decides whether that caller may perform this action on this resource.

blocks.title: How does a token bucket rate limiter work?
blocks.text: A bucket holds up to N tokens and refills at a steady rate. Each request takes one token and is rejected when the bucket is empty, which allows short bursts but limits the average rate.

A real service needs three habits. **Configuration** comes from environment variables, so the same code runs on your laptop, in staging and in production. **Dependencies** such as the database session or settings are handed to a function instead of created inside it, so tests can swap them. **Errors** are raised as specific exceptions and converted to HTTP responses in one place.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `Depends(...)` is dependency injection: the same idea as passing a repository into a view model or providing a bloc. An exception handler is a global error interceptor. Environment variables are your build configurations and `.xcconfig` values, decided at run time instead of build time.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Business rules inside route functions. They become impossible to reuse from a background job or test without HTTP.
`print` for logging. Use `logging` with levels and include ids (request id, order id) so one request can be traced.
Logging secrets or personal data such as tokens, phone numbers and addresses.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is dependency injection and why use it?
blocks.text: A function receives the things it needs as parameters instead of creating them. Tests can then pass fakes, and real wiring lives in one place.

blocks.title: Why should a service be stateless?
blocks.text: So any instance can serve any request. That allows running many copies behind a load balancer, restarting them and scaling up or down freely. State goes in a database or cache.

blocks.title: What belongs in a log line?
blocks.text: A level, a short event name, and identifying fields such as request id, user id and order id. No secrets and no personal data.

`pytest` finds files named `test_*.py`, runs every function named `test_*` and reports which `assert` failed and why. A **fixture** is a function that prepares something a test needs, such as a client or a clean database. **Parametrize** runs one test with many inputs.
Test the business rules heavily with plain function tests, and test each endpoint a little through the HTTP layer.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A fixture is `setUp` you can share and compose. `TestClient` is a widget test for an API: it calls the app in memory with no network. Overriding a dependency is injecting a mock repository.

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Boundary values catch real bugs. The rule says "free above 500". Is exactly 500 free? The parametrised test with 499 and 500 forces someone to decide, and it fails loudly if a later change flips the answer.
Pitfalls

items: Tests that depend on each other or on order. Each test should set up what it needs.
Calling real payment gateways or AI models in unit tests. Replace them with fakes and test the real thing separately.
Chasing 100% coverage instead of testing the rules that cost money when wrong.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a fixture?
blocks.text: A function that builds something a test needs. pytest passes its result to any test that names it as a parameter and can clean up afterwards.

blocks.title: Mock versus fake?
blocks.text: A mock records how it was called so you can assert on the calls. A fake is a simple working replacement, such as an in-memory repository. Fakes usually make sturdier tests.

blocks.title: What should you not unit test?
blocks.text: Third-party library internals and trivial getters. Test your own decisions and the boundaries between components.
Mocks, fakes and controlling time
A unit test must not call a payment gateway, send an SMS or depend on today's date. You replace those collaborators with **test doubles**.

A **fake** is a small working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A **mock** records how it was called so the test can assert on the calls, and can be told what to return or raise. `unittest.mock` in the standard library provides both `Mock` and `AsyncMock`, and `patch` temporarily swaps an attribute.

The cleanest way to make code testable is to **pass dependencies in** as arguments. Time is the classic case: a function that calls `datetime.now()` inside is hard to test, and one that accepts a clock is trivial.
This sample uses only the standard library and plain `assert`, so it runs anywhere. In a project you would put the same assertions in test functions.

blocks.code:
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, Mock, patch

@dataclass
class Order:
    id: int
    total: int
    placed_at: datetime

def can_cancel(order: Order, now: datetime) -> bool:          # the clock is an argument
    return now - order.placed_at <= timedelta(minutes=5)

placed = datetime(2026, 11, 11, 9, 0)
assert can_cancel(Order(1, 500, placed), now=placed + timedelta(minutes=4))
assert not can_cancel(Order(1, 500, placed), now=placed + timedelta(minutes=6))

@dataclass
class FakeOrders:                                              # a fake: real behaviour, in memory
    rows: dict[int, Order] = field(default_factory=dict)
    def get(self, order_id: int) -> Order | None:
        return self.rows.get(order_id)

def refund(order_id: int, orders, gateway, notifier) -> str:
    order = orders.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        return "not_found"
    gateway.refund(order_id=order.id, amount=order.total)
    notifier.send(f"Refund of {order.total} started")
    return "refunded"

orders = FakeOrders({184: Order(184, 70900, placed)})
gateway, notifier = Mock(), Mock()                            # mocks: record every call
assert refund(184, orders, gateway, notifier) == "refunded"
gateway.refund.assert_called_once_with(order_id=184, amount=70900)
notifier.send.assert_called_once()
assert refund(999, orders, gateway, notifier) == "not_found"
assert gateway.refund.call_count == 1                         # no second refund

gateway.refund.side_effect = TimeoutError("gateway timeout")  # make the collaborator fail
try:
    refund(184, orders, gateway, notifier)
except TimeoutError:
    assert notifier.send.call_count == 1                      # no "refund started" message was sent

async def eta_message(client) -> str:
    data = await client.get_eta(order_id=184)
    return f"Arriving in {data['minutes']} min"

client = AsyncMock()
client.get_eta.return_value = {"minutes": 12}
assert asyncio.run(eta_message(client)) == "Arriving in 12 min"
client.get_eta.assert_awaited_once_with(order_id=184)

import random
with patch.object(random, "random", return_value=0.5):        # patch: swap, then restore automatically
    assert random.random() == 0.5
print("all assertions passed")

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Mock versus fake versus stub?
blocks.text: A stub returns canned answers. A mock additionally records calls so you can assert on them. A fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory database.

blocks.title: How do you test code that depends on the current time?
blocks.text: Pass the time or a clock function into the code and supply a fixed value in the test, instead of calling `datetime.now()` inside.

blocks.title: What does `side_effect` do on a mock?
blocks.text: It makes the mock raise an exception, or return successive values from an iterable, or call a function when invoked.

blocks.title: Why is over-mocking a problem?
blocks.text: Tests end up asserting how the code is written instead of what it does, so they break on harmless refactoring and pass even when the real integration is wrong.

blocks.title: What is `AsyncMock`?
blocks.text: A mock whose calls return awaitables, for replacing `async` functions, with assertions such as `assert_awaited_once_with`.

Two tools make an API fast. A **cache** (usually Redis) keeps the answer to an expensive question for a short time so the next request skips the work. A **job queue** moves slow work out of the request: the API puts a message on a queue and answers at once, and a separate **worker** process does the work later.
Rule of thumb: anything over about half a second that the user does not need to wait for should be a background job.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The cache is the answer you wrote on a sticky note so you do not look it up again. The queue is the ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen: the waiter clips a ticket and walks away, and cooks take tickets when free.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The cache is `NSCache` or an in-memory map with expiry, but shared by every server instance. The queue is a persistent `OperationQueue` that survives restarts and is consumed by other machines.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, time

class TTLCache:
    def __init__(self, seconds: float):
        self.seconds, self.store = seconds, {}
    def get(self, key):
        hit = self.store.get(key)
        if hit and hit[1] > time.monotonic():
            return hit[0]
        self.store.pop(key, None)
        return None
    def set(self, key, value):
        self.store[key] = (value, time.monotonic() + self.seconds)

cache = TTLCache(seconds=60)

async def slots_for(pincode: str) -> list[str]:
    cached = cache.get(pincode)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached                         # cache hit: no database work
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)                  # the slow query
    slots = ["7-9", "9-11"]
    cache.set(pincode, slots)
    return slots

async def worker(name: str, queue: asyncio.Queue) -> None:
    while True:
        job = await queue.get()
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)          # send email, build invoice PDF, ...
            print(f"{name} finished {job}")
        finally:
            queue.task_done()

async def main() -> None:
    for _ in range(2):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        await slots_for("560103")
        print(f"slots in {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.0f} ms")

    queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()
    workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(f"worker-{i}", queue)) for i in range(2)]
    for order_id in (184, 185, 186):
        queue.put_nowait({"job": "send_invoice", "order_id": order_id})   # API returns immediately
    await queue.join()
    for task in workers:
        task.cancel()

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Caching without an expiry or without a plan to invalidate on change. Stale prices are worse than slow prices.
Jobs that are not idempotent. A queue can deliver a job twice, so "send invoice" must cope with running again.
A cache stampede: a popular key expires and 500 requests all recompute it at once. Add jitter to expiry times or lock the recompute.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is cache-aside?
blocks.text: The application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, writes the result into the cache with an expiry and returns it.

blocks.title: Why must background jobs be idempotent?
blocks.text: Queues usually guarantee at-least-once delivery. A worker may crash after doing the work but before acknowledging it, so the job runs again.

blocks.title: When do you use a queue instead of doing work in the request?
blocks.text: When the work is slow, can fail and be retried, or the user does not need the result immediately: emails, notifications, reports, calls to slow third parties.

blocks.title: What are the two hard problems of caching?
blocks.text: Knowing when cached data is stale (invalidation) and choosing how long to keep it (expiry).
Idempotency keys, single-flight and the outbox
Three patterns make queues and caches safe under failure.

An **idempotency key** makes "do this once" true even when the request or job is delivered twice. The caller sends a unique key. The first execution stores the key with its result. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result without doing the work again. The check and the store must be atomic, or two simultaneous duplicates both pass the check.

**Single-flight** protects against a cache stampede. When a popular key expires, a hundred concurrent requests would all run the same expensive query. Single-flight lets the first one run it and makes the other ninety-nine wait for that same result.

The **outbox pattern** solves "I saved the order but crashed before publishing the event". The event is written to an `outbox` table in the same database transaction as the order. A separate process reads the table and publishes. The order and its event are saved together or not at all.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

charges = 0
results: dict[str, asyncio.Future] = {}                 # production: a table with a unique key column

async def charge(idempotency_key: str, amount: int) -> str:
    global charges
    if idempotency_key in results:                      # seen before: return the first outcome
        return await results[idempotency_key] + " (replayed)"
    future = results[idempotency_key] = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()   # claimed, no await in between
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)                           # talk to the payment gateway
    charges += 1
    future.set_result(f"charged {amount}")
    return future.result()

class SingleFlight:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.in_flight: dict[str, asyncio.Task] = {}
    async def do(self, key: str, loader):
        task = self.in_flight.get(key)
        if task is None:                                # first caller starts the work
            task = self.in_flight[key] = asyncio.create_task(loader())
            task.add_done_callback(lambda _: self.in_flight.pop(key, None))
        return await task                               # everyone awaits the same task

queries = 0
async def load_slots() -> list[str]:
    global queries
    queries += 1
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)                           # the expensive query
    return ["7-9", "9-11"]

async def main() -> None:
    outcomes = await asyncio.gather(*(charge("order-184-pay", 70900) for _ in range(3)))   # retries and duplicates
    print(outcomes, "| card charged", charges, "time(s)")

    flight = SingleFlight()
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(flight.do("slots:560103", load_slots) for _ in range(100)))
    print(len(answers), "requests served by", queries, "database query")

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: Delivery guarantees

rows: In practice: at least once plus idempotency

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is an idempotency key?
blocks.text: A unique value the client sends with a request. The server stores it with the outcome and returns that outcome for any repeat, so retries cannot perform the action twice.

blocks.title: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
blocks.text: Many requests recomputing the same expired cache entry at once. Prevent it with single-flight or a lock so one request recomputes, with jittered expiry, or by refreshing before expiry.

blocks.title: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
blocks.text: The dual-write problem: saving to the database and publishing to a broker cannot be made atomic. Writing the event to a table in the same transaction and publishing it afterwards guarantees it is never lost.

blocks.title: Why is exactly-once delivery hard?
blocks.text: The sender cannot know whether a message was processed when an acknowledgement is lost, so it must resend. Systems therefore deliver at least once and rely on idempotent processing.
Normal HTTP is one question, one answer. Real-time features keep the connection open so the server can push more data when something changes.

**Server-sent events (SSE)** is a one-way stream from server to client over ordinary HTTP. It suits live order status and streamed AI answers. A **WebSocket** is a two-way channel. It suits chat and live location where the client also sends constantly.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: SSE is what you consume when a chat app shows an AI answer word by word, and it is an `AsyncSequence` / Dart `Stream` on the client. On the server it is an async generator, the same `yield` you met earlier.

blocks.code:
import asyncio, json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
STAGES = ["placed", "packed", "out_for_delivery", "delivered"]

async def order_events(order_id: int):
    for stage in STAGES:                      # production: await messages from Redis pub/sub
        payload = json.dumps({"order_id": order_id, "status": stage})
        yield f"event: status\ndata: {payload}\n\n"      # the SSE wire format
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)

@app.get("/orders/{order_id}/events")
async def events(order_id: int) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(order_events(order_id), media_type="text/event-stream")

with TestClient(app).stream("GET", "/orders/184/events") as response:
    for line in response.iter_lines():
        if line.startswith("data:"):
            print("phone received:", json.loads(line[5:]))

nodes.label: API instance holding the phone's SSE connection

blocks.text: Which one

rows: Automatic in browsers, simple on mobile

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Keeping connection state only in one server's memory. With several instances the event may arrive at a different instance than the one holding the connection. Use Redis pub/sub or similar between them.
No heartbeat. Proxies close idle connections after about a minute. Send a comment line or ping regularly.
Forgetting the phone goes offline. On reconnect, send the current state first, then live updates.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: SSE versus WebSocket versus polling?
blocks.text: Polling asks repeatedly and wastes requests. SSE keeps one HTTP response open for server-to-client events. WebSocket is a two-way channel for when the client also sends frequently.

blocks.title: How do you scale real-time connections across many servers?
blocks.text: Each server holds its own connections, and a shared pub/sub system (Redis, Kafka) delivers each event to every server so the one holding the right connection can push it.

blocks.title: Why does async matter here?
blocks.text: Each open connection is mostly idle. An event loop can hold tens of thousands of idle connections in one process, which threads cannot do cheaply.

Deploying means packaging your code with its exact dependencies and running it somewhere reliable. The package is a **Docker image**. Inside it, a server program (`uvicorn`, often several worker processes) runs your app. A load balancer in front spreads requests over several copies.
Running in production means you can answer three questions at any moment: is it up, is it fast and what went wrong. Those are health checks, metrics and logs.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The Docker image is your `.ipa` / app bundle: one artefact, built once by CI, promoted through environments. A rolling deploy is a phased release. Environment variables per environment are your schemes and flavours.

blocks.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app ./app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "4"]

curl http://localhost:8000/health

blocks.text: What to watch

rows: CPU, memory, DB connections in use

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A deploy at 6 pm doubles p95 latency on `GET /slots`. Because every request log line carries a request id, route and duration, you find the slow route in a minute, see a new query without an index, roll back the image to the previous tag and fix forward the next morning. Without those logs the same incident takes hours.
Pitfalls

items: More workers than the database can serve. Workers times pool size must stay under the database connection limit.
No health endpoint, so the platform sends traffic to an instance that is still starting or already broken.
Running database migrations that lock a big table during peak traffic.
Baking secrets into the image.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between uvicorn and gunicorn?
blocks.text: Uvicorn is an ASGI server that runs async apps. Gunicorn is a process manager. A common setup runs several uvicorn workers, either with `uvicorn --workers` or managed by gunicorn.

blocks.title: How many workers should you run?
blocks.text: Roughly one per CPU core for async apps, then measure. Each worker is a separate process with its own memory and its own database connections.

blocks.title: What is a rolling deployment?
blocks.text: New instances are started and checked before old ones are removed, a few at a time, so there is no downtime and a bad release can be stopped early.

blocks.title: What does p95 latency mean?
blocks.text: 95% of requests were faster than this value. It shows what slow requests feel like, which averages hide.

blocks.title: Liveness versus readiness check?
blocks.text: Liveness asks "is the process alive, or should it be restarted". Readiness asks "can it take traffic right now", which is false during startup or when a dependency is down.
Percentiles, structured logs and a local production-like stack

Averages hide pain. If nine requests in ten take 50 ms and the tenth takes two seconds, the average is about 250 ms and looks acceptable, while one user in ten waits two seconds. **Percentiles** describe what users feel: p50 is the typical request, p95 and p99 are the slow tail. Set targets and alerts on p95 or p99.
**Structured logs** are one JSON object per line with fixed field names. A machine can then filter by `order_id` or `request_id` across millions of lines. Free-text logs cannot be searched reliably.

**Docker Compose** starts your API, PostgreSQL and Redis together on your laptop with one command, wired the way they are in production. It is the fastest way to reproduce a production problem locally.

blocks.code:
import json, logging, statistics, sys

latencies_ms = [48, 52, 50, 47, 55, 51, 49, 53, 50, 46] * 18 + [900, 1200, 1500, 2100, 2400, 2800, 3000, 3100, 3300, 3500] * 2   # 10% slow

def percentile(values: list[float], p: float) -> float:
    ordered = sorted(values)
    index = min(len(ordered) - 1, round(p / 100 * (len(ordered) - 1)))
    return ordered[index]

print(f"requests {len(latencies_ms)} | mean {statistics.mean(latencies_ms):.0f} ms | "
      f"p50 {percentile(latencies_ms, 50)} | p95 {percentile(latencies_ms, 95)} | p99 {percentile(latencies_ms, 99)} ms")

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        entry = {"level": record.levelname, "event": record.getMessage(), "logger": record.name}
        entry.update(getattr(record, "fields", {}))
        if record.exc_info:
            entry["error"] = repr(record.exc_info[1])
        return json.dumps(entry)

handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
log = logging.getLogger("shop.orders")
log.addHandler(handler)
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

log.info("order.placed", extra={"fields": {"request_id": "a1b2c3", "order_id": 184, "user_id": 7, "duration_ms": 82}})
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    log.error("order.price_failed", exc_info=True, extra={"fields": {"request_id": "a1b2c3", "order_id": 184}})

error_budget = 1 - 0.999                                   # a 99.9% availability target
print(f"99.9% per 30 days allows {error_budget * 30 * 24 * 60:.0f} minutes of downtime")

services:

    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql+psycopg://shop:shop@db:5432/shop
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }

  worker:
    build: .

    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql+psycopg://shop:shop@db:5432/shop

  db:

    healthcheck:

    image: redis:7

blocks.title: Why use percentiles instead of the average?
blocks.text: A small share of very slow requests barely moves the average but is exactly what users complain about. p95 and p99 expose that tail.

blocks.title: What is structured logging?
blocks.text: Emitting logs as machine-readable records with consistent fields, usually JSON, so they can be filtered and aggregated by request id, user or route.

blocks.title: What are an SLI, SLO and error budget?
blocks.text: An SLI is a measured indicator such as the share of successful requests. An SLO is its target, such as 99.9%. The error budget is the allowed failure, 0.1%, which a team can spend on risk such as deploys.

blocks.title: What is Docker Compose used for?
blocks.text: Defining and running several containers together, typically the app with its database and cache, for local development and integration tests.

blocks.title: What do you do first when a deploy makes things worse?
blocks.text: Roll back to the previous version to restore service, then investigate with the evidence you collected.

modules.title: Python: Stage 6 · AI
modules.summary: Putting a model behind your API

lessons.title: NumPy and pandas in one sitting

blocks.text: **NumPy** gives you arrays of numbers and maths on whole arrays at once, running in fast C code. Every AI library is built on this idea. **pandas** gives you a table (a `DataFrame`) with named columns, for loading, filtering and summarising data.
You do not need to master either to build AI features on an API. You need to read them, because vectors, embeddings and evaluation results all arrive as arrays and tables.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A NumPy array is `[Double]` with SIMD-style maths built in: `a * b` multiplies element by element with no loop in your code. A DataFrame is a spreadsheet you query with code, or a SQL table in memory.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

prices = np.array([62, 45, 540, 189])
qty = np.array([2, 1, 1, 3])
print((prices * qty).sum(), prices[prices > 100], prices.mean())    # no loops

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
b = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 4.1])
cosine = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))            # how similar two vectors point
print("similarity", round(float(cosine), 4))

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["blr", "del", "blr", "mum", "blr"],
    "total": [320, 90, 760, 410, 150],
    "status": ["delivered", "cancelled", "delivered", "delivered", "delivered"],
})
delivered = orders[orders["status"] == "delivered"]
print(delivered.groupby("city")["total"].agg(["count", "sum", "mean"]))
print(orders["status"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(2).to_dict())

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: "Which city cancels most, and is it getting worse week by week" is five lines of pandas over an export from the orders table. Analysts and ML engineers live in this tool, so reading it lets you work with them.
Pitfalls

items: Looping over a NumPy array or DataFrame row by row in Python. Use whole-column operations, which are often 100 times faster.
Loading a 20 GB table into pandas on a server. Aggregate in SQL first.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is NumPy faster than a Python list for maths?
blocks.text: Values are stored in one contiguous block of a single type, and operations run as compiled loops over that block instead of interpreting Python per element.

blocks.title: What is cosine similarity?
blocks.text: The cosine of the angle between two vectors: their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. 1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated.

blocks.title: What is vectorisation?
blocks.text: Expressing an operation on whole arrays so the loop happens inside optimised native code.

A large language model takes text in and produces text out, one small piece (**token**) at a time. Your code sends a list of **messages** and gets a message back. The model has no memory between calls: every request must contain everything it should know, including earlier turns of the conversation.
You pay per token, both in and out, and each model has a maximum amount of text it can consider at once, called the **context window**.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A brilliant temp who has read everything but started work this minute and knows nothing about your company. The prompt is the briefing note you hand over. A vague note gets a vague result.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: From your side it is one more HTTP API: you already call REST endpoints from Dio. The differences are that the response is slow (seconds), costs money per call, is not identical each time and can decline. So you treat it like an unreliable but valuable third-party service.

blocks.code:
pip install anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."      # from the console; never commit it

blocks.text: A conversation is a growing list you resend

rows: Turn 1. You send the system prompt and one user message.
system, user: what can I cook?
Turn 2. The model remembers nothing, so you send the whole history plus the new question.
system, user: what can I cook?, assistant: Paneer capsicum..., user: make it less spicy
Turn 3. The list keeps growing, and so do input tokens and cost. Long chats need trimming or summarising.
system, user, assistant, user, assistant, user: add a shopping list

diagram.title: One model call from your API

blocks.text: Parts of a request

rows: Which model answers. Larger models are smarter, slower and cost more
Standing instructions: role, tone, rules, format
The conversation so far, alternating user and assistant
Hard ceiling on the length of the answer
Why it stopped: finished, hit the limit, wants a tool, or declined

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Calling the model from the phone with the API key inside the app. Keys in a mobile binary can be extracted. Always go through your backend.
Assuming the answer is correct. Models state wrong things confidently. Ground them with your own data (RAG) and check outputs.
Not reading `stop_reason`. An answer cut off at `max_tokens` looks like a normal answer.
Putting untrusted text (reviews, web pages) into the prompt and trusting what comes back. That text can contain instructions (prompt injection).

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a token?
blocks.text: A piece of text the model reads and writes, roughly three quarters of an English word. Limits and prices are counted in tokens.

blocks.title: Why must you resend the conversation each time?
blocks.text: The API is stateless. The model only knows what is in the current request.

blocks.title: What is a system prompt?
blocks.text: Instructions that set the model's role and rules for the whole conversation, separate from the user's messages.

blocks.title: Why should model calls go through your backend?
blocks.text: To keep the API key secret, to add your own data and rules, to rate-limit and log, and to swap models without an app release.

blocks.title: What is a context window?
blocks.text: The maximum amount of text, in tokens, the model can take into account in one request: prompt, history, documents and its own answer.
Writing prompts, managing context and caching

A prompt is a specification. The model does what the text says, so quality comes from being specific. A reliable structure is: who the model is acting as, the task, the context it needs, the rules, and the exact output wanted. Put long documents first and the question last. Show one or two examples of the output you want.

The context window is a budget. A long chat eventually exceeds it and gets expensive well before that. Common tactics are to keep the system prompt and the most recent turns, and replace older turns with a summary.

Many requests share a long, identical beginning: the system prompt, tool definitions, a policy document. **Prompt caching** lets the provider reuse its work on that prefix, so repeated requests are cheaper and faster. Caching matches on an exact prefix, so keep the stable part first and anything that changes (the user's question, the time) last.

blocks.code:
SYSTEM = """You are the support assistant for a grocery delivery app.

Rules:
- Answer only from the policy text and tool results you are given.
- If the answer is not there, say you do not know and offer a human agent.
- Never state an order status without calling the order tool.
- Reply in at most three short sentences, in the user's language.

Output: plain text, no markdown."""

def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)             # rough rule: about 4 characters per token in English

def trim_history(history: list[dict], budget_tokens: int) -> list[dict]:
    """Keep the newest turns that fit. Older turns become one summary line."""
    kept, used = [], 0
    for message in reversed(history):
        cost = estimate_tokens(message["content"])
        if used + cost > budget_tokens:
            break
        kept.append(message)
        used += cost
    kept.reverse()
    dropped = len(history) - len(kept)
    if dropped:
        if kept and kept[0]["role"] == "assistant":       # a conversation must start with the user
            kept, dropped = kept[1:], dropped + 1
        summary = {"role": "user", "content": f"(Summary of {dropped} earlier messages: user asked about a late order and a refund.)"}
        ack = {"role": "assistant", "content": "Understood."}
        kept = [summary, ack] + kept
    return kept

history = []
for turn in range(1, 9):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Question {turn}: " + "details " * 30})
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": f"Answer {turn}: " + "explanation " * 30})
history.append({"role": "user", "content": "So when will order 184 arrive?"})

trimmed = trim_history(history, budget_tokens=400)
print(len(history), "messages ->", len(trimmed), "| roles:", [m["role"][0] for m in trimmed])
print("system prompt tokens (estimate):", estimate_tokens(SYSTEM))

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
POLICY = open("refund_policy.md").read()          # long and identical on every request

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},          # cache the stable prefix automatically
    system=f"You answer from this policy only.\n\n{POLICY}",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Can I return opened milk?"}],   # the part that changes goes last
)
print(response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens, response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)
# First call: tokens are written to the cache. Later calls: read from it at a lower price.

blocks.text: Fixing a weak prompt

rows: "Summarise for a delivery partner in 3 bullet points: what to deliver, where, by when."
Audience, length and content are stated
"Answer only from the sources. If they do not cover it, say so."
A checkable rule instead of a wish
Shape is enforced, not hoped for

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What makes a good prompt?
blocks.text: It states the role, the task, the needed context, explicit rules and the exact output format, gives an example, and tells the model what to do when it lacks information.

blocks.title: How do you handle conversations longer than the context window?
blocks.text: Keep the system prompt and the most recent turns, summarise or drop older ones, and retrieve past details on demand instead of resending everything.

blocks.title: What is prompt caching and when does it help?
blocks.text: The provider stores its processing of a repeated prompt prefix and reuses it on later requests at a lower price and latency. It helps when many requests share a long, identical beginning.

blocks.title: Why must cached content come first in the request?
blocks.text: Caching matches on an exact prefix. Any change early in the prompt, such as a timestamp, invalidates everything after it.

blocks.title: What do temperature and similar sampling settings do?
blocks.text: They control how random the choice of each next token is. Lower means more predictable output. Some current models fix these settings, in which case you steer with instructions instead.

lessons.title: Structured output: text in, typed data out

blocks.text: An app cannot use a paragraph. It needs fields. **Structured output** makes the model fill in a schema you define, so you get an object you can validate and store instead of free text you have to parse with guesswork.
You describe the shape with a Pydantic model, the same tool you used for request bodies.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: It is `Codable` for model answers: you declare the struct and get a decoded instance or an error, instead of scraping strings with regular expressions.

blocks.code:
import anthropic
from pydantic import BaseModel

class CartLine(BaseModel):
    product: str
    quantity: float
    unit: str

class ParsedList(BaseModel):
    lines: list[CartLine]
    unclear: list[str]

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
note = "2 kg aloo, half litre milk, dhaniya, 6 eggs and that biscuit we had last time"

response = client.messages.parse(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    system="Turn a shopping note into cart lines. Put anything you cannot identify in `unclear`.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": note}],
    output_format=ParsedList,
)
parsed = response.parsed_output          # a validated ParsedList instance
for line in parsed.lines:
    print(line.quantity, line.unit, line.product)
print("ask the user about:", parsed.unclear)

Match each product against the catalogue (your code)

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: "Add my usual Sunday list" becomes cart lines. The model does the language part: "aloo" is potato, "half litre" is 0.5 l. Your code does the facts: which exact product, the current price, whether it is in stock. The user confirms before anything is ordered. Language to the model, facts and money to your code.
Pitfalls

items: Asking for "JSON" in the prompt and parsing whatever comes back. Use the schema feature so the shape is guaranteed.
Letting the model invent product ids or prices. It should extract and classify. Lookups come from your database.
No escape hatch in the schema. Give it an `unclear` or `none` option, or it will guess.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use structured output instead of asking for JSON in the prompt?
blocks.text: The schema is enforced and validated, so you do not get missing fields, extra prose or broken JSON.

blocks.title: What should the model decide and what should your code decide?
blocks.text: The model handles language: understanding, extracting, classifying. Your code handles facts and actions: ids, prices, stock, permissions and anything involving money.
A long answer can take ten seconds or more. Waiting for all of it feels broken. **Streaming** sends each piece of text as soon as the model produces it, so the first words appear in under a second.
Your server sits in the middle: it reads the model's stream and forwards each piece to the phone over server-sent events. This is the async generator and SSE from earlier lessons joined together.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: On the client you already consume this as `URLSession.bytes(for:)` or a Dart `Stream` from Dio with `ResponseType.stream`. The server side is the producer of that stream.

blocks.code:
import json
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
client = AsyncAnthropic()

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

async def answer_events(question: str):
    async with client.messages.stream(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=64000,
        system="You are a cooking assistant for a grocery app.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    ) as stream:
        async for text in stream.text_stream:                 # one small piece at a time
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'text': text})}\n\n"
        final = await stream.get_final_message()
    done = {"output_tokens": final.usage.output_tokens, "stop_reason": final.stop_reason}
    yield f"event: done\ndata: {json.dumps(done)}\n\n"

@app.post("/assistant")
async def assistant(body: Ask) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(answer_events(body.question), media_type="text/event-stream")

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Buffering somewhere in the chain (a proxy, gzip, a framework default) so the user gets everything at the end anyway. Test with a real device on a real network.
Using the sync client inside an async endpoint. It blocks the event loop for the whole answer.
Not handling the user closing the screen. Stop reading from the model when the client disconnects, or you pay for an answer nobody sees.
Saving nothing. Log the final text and usage when the stream ends.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why stream model output?
blocks.text: Perceived speed. Total time is the same, but the user sees the first words almost immediately and can start reading or cancel.

blocks.title: What is time to first token?
blocks.text: The delay between sending the request and receiving the first piece of the answer. It is the main latency number for chat-style features.

blocks.title: Why is async a good fit for streaming endpoints?
blocks.text: Each request is a long-lived, mostly idle connection. One event loop can serve many of them without a thread per user.

A model on its own can only write text. **Tools** let it act. You describe functions it may call (name, purpose, parameters). When the model decides it needs one, it replies with a tool request instead of an answer. Your code runs the function and sends the result back. The model then continues, possibly asking for another tool.
That repeat-until-done cycle is the **agent loop**. An agent is a model, a set of tools and this loop.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A manager on the phone who cannot touch the computer. They tell you "look up order 184". You look it up and read out the result. They decide what to ask next. You are the hands, they are the planner.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: It is a delegate or callback pattern across a network: the model calls back into your code with a function name and JSON arguments, and you return a result.
The loop, turn by turn

rows: Your code sends the user's message and the tool descriptions.
The model answers with tool requests instead of text. `stop_reason` is `tool_use`.
Your code runs both functions and appends the results.
user message, assistant tool requests, tool results
The model reads the results and asks for one more tool.
Your code runs it and returns the result.
No more tools needed. The model writes the final answer and the loop ends.
Order 184 arrives in 12 minutes. I opened a refund request for 185.

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Your tool functions are the security boundary. `create_refund_request` must check, in your code, that the order belongs to the logged-in user and is refundable. The model may ask for anything, including things a malicious message told it to ask for. It can only do what your functions allow.
Pitfalls

items: Giving a tool more power than the user has. Check permissions inside every tool with the real user's identity.
Tools that do irreversible things with no confirmation step (payments, cancellations).
Vague tool descriptions. The description is the only documentation the model has. Say what it does and when to use it.
No limit on loop iterations or cost.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is tool use (function calling)?
blocks.text: The model returns a structured request to call a function you described. Your code executes it and returns the result so the model can continue.

blocks.title: What is an agent?
blocks.text: A model running in a loop with tools, deciding itself which tool to call next until the task is finished.

blocks.title: Who executes a tool?
blocks.text: Your code, on your servers, with your permissions checks. The model only asks.

blocks.title: How do you stop an agent from doing damage?
blocks.text: Narrow tools, permission checks inside each tool, confirmation before irreversible actions, iteration and budget limits, and logs of every call.

blocks.title: What is prompt injection?
blocks.text: Text inside data the model reads (a review, a web page, an email) that tries to give it instructions. Treat everything the model reads as untrusted, and never let it be the only safeguard.
The loop written by hand
The SDK's tool runner hides the loop. Writing it once by hand shows exactly what travels over the wire, which is what you need when debugging or when an interviewer asks you to explain an agent.

Each round has the same shape. Send the conversation and the tool definitions. If `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, the reply contains one or more `tool_use` blocks, each with an id, a tool name and JSON input. Run them, then send back one user message containing a `tool_result` block per call, matched by id. Repeat until the model stops asking for tools.
Two rules prevent subtle failures. Append the model's **whole** content list to the conversation, not only its text. And return **all** tool results in a single message.
What the `messages` list looks like as the loop runs

rows: The model replies with a tool request. Its content list is appended as the assistant turn.
Your code runs the tool and appends one user message holding the result, matched by id.
The model now has the fact and writes the answer. The loop ends.
user, assistant [tool_use], user [tool_result], assistant "It arrives in about 12 minutes."

rows: Your code, in a fixed order
Steps depend on what is found along the way

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Describe the tool-use message cycle.
blocks.text: Send messages and tool definitions. The model returns `tool_use` blocks with ids and inputs and `stop_reason: tool_use`. Execute them, append the assistant turn, then send a user message with a `tool_result` per id. Repeat until no tool is requested.

blocks.title: Why append the full content list instead of just the text?
blocks.text: The assistant turn contains the `tool_use` blocks that the following `tool_result` blocks refer to by id. Dropping them makes the next request invalid.

blocks.title: How do you report a failed tool call to the model?
blocks.text: Return a `tool_result` for that id with `is_error` set and a short message, so the model can retry, choose another path or tell the user.

blocks.title: Workflow versus agent?
blocks.text: In a workflow your code fixes the sequence of model calls. In an agent the model chooses the next tool in a loop. Prefer the simplest shape that solves the task.

A model does not know your refund policy or today's catalogue. **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** fixes that: find the few pieces of your own text that relate to the question, paste them into the prompt and tell the model to answer only from them.
Finding relevant text uses **embeddings**. An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector) so that texts with similar meaning have vectors that point in similar directions.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An open-book exam. The model is a strong student, retrieval hands it the right two pages, and the instruction is "answer from these pages and say so if the answer is not there".

blocks.code:
import re
import numpy as np

DOCS = [
    "Refunds for damaged items are issued to the original payment method within 5 days.",
    "Delivery is free for orders above 500 rupees. Below that a fee of 40 rupees applies.",
    "Fresh milk can be returned at the door if the seal is broken.",
    "Membership gives free delivery on every order and early access to slots.",
]

def words(text: str) -> list[str]:
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())

VOCAB = sorted({w for doc in DOCS for w in words(doc)})

def embed(text: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """Toy embedding: word counts. A real system calls an embedding model here."""
    counts = np.array([words(text).count(w) for w in VOCAB], dtype=float)
    length = np.linalg.norm(counts)
    return counts / length if length else counts

INDEX = np.stack([embed(doc) for doc in DOCS])        # done once, stored in a vector database

def retrieve(question: str, k: int = 2) -> list[tuple[float, str]]:
    scores = INDEX @ embed(question)                   # cosine similarity with every chunk
    best = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k]
    return [(round(float(scores[i]), 2), DOCS[i]) for i in best]

question = "is delivery free above 500 rupees"
hits = retrieve(question)
for score, doc in hits:
    print(score, doc)

context = "\n".join(f"[{n}] {doc}" for n, (_, doc) in enumerate(hits, 1))
prompt = (
    "Answer using only the numbered sources. Cite the source number. "
    "If the sources do not contain the answer, say you do not know.\n\n"
    f"Sources:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
)
print(prompt)       # this prompt is what you send to the model
