blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A support assistant answers "can I return opened milk" from the actual policy pages, and shows which page it used. When the policy changes, you re-index that page and the answer changes with no retraining. When retrieval finds nothing relevant, the assistant says it does not know and offers a human.
Pitfalls

items: Blaming the model when the retrieval step returned the wrong chunks. Log the retrieved text and check it first.
Chunks that are too big (noise, cost) or too small (no context). Start around a few hundred words with some overlap, then measure.
No "I do not know" instruction, so the model fills gaps from its general knowledge.
Skipping access control. Retrieval must only search documents this user is allowed to see.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is RAG?
blocks.text: Retrieve relevant pieces of your own data for a question, add them to the prompt and have the model answer from them. It grounds answers in current, private information.

blocks.title: What is an embedding?
blocks.text: A vector that represents the meaning of a text, produced by an embedding model. Similar texts get nearby vectors.

blocks.title: RAG versus fine-tuning?
blocks.text: RAG supplies knowledge at question time and is updated by changing documents. Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour or style through training. For facts that change, use RAG.

blocks.title: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
blocks.text: Separately measure retrieval (did the right chunk come back in the top results) and generation (is the answer supported by the retrieved text and correct).

blocks.title: What is a vector database?
blocks.text: A store that keeps vectors with their source text and finds the nearest ones quickly. PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension is a common first choice.
Chunking, hybrid search and measuring retrieval
Three decisions determine RAG quality more than the choice of model.

**Chunking**: how documents are split. Chunks should be self-contained units of meaning, a few hundred words long, with a small overlap so a sentence cut at a boundary still appears whole in one chunk. Keep the document title and section heading with every chunk.

**Search method**: vector search finds similar meaning but can miss exact terms such as product codes or names. Keyword search (BM25) is the opposite. **Hybrid search** runs both and merges the rankings. A **reranker** that rescores the top 20 or so against the question usually lifts quality further.

**Measurement**: build a small set of questions with the chunk that should answer each. **Recall@k** is the share of questions whose correct chunk appears in the top k results. If recall is low, no prompt will fix the answers.

nodes.label: Vector search top 20 + keyword search top 20

blocks.text: When answers are wrong, look here first

rows: Too many or too long chunks
Send fewer, put the best first
Chunks lack their heading or product name
Add title and section to each chunk
Exact code or name not found

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you choose a chunk size?
blocks.text: Start with self-contained passages of a few hundred words with some overlap, keep headings with each chunk, then tune by measuring recall on real questions.

blocks.title: What is hybrid search?
blocks.text: Running semantic vector search and keyword search together and merging the results, so both paraphrases and exact terms are found.

blocks.title: What is recall@k?
blocks.text: The fraction of test questions for which a relevant chunk appears among the top k retrieved results.

blocks.title: What does a reranker do?
blocks.text: It rescores a small candidate list against the query with a more accurate, slower model and reorders it, improving what ends up in the prompt.

blocks.title: How do you keep RAG from leaking data between users?
blocks.text: Store access metadata with each chunk and filter retrieval by the requesting user's permissions before anything reaches the prompt.

You cannot test an AI feature with one `assert`, because the output varies. An **eval** is a set of realistic inputs with a way to score each output. You run it whenever the prompt, the model or the retrieval changes, and compare the score with the previous run.
Without evals, every prompt change is a guess. With them, AI work becomes normal engineering: change, measure, keep or revert.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: An eval set is a regression test suite whose assertions are graders instead of exact equality. A score dropping from 92% to 85% is a failing build.
Three ways to grade

rows: Exact match, contains, valid JSON, right tool called
A second model scores the answer against a rubric
Calibrating the other two, high-risk features

blocks.text: Cost and latency levers

rows: Prompt caching for the stable prefix
Repeated prefix billed at a fraction
Lower price and latency per call
Same total time, much better perceived speed

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A worked cost estimate. Say a feature sends 2,000 input tokens and gets 500 output tokens per request, one million requests a month. At 4 dollars per million input tokens and 20 per million output tokens that is 8,000 + 10,000 = 18,000 dollars a month. Halving the prompt saves 4,000. Prices change, so always take current numbers from the provider's pricing page, but do this arithmetic before you ship.
Pitfalls

items: Shipping a prompt change because three hand-tried examples looked good.
An eval set of only easy cases. Include the questions that should be refused and the ones with no answer.
No per-user rate limit on an AI endpoint. One script can spend your monthly budget overnight.
Logging full prompts that contain personal data without a retention plan.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is an eval?
blocks.text: A repeatable test for an AI feature: a fixed set of inputs, a grading method and a score you track across changes.

blocks.title: What is a hallucination and how do you reduce it?
blocks.text: A fluent answer that is not true. Reduce it by grounding in retrieved sources, requiring citations, allowing "I do not know" and measuring with evals.

blocks.title: How do you control the cost of an AI feature?
blocks.text: Measure tokens per request, trim prompts, cache stable prefixes, use the smallest model that passes your eval, cap output and iterations, and rate-limit users.

blocks.title: What are guardrails?
blocks.text: Checks around the model: input validation, permission checks in tools, output validation against a schema or policy, and human approval for risky actions.
Scoring classifiers, model-graded evals and a release gate
Different features need different scores.

For a **classifier**, such as "is this message a complaint", accuracy alone misleads when one class is rare. **Precision** asks: of the items flagged, how many were right. **Recall** asks: of the items that should have been flagged, how many were found. Which matters more depends on the cost of each mistake.

For **open-ended answers**, code cannot judge tone or correctness, so a second model grades each answer against a written rubric and returns a structured verdict. Check the judge against human labels on a sample before trusting it.

A **release gate** turns this into engineering. Store the score of the version in production as the baseline. In CI, run the eval on the candidate and fail the build if the score drops by more than the noise you measured.

blocks.code:
import anthropic
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Verdict(BaseModel):
    grounded: bool          # every claim is supported by the sources
    answers_question: bool
    reason: str

RUBRIC = """You grade a support assistant's answer.
grounded: true only if every factual claim appears in the sources.
answers_question: true only if the user's question is directly answered.
Give a one-sentence reason."""

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def judge(question: str, sources: str, answer: str) -> Verdict:
    response = client.messages.parse(
        model="claude-opus-5-5",
        max_tokens=16000,
        system=RUBRIC,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Sources:\n{sources}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nAnswer: {answer}"}],
        output_format=Verdict,
    )
    return response.parsed_output

blocks.title: Precision versus recall?
blocks.text: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct. Recall is the share of actual positives that were found. Improving one often lowers the other.

blocks.title: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
blocks.text: If 95% of messages are not complaints, a classifier that always says "not a complaint" is 95% accurate and useless.

blocks.title: How do you trust a model-graded eval?
blocks.text: Write a specific rubric, ask for a structured verdict with a reason, and compare the judge's verdicts with human labels on a sample. Use it only where they agree well.

blocks.title: How do you stop prompt changes from causing regressions?
blocks.text: Keep an eval set in the repository, record the production score as a baseline and fail CI when a change scores worse beyond the measured noise.

blocks.title: Where do eval cases come from?
blocks.text: Real user inputs, past failures and bug reports, and deliberately hard or adversarial cases, each with the expected behaviour written down.
Make it correct, then measure, then make the slow part fast. Guessing which part is slow is wrong most of the time. A **profiler** tells you where the time went.

Most speed-ups in backend Python come from three places, in this order: doing less I/O (fewer queries, a cache), choosing the right data structure (a set instead of a list) and moving heavy loops into a library written in C.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `cProfile` is Instruments' Time Profiler or the Flutter CPU profiler in text form: a table of functions sorted by time.

blocks.code:
import cProfile, pstats, timeit

blocked_list = list(range(20_000))
blocked_set = set(blocked_list)

def slow(ids):
    return [i for i in ids if i in blocked_list]      # scans the list each time

def fast(ids):
    return [i for i in ids if i in blocked_set]       # one hash lookup each time

ids = list(range(0, 40_000, 20))
print(f"list: {timeit.timeit(lambda: slow(ids), number=3):.3f}s")
print(f"set : {timeit.timeit(lambda: fast(ids), number=3):.5f}s")

profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.enable()
slow(ids)
profiler.disable()
pstats.Stats(profiler).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(3)

Micro-tuning Python while the endpoint makes 200 database queries.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you find a bottleneck?
blocks.text: Measure. Start from production metrics to find the slow route, then profile that code path or inspect its queries, and change only what the measurements point to.

blocks.title: Why is `x in list` slower than `x in set`?
blocks.text: A list is searched item by item, O(n). A set hashes the value and jumps to its slot, O(1) on average.

blocks.title: What options exist for CPU-heavy Python?
blocks.text: Vectorised libraries such as NumPy, multiple processes, a job queue to move work off the request path, or native extensions.

A professional Python project has one config file, `pyproject.toml`, that lists dependencies and configures the tools. Four tools run on every commit: a **formatter and linter** (`ruff`), a **type checker** (`mypy` or `pyright`), the **tests** (`pytest`) and a **lock file** that pins exact dependency versions.
Continuous integration runs the same four on every pull request, so problems are found before review.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `pyproject.toml` is `pubspec.yaml` plus `analysis_options.yaml` in one file. `ruff` is `dart format` plus `flutter analyze` or SwiftLint. The lock file is `pubspec.lock`.

modules.summary: What Node is, install it, run one file

lessons.title: What Node.js is and the whole path

blocks.text: JavaScript was built to run inside web browsers. **Node.js** is a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on a laptop or a server. It takes the JavaScript engine from Chrome (called **V8**) and adds what a server needs: reading files, opening network connections and talking to databases.
Node is popular for backends because it handles a large number of simultaneous connections with very little memory, and because web teams can use one language on both sides.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: V8 is the engine. Node is the car built around it: wheels (file system), steering (network) and a dashboard (the `process` object). The browser is a different car using the same engine.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Node feels close to Dart. Both are single-threaded with an event loop, both use `async` / `await` and `Future` / `Promise`, both have a package manager with a manifest file (`pubspec.yaml`, `package.json`). TypeScript is to JavaScript roughly what sound null-safe Dart is to early untyped Dart.
Python or Node for the same job

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A chat feature and live order tracking hold a connection open per user. Ten thousand users online means ten thousand mostly idle connections. Node keeps all of them in one process with one thread, which is the workload it was designed for.
Check yourself

blocks.title: What is Node.js?
blocks.text: A JavaScript runtime built on the V8 engine and the libuv library. It runs JavaScript outside the browser with APIs for files, networking and processes.

blocks.title: Is Node a language or a framework?
blocks.text: Neither. JavaScript is the language, Node is the runtime that executes it, and Express or NestJS are frameworks that run on Node.

blocks.title: What is libuv?
blocks.text: The C library inside Node that provides the event loop, non-blocking network I/O and a small thread pool for work the OS cannot do asynchronously, such as file access.

blocks.title: When is Node a poor fit?
blocks.text: CPU-heavy work such as image processing or large computations, because one long calculation blocks the single JavaScript thread.
Install Node with a version manager so each project can pin its own Node version. `nvm` is the common one. Node ships with `npm`, the package manager.

A project is a folder with a `package.json` file. That file names the project, lists the libraries it needs and defines shortcut commands called **scripts**. Installed libraries go into `node_modules`, and exact versions are recorded in `package-lock.json`.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `package.json` is `pubspec.yaml` / `Podfile`. `package-lock.json` is the lock file. `node_modules` is `.pub-cache` or `Pods/`, except it lives inside every project and is never committed. `npm run dev` is like a named scheme or a `Makefile` target.

Pitfalls

items: Committing `node_modules`. Add it to `.gitignore` and commit the lock file instead.
Using `npm install` in CI. Use `npm ci`, which installs exactly what the lock file says and fails if it is out of date.
Installing a package after reading only its name. Check downloads, maintenance and the exact spelling: typo-squatted packages exist.

blocks.title: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
blocks.text: `dependencies` are needed to run the app in production. `devDependencies` are only needed to build and test it, such as TypeScript and test tools.

blocks.title: What is `package-lock.json` for?
blocks.text: It records the exact version of every direct and indirect dependency so every install is identical.

blocks.title: `npm install` versus `npm ci`?
blocks.text: `npm install` may update the lock file to satisfy ranges. `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` and installs strictly from the lock file, which is what build servers should do.

blocks.title: What does `npx` do?
blocks.text: Runs a package's command without installing it globally, for example `npx prisma migrate dev`.

modules.title: Node.js: Stage 1 · Language
modules.summary: The JavaScript you need for servers

blocks.text: Declare variables with `const` by default and `let` only when you must reassign. Never use `var`.
The basic value types are `number` (one type for integers and decimals), `string`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `bigint` and `object`. Arrays and functions are objects.
JavaScript converts between types by itself in ways that surprise people. The rule that removes most surprises: always compare with `===`, never `==`.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `const` is `let` in Swift and `final` in Dart. `let` is `var`. There are two "nothing" values: `undefined` means "never set" and `null` means "deliberately empty". `?.` and `??` work the same as in Swift and Dart.
The falsy values (everything else is truthy)

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A price arrives from a form as the string `"49"`. `"49" + 1` is `"491"`, and that bug charges the wrong amount. Convert and validate at the boundary (`Number(value)` plus a schema check), and keep money as whole paise in an integer, since `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3` here either.
Pitfalls

items: Using `==`. `0 == ""` and `null == undefined` are both true.
`const` does not freeze an object. `const cart = []; cart.push(1)` works. Only the binding is constant.
`typeof null` is `"object"`, a historical bug. Check with `value === null`.
Ids larger than 2^53 lose precision as numbers. Send them as strings.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: `==` versus `===`?
blocks.text: `==` converts the two sides to a common type before comparing. `===` compares without conversion, so different types are never equal. Use `===`.

blocks.title: `null` versus `undefined`?
blocks.text: `undefined` means a value was never assigned. `null` is an explicit "no value". `value ?? fallback` treats both as missing.

blocks.title: `var` versus `let` versus `const`?
blocks.text: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted. `let` and `const` are block-scoped. `const` cannot be reassigned.

blocks.title: What is hoisting?
blocks.text: Declarations are processed before code runs. A `var` is usable (as `undefined`) before its line, and function declarations can be called before they appear. `let` and `const` exist but cannot be read before their line.
Coercion rules, number limits and dates
JavaScript converts types for you when an operator gets something unexpected. Three rules explain almost every surprise.

`+` with a string on either side **joins text**. Every other arithmetic operator converts both sides **to numbers**. And a value that cannot become a number becomes `NaN`, a special number that is not equal to anything, including itself.

All ordinary numbers are 64-bit floating point. Integers are exact only up to 2^53, and decimal fractions such as 0.1 are approximations. Use whole paise for money and `BigInt` or strings for very large ids.
A `Date` stores one thing: milliseconds since 1970 in UTC. Time zones only appear when you format it. Send and store dates as ISO 8601 strings in UTC, and convert to the user's zone at the edge.
`let` and `const` exist from the top of their block but cannot be read until their line runs. That gap is the **temporal dead zone**, and reading inside it throws.
What an operator does with mixed types
The temporal dead zone

rows: The block starts. `early` is known to exist but is uninitialised.
Had execution reached `let early = 1`, the dead zone would end.
A `var` in the same position would have been `undefined` instead of throwing, which hides the mistake.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`?
blocks.text: Numbers are binary floating point, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation. The tiny errors add up. Compare with a tolerance or use integers.

blocks.title: What is `NaN` and how do you test for it?
blocks.text: "Not a number", the result of an invalid numeric operation. It is not equal to itself, so test with `Number.isNaN(value)`.

blocks.title: What is the largest safe integer?
blocks.text: 2^53 - 1, `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Beyond it integers lose precision. Use `BigInt` or strings.

blocks.title: What is the temporal dead zone?
blocks.text: The span from the start of a block to the line where a `let` or `const` is declared. Reading the variable there throws a `ReferenceError`.

blocks.title: How should dates be exchanged between client and server?
blocks.text: As ISO 8601 strings in UTC, or as epoch milliseconds. Convert to a local time zone only for display.
Functions are values. You pass them as arguments, return them and store them. An **arrow function** `(x) => x * 2` is the short form used for callbacks.
A **closure** is a function that keeps access to the variables around it after the outer function has returned. Most Node patterns rely on it: middleware, event handlers, factories.

`this` is the object a method was called on. It depends on **how** the function is called, not where it was written. Arrow functions do not have their own `this`, which is why they are safe as callbacks.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Arrow functions are Swift closures and Dart lambdas. Closures capture variables the same way. The `this` rules are the part with no equivalent: imagine `self` could silently become `nil` when you pass a method as a callback.
A closure keeps its variable alive

rows: `makeCounter(183)` runs. A variable `count` is created inside it.
It returns an object with two arrow functions and finishes. `count` is not destroyed, because the returned functions still refer to it.
`orderIds.next()` runs. It reads and changes the same `count`.
Called again. The state persisted between calls, and nothing outside can touch `count` directly.

nodes.label: this comes from the surrounding code

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Passing a method as a callback (`setTimeout(cart.describe, 0)`) and losing `this`. Wrap it: `() => cart.describe()`.
A closure holding a large object alive for the life of the server. This is a common memory leak.
Default parameter objects without `= {}`. Calling `fee(300)` would throw on destructuring.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a closure?
blocks.text: A function together with the variables from the scope where it was defined. It can read and update them after the outer function has returned.

blocks.title: How do arrow functions differ from normal functions?
blocks.text: They have no own `this`, `arguments` or `new`. They use `this` from the surrounding scope, which makes them predictable as callbacks.

blocks.title: What do `call`, `apply` and `bind` do?
blocks.text: They set `this` explicitly. `call` and `apply` invoke immediately (arguments listed versus as an array). `bind` returns a new function with `this` fixed.

blocks.title: What is a higher-order function?
blocks.text: A function that takes a function as an argument or returns one, such as `map`, `filter` or an Express middleware factory.
Prototypes, classes and two utilities you will be asked to write

JavaScript objects inherit from other **objects**, not from classes. Every object has a hidden link to another object called its **prototype**. When you read `obj.method` and the object does not have it, JavaScript follows the link and looks there, then follows that object's link, until it finds the property or reaches the end of the chain.

The `class` keyword is a cleaner way to set those links up. Methods you write in a class body are stored once, on `ClassName.prototype`, and every instance links to it. Fields set in the constructor are stored on each instance.
Classes add a few features of their own: `#private` fields that are inaccessible from outside, `static` members that belong to the class, and getters that compute a value on access.
Looking up `milk.lineTotal` and `milk.toString`

rows: `milk.lineTotal`: not on the instance. Follow the prototype link.
Inside it, `super.lineTotal` starts the search one level further up.
`milk.toString`: not on any of those. One more link up.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is prototypal inheritance?
blocks.text: Objects delegate to other objects. Each object has a prototype link, and a property that is not found on the object is looked up along that chain.

blocks.title: Is `class` in JavaScript a new object model?
blocks.text: No. It is syntax over prototypes. Methods live on the constructor's `prototype` object and instances link to it. Classes do add private fields, `static` and stricter rules.

blocks.title: `__proto__` versus `prototype`?
blocks.text: `prototype` is a property of a constructor function or class: the object that becomes the prototype of instances it creates. `__proto__` (better read with `Object.getPrototypeOf`) is an instance's actual link to that object.

blocks.title: Debounce versus throttle?
blocks.text: Debounce waits until calls have stopped for a period and then runs once. Throttle runs at most once per period while calls keep coming.

blocks.title: What is memoization?
blocks.text: Caching a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same input skip the computation. It requires a pure function.
Objects (`{}`) are key-value records and arrays (`[]`) are ordered lists. JSON is this same syntax written as text, which is why JavaScript handles API data so naturally.

Three tools are used constantly: **destructuring** pulls fields out into variables, **spread** (`...`) copies and merges, and the array methods `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find` and `some` replace most loops.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `map` / `filter` / `reduce` are the same as in Swift and Dart. Spread `{ ...order, status: "packed" }` is `copyWith`. Objects are reference types like Dart `Map` and Swift classes: assigning one does not copy it.
Does it change the original array?

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A request handler receives a shared configuration object and "just adds a field" to it. Every later request now sees that field, because the object was shared, not copied. Treat inputs as read-only and build new objects with spread. This single habit prevents a class of bugs that only appear under load.
Pitfalls

items: `array.sort()` without a comparator sorts as strings: `[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`.
Spread and `Object.assign` copy one level only. Nested objects are still shared. Use `structuredClone` for a deep copy.
`for...in` on arrays. Use `for...of` or the array methods.
Using a plain object as a map with user-supplied keys. Use `Map`.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: `map` versus `forEach`?
blocks.text: `map` returns a new array of the callback results. `forEach` returns nothing and is only for side effects.

blocks.title: Shallow copy versus deep copy?
blocks.text: A shallow copy duplicates the top level and shares nested objects. A deep copy (`structuredClone`) duplicates everything.

blocks.title: `Map` versus plain object?
blocks.text: `Map` accepts any key type, keeps insertion order, has `size` and has no inherited keys. Plain objects are best for fixed-shape records.

blocks.title: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
blocks.text: `[...new Set(array)]`.
References, freezing, grouping, iterators and JSON traps

Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) are copied when assigned. Objects and arrays are not: a variable holds a **reference**, and two variables can point at the same object. Passing an object to a function passes that reference, so the function can change the caller's data.

`Object.freeze` makes an object read-only: writing to it throws in modules and classes (and is silently ignored in old non-strict scripts). It is only one level deep. Nested objects stay changeable unless you freeze them too.
Any object can be made usable in `for...of` and spread by implementing `[Symbol.iterator]`. A generator method is the short way to write it.
`JSON.stringify` silently changes data. `undefined` and functions vanish, `NaN` becomes `null`, a `Date` becomes a string and never comes back as a `Date`, and a `Map` becomes `{}`.
Two variables, one object

rows: `const first = { qty: 1 }` creates an object and stores a reference to it.
`const second = first` copies the reference, not the object.
`second.qty++` changes the one object. Both variables see it.
`{ ...first }` would create a second object with the same top-level fields.

blocks.text: What survives `JSON.stringify` then `JSON.parse`

rows: A plain object: methods are gone

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Are objects passed by value or by reference?
blocks.text: The reference is passed by value. The function gets a copy of the reference, so it can mutate the object but reassigning its parameter does not affect the caller.

blocks.title: Is `Object.freeze` deep?
blocks.text: No. It prevents changes to the object's own properties only. Nested objects must be frozen separately.

blocks.title: What makes an object iterable?
blocks.text: A `[Symbol.iterator]` method that returns an iterator: an object with `next()` returning `{ value, done }`. Generators implement it for you.

blocks.title: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` versus `structuredClone(x)`?
blocks.text: The JSON trick loses dates, maps, sets and `undefined`, and fails on BigInt and cycles. `structuredClone` preserves those types and handles cycles, but cannot clone functions.

blocks.title: Why does `["b", "a", "C"].sort()` put "C" first?
blocks.text: The default sort compares UTF-16 code units, where capital letters come before lowercase. Pass a comparator such as `localeCompare`.
Each file is a module with its own scope. `export` makes something available and `import` brings it in. This standard system is called **ES modules (ESM)**.
Node also has an older system, **CommonJS**, which uses `require()` and `module.exports`. You will meet both. New projects should use ESM by setting `"type": "module"` in `package.json`.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A named export is a public top-level declaration in Swift or Dart. `import { fee } from "./pricing.js"` is `import 'pricing.dart' show fee;`. A default export is one unnamed main thing per file.
ESM versus CommonJS

rows: Synchronous, at the line that calls it

nodes.label: Look in node_modules, walking up folders

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Leaving the `.js` extension off a relative import in ESM.
Using `__dirname` or `require` in an ES module.
Circular imports between two files, which leave one side `undefined` at load time.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What are the differences between ESM and CommonJS?
blocks.text: ESM uses `import` / `export`, loads asynchronously, supports top-level `await` and is the language standard. CommonJS uses `require`, loads synchronously and is Node's original system.

blocks.title: Is a module run every time it is imported?
blocks.text: No. It runs once, the first time, and the result is cached. Later imports get the same instance.

blocks.title: Named versus default export?
blocks.text: A file can have many named exports imported by their exact names, and at most one default export imported under any name you choose.
Module instances, live bindings, cycles and package entry points

A module is evaluated **once per process**, the first time it is imported. Every other import receives the same instance. That is why a module that exports a database pool or a counter behaves as a singleton, and also why module-level state is shared by every request.

ES module exports are **live bindings**. An importer does not get a copy of the value. It sees the exporter's variable, including later changes. CommonJS, in contrast, hands over a snapshot of `module.exports`.

**Circular imports** are legal, but one of the two modules is evaluated first and sees the other's exports before they are initialised. Reading one at the top level throws. The fix is to move the shared piece into a third module.
A package decides what can be imported from it through the `exports` field of its `package.json`.

blocks.caption: A package's public surface

blocks.text: Why the circular import fails

rows: `x.mjs` is imported. Before running it, Node loads its dependency `y.mjs`.
`y.mjs` imports `x.mjs`, which is already being loaded, so Node does not start it again. `y.mjs` runs first.
`y.mjs` reads `x` at its top level. `x.mjs` has not run yet, so `x` is in its dead zone.
Had `y.mjs` only used `x` inside a function called later, it would have worked. Top-level use across a cycle is the problem.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How many times is a module evaluated?
blocks.text: Once per process for a given resolved URL. Later imports reuse the cached module instance and its state.

blocks.title: What are live bindings?
blocks.text: ES module imports refer to the exporting module's variables, not to copies. If the exporter reassigns an exported `let`, importers see the new value.

blocks.title: Why are circular dependencies a problem?
blocks.text: One module in the cycle is evaluated before the other has finished, so it may see uninitialised exports. Top-level use then throws in ESM or yields `undefined` in CommonJS.

blocks.title: Can ESM import CommonJS and the reverse?
blocks.text: ESM can import a CommonJS module, receiving `module.exports` as the default export. CommonJS can load ESM with dynamic `import()`, and recent Node versions also allow `require()` of ES modules that have no top-level await.

blocks.title: What does the `exports` field in `package.json` do?
blocks.text: It defines the package's entry points and blocks imports of any other internal file. It can map different files for `import`, `require` and types.
TypeScript is JavaScript with types added. A tool called `tsc` checks the types and then removes them, leaving plain JavaScript. Nothing typed exists at run time.
Almost every professional Node backend is written in TypeScript. It catches the mistakes JavaScript lets through: a misspelled field, a missing `await`, a value that might be `undefined`.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: This will feel like home. `interface` is a protocol or abstract class for data shapes. `string | undefined` is `String?`. Union types with a `kind` field are Swift enums with associated values or Dart sealed classes, and `switch` over them is exhaustively checked.

blocks.code:
npm install -D typescript @types/node tsx
npx tsc --init --strict
npx tsx watch src/server.ts      # run TypeScript directly while developing
npx tsc --noEmit                 # type-check only, used in CI

nodes.label: Data from outside must be validated (Zod)

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Trusting `as T` or `any` on data from a request or an API. A type is a claim, not a check. Validate with a schema at the boundary.
Turning off `strict`. Most of TypeScript's value comes from strict null checks.
Writing types for everything by hand. Let the compiler infer local variables and annotate function boundaries.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Does TypeScript check types at run time?
blocks.text: No. Types are removed during compilation. Run-time safety for external data needs a validation library.

blocks.title: `interface` versus `type`?
blocks.text: Both describe object shapes. `interface` can be extended and merged, `type` can also express unions, tuples and mapped types. Use either consistently.

blocks.title: `any` versus `unknown`?
blocks.text: `any` switches type checking off for that value. `unknown` forces you to narrow it (check its type) before using it, so it is the safe choice for external data.

blocks.title: What is a discriminated union?
blocks.text: A union of object types that share a literal field such as `kind`. Checking that field narrows the type, and the compiler can verify every case is handled.
Generics, narrowing and types built from other types
Three ideas take you from writing interfaces to using TypeScript well.
**Generics** let a function or type work with many types while keeping the link between input and output. A constraint (`T extends { id: number }`) says what the type must at least have.

**Narrowing** is the compiler following your checks. After `if (!result.ok) return`, it knows `result` is the success shape. A **type guard** is a function that performs such a check for a value of unknown origin. Assigning to `never` in a `default` branch makes the compiler prove you handled every case.

**Types from types**: `keyof` gives the union of an object type's keys, mapped types transform every property, and conditional types choose a type by a test. Most utility types (`Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `ReturnType`) are built from these.

blocks.caption: Compiled with `tsc --strict`

blocks.text: Utility types you will use weekly

rows: Object with keys K and values V
The type a promise resolves to

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a generic?
blocks.text: A type parameter that lets a function, class or type work over many types while preserving the relationship between its inputs and outputs.

blocks.title: What is type narrowing?
blocks.text: The compiler refining a variable's type inside a branch based on a check such as `typeof`, `in`, equality on a literal field or a type guard.

blocks.title: What is a type guard?
blocks.text: A function whose return type is `value is T`. When it returns true the compiler treats the argument as `T` in that branch.

blocks.title: How do you make a `switch` exhaustive?
blocks.text: In the `default` branch assign the value to a variable of type `never`. If a case is missing the assignment does not compile.

blocks.title: What does `satisfies` do?
blocks.text: It checks that a value conforms to a type without widening the value's own inferred type, so literal keys and values stay precise.

blocks.title: `unknown` versus `never`?
blocks.text: `unknown` is the type of any value you have not checked yet. `never` is the type with no values, for code that cannot be reached or functions that never return.

modules.title: Node.js: Stage 2 · Async core
modules.summary: The model that makes Node, Node

blocks.text: In Node, slow operations do not make your code wait. You start the operation and say what should happen when it finishes. There have been three ways to say that.

A **callback** is a function you hand over to be called later. A **promise** is an object that stands for a result that will arrive later. **async / await** is syntax that lets promise code read top to bottom like ordinary code. Write new code with async / await, and understand the other two because libraries and old code use them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A callback is "call this number when it is ready". A promise is the token you get at a food counter: you hold it, and it turns into food or an apology. `await` is standing aside until your token is called while the counter serves others.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A `Promise` is a Dart `Future` and behaves like a Swift `Task` value. `Promise.all` is `Future.wait` or `async let`. `try / catch` around `await` works the same in all three.
What `await` does to a function

rows: `productPage()` is called and runs synchronously until the first `await`.
At `await wait(100)` the function is paused and removed from the stack. Its state is saved.
The timer fires. The promise resolves and the rest of the function is queued as a microtask.
The function resumes on the stack with the value 62 and runs to the next `await`.

blocks.text: Combining promises

rows: All succeed (fails fast on the first error)
A page that can show partial data

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A missing `await`. The function carries on with a promise instead of a value, and errors vanish.
`await` inside a `for` loop when the calls are independent. Use `Promise.all` with `map`.
`array.forEach(async ...)`. `forEach` does not wait for the promises. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all`.
An unhandled rejection. In current Node it crashes the process.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is a promise?
blocks.text: An object representing a value that will be available later. It is pending, then either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error, and never changes after that.

blocks.title: What is callback hell and how was it solved?
blocks.text: Deeply nested callbacks that are hard to read and to handle errors in. Promises flattened the nesting with chaining, and async / await made it read like sequential code.

blocks.title: `Promise.all` versus `Promise.allSettled`?
blocks.text: `all` rejects as soon as one promise rejects. `allSettled` waits for every promise and reports each outcome.

blocks.title: Does `await` block the thread?
blocks.text: No. It pauses only that function. The event loop keeps running other callbacks until the awaited promise settles.
Cancellation, limits, retries and async iteration
Four patterns turn basic `await` into production code.

**Cancellation** uses `AbortController`. You pass its `signal` into an operation and call `abort()` to stop it. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives a signal that aborts by itself, which is the standard way to put a deadline on `fetch`.
**Concurrency limits** matter because `Promise.all` over 10,000 items starts 10,000 operations at once. A small worker loop keeps only N running.
**Retries** should back off exponentially and add random jitter, so that many clients do not retry in step and knock a recovering service over again. Retry only errors that can succeed later.
**Async iteration** with `for await` consumes data that arrives in pages or chunks, one piece at a time.
Retries with backoff and jitter

rows: Attempt 1 fails with a 503. The error is marked retryable.
Attempt 2 fails. The maximum wait doubles.
Attempt 3 succeeds. The result is returned and no more delay is spent.
Had it kept failing, attempt 4 would be the last and its error would be thrown to the caller.

blocks.text: Which errors to retry

rows: 401 and 403: retrying will not grant access
404, 409: the state will not change by waiting
A POST without an idempotency key

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you cancel an async operation in Node?
blocks.text: Pass an `AbortSignal` from an `AbortController` to the operation and call `abort()`. Operations that support signals, such as `fetch`, timers and streams, reject with an abort error.

blocks.title: How do you add a timeout to `fetch`?
blocks.text: Pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`. The request is aborted and the promise rejects with a `TimeoutError` when the time is up.

blocks.title: How do you limit concurrency over a large array?
blocks.text: Run a fixed number of worker loops that each take the next item until none remain, or use a library such as `p-limit`.

blocks.title: Why add jitter to retry delays?
blocks.text: Without it, clients that failed together retry together and create repeated spikes. Randomising the delay spreads them out.

blocks.title: What is an async iterator?
blocks.text: An object whose `next()` returns a promise. `for await` consumes it. Async generators, streams and paginated API clients produce them.

Node runs your JavaScript on **one thread**. The **event loop** is the cycle that decides what that thread does next. It picks a callback, runs it to completion, picks the next one and so on, forever.

Slow I/O does not happen on that thread. Network work is handed to the operating system, and file and crypto work goes to a small thread pool. When the work finishes, its callback is put in a queue and the loop runs it when the thread is free.
One rule follows from this and explains most Node performance bugs: **never do long CPU work on the main thread**, because nothing else can run until it finishes.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: One chef, many timers. The chef starts ten dishes, sets timers and works on whichever timer rings. It works beautifully until the chef decides to peel 500 potatoes by hand. Every dish burns while that happens.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: This is the Dart event loop with its microtask queue and event queue, and the idea behind the main run loop in iOS. "Do not block the main thread" is the same rule, except here the main thread serves every user, not one screen.
Follow the code above through the queues

rows: Synchronous code runs. `setTimeout` registers a timer, the promise queues a microtask, `readFile` hands work to the thread pool.
The script ends. Before anything else, the microtask queue is emptied.
The loop enters the timers phase and runs the expired timer.
The file read finishes. In the poll phase its callback runs and schedules three things.
Microtasks run immediately after that callback.
Next is the check phase, so `setImmediate` runs before the new timer.
A, B, C, D, E, F
A new round begins. The timers phase runs G. Nothing is left, so the process exits.
A, B, C, D, E, F, G

File system, DNS lookup, crypto, zlib
libuv thread pool (4 threads by default)

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: An endpoint builds a 50 MB report with a synchronous loop that takes 3 seconds. For those 3 seconds the server answers nobody: health checks time out, the load balancer marks the instance dead and other users see errors. The fix is to stream the report in pieces, move the work to a worker thread, or make it a background job.
Pitfalls

items: Synchronous APIs in request handlers: `readFileSync`, `JSON.parse` on huge strings, big loops, synchronous crypto.
Believing `async` makes CPU work non-blocking. `async` only helps with waiting.
A promise chain that keeps queuing microtasks forever. It starves timers and I/O.
Expecting `setTimeout(fn, 0)` to run immediately. It runs after the current code, all microtasks, and when the timers phase comes round.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does Node handle many requests on one thread?
blocks.text: The thread only runs short callbacks. Waiting on the network, disk and databases happens outside it. When an operation completes, its callback is queued and run. So the thread is rarely idle and rarely busy for long.

blocks.title: Microtask versus macrotask?
blocks.text: Microtasks (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`) run right after the current callback, before the loop moves on. Macrotasks (timers, I/O, `setImmediate`) run one per turn in their loop phase.

blocks.title: `setImmediate` versus `setTimeout(fn, 0)` versus `process.nextTick`?
blocks.text: `nextTick` runs before any other queued work, right after the current operation. `setTimeout 0` runs in the next timers phase. `setImmediate` runs in the check phase, right after I/O callbacks.

blocks.title: What blocks the event loop?
blocks.text: Any long synchronous work: heavy computation, synchronous file or crypto calls, parsing very large JSON, catastrophic regular expressions.

blocks.title: What is the libuv thread pool used for?
blocks.text: Operations without a non-blocking OS interface: file system calls, DNS lookups via `getaddrinfo`, and CPU-heavy built-ins such as `crypto.scrypt` and `zlib`. Its size defaults to 4 and is set with `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`.
The thread pool, starvation and yielding

The libuv **thread pool** has four threads by default. File system calls, DNS lookups through `dns.lookup`, and CPU-heavy built-ins such as `crypto.pbkdf2`, `crypto.scrypt` and `zlib` all share those four. If four slow hashes are running, the fifth waits, and so does an unrelated file read. Network sockets do not use the pool.

**Microtask starvation** is the opposite problem. The microtask queue is emptied completely before the loop moves on. Code that keeps queuing microtasks, such as a promise chain that never waits on real I/O, stops timers and network callbacks from running.
When a long calculation must stay on the main thread, split it into chunks and **yield** between them with `setImmediate`, so pending I/O callbacks get a turn.

One more detail for interviews: in CommonJS files `process.nextTick` callbacks run before promise callbacks. In ES modules the top-level code is itself running inside a promise job, so there the promise callbacks come first.
Six hashes, four threads

rows: Six `pbkdf2` calls are made. Four start at once on the pool's four threads. Two wait in the pool's queue.
The main thread is not blocked. It could serve network requests now. But any file read would queue behind hashes 5 and 6.
hash 5, hash 6, (a file read would wait here)
The first four finish at about the same time. Their callbacks are queued for the main thread.
The last two finish one round later, which is the second group of timestamps in the output.

blocks.text: What runs where

rows: Yes, for as long as it runs
No, but they queue behind each other

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How big is the libuv thread pool and how do you change it?
blocks.text: Four threads by default. Set the `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` environment variable before the process starts, up to 1024.

blocks.title: Which operations use the thread pool?
blocks.text: File system operations, `dns.lookup`, and CPU-intensive built-ins in `crypto` and `zlib`. Network I/O does not.

blocks.title: What is microtask starvation?
blocks.text: Continuously queuing microtasks so the queue never empties. The loop cannot advance to timers or I/O, and the process appears frozen even though each callback is short.

blocks.title: How do you keep the loop responsive during a long calculation?
blocks.text: Move it to a worker thread or job queue. If it must stay on the main thread, process it in chunks and yield with `setImmediate` between chunks.

blocks.title: Does `process.nextTick` run before promise callbacks?
blocks.text: In CommonJS, yes: the nextTick queue is drained first. In ES modules, top-level code runs inside a promise job, so already-queued promise callbacks run before nextTick callbacks.

Errors in Node come in two kinds. **Operational errors** are expected failures of a correct program: a timeout, invalid input, a missing record. Handle them and give a useful response. **Programmer errors** are bugs: reading a property of `undefined`, a wrong argument. Do not try to recover from them. Log, let the process restart, and fix the code.
With async / await, `try / catch` handles both synchronous throws and rejected promises, provided every promise is awaited.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Same model as Swift `do / catch` and Dart `try / catch`. The difference is that nothing forces you to handle a failure. A forgotten `await` is like an unobserved `Task` whose error crashes the app later.

diagram.title: Where an error ends up in a web app

nodes.label: Handler throws or a promise rejects

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: An empty `catch {}`. The failure still happened and now nobody knows.
Throwing strings or plain objects. Throw `Error` instances so there is a stack trace.
Sending `err.message` or the stack to clients. It leaks internals. Send a stable code and a safe message.
Trying to keep a process alive after an unknown exception. Its state may be corrupt. Exit and restart.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Operational versus programmer errors?
blocks.text: Operational errors are expected run-time failures such as timeouts and bad input, which you handle. Programmer errors are bugs, which you fix. Do not write recovery code for bugs.

blocks.title: What happens on an unhandled promise rejection?
blocks.text: Current Node versions print the error and terminate the process with a non-zero exit code.

blocks.title: Why add a `cause` to an error?
blocks.text: It keeps the original low-level error attached to the higher-level one, so logs show the full chain without losing the meaningful message.

blocks.title: How do you handle errors in async Express handlers?
blocks.text: Express 5 forwards a rejected promise from a handler to the error middleware. In Express 4 you must catch and call `next(err)` or use a wrapper.
Where errors escape, and returning results instead of throwing
`try / catch` only catches what happens **while the `try` block is on the call stack**, including promises you `await` inside it. Three kinds of failure get away.

A callback that runs later, such as a timer or an event handler, throws when the `try` block is long gone. That becomes an **uncaught exception**. A promise that rejects without being awaited or given a `.catch` becomes an **unhandled rejection**. An `EventEmitter` that emits `error` with no listener throws on the spot. All three end the process by default.

For failures that are an expected part of normal operation, such as validation, many codebases **return a result object** instead of throwing: `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, error }`. The caller must look at `ok`, and TypeScript enforces that it does.

diagram.title: Does this error reach my catch block?

nodes.label: Rejected promise that is awaited inside try
Thrown in a timer or event callback

blocks.text: Throw or return a result

rows: Invalid user input, "not found", business rule refused
Return a result, or throw a typed `AppError` handled centrally
Deep call chain where only the top can respond
Avoids passing results through every layer

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why does `try / catch` not catch an error thrown in a `setTimeout` callback?
blocks.text: The callback runs in a later turn of the event loop, after the `try` block has finished. There is no enclosing frame left to catch it.

blocks.title: What causes an unhandled rejection?
blocks.text: A promise rejects and has no rejection handler attached: usually a missing `await` or `.catch`. Node terminates the process by default.

blocks.title: What should an `uncaughtException` handler do?
blocks.text: Log the error, perhaps flush logs and metrics, and exit. The process state is unknown, so it should not keep serving requests.

blocks.title: What is the result pattern?
blocks.text: Returning an object that says whether the operation succeeded, with either the value or an error, instead of throwing. It makes failure part of the function's type.

blocks.title: What is `AggregateError`?
blocks.text: An error holding several errors in its `errors` array. `Promise.any` rejects with it when every promise fails.

Much of Node is built on one pattern: an object **emits** named events and other code **listens** for them. Servers emit `request`, streams emit `data` and `end`, processes emit `exit`. `EventEmitter` is the class behind it, and you can use it for your own events.
It decouples parts of a program: the code that places an order does not need to know who cares about it.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: It is `NotificationCenter` in iOS or a broadcast `StreamController` in Dart: named events, many listeners, synchronous delivery in registration order.

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: Inside one process an emitter is fine for decoupling. Across several servers it is not enough, because the event only exists in the memory of one instance. Then the same idea moves to a message broker such as Redis pub/sub, RabbitMQ or Kafka. The pattern is identical and the transport changes.
Pitfalls

items: Emitting `error` with no listener. Node throws and the process crashes.
Adding a listener per request and never removing it. Memory grows and Node warns about a possible leak after 10 listeners.
Assuming listeners run asynchronously. `emit` calls them one by one before returning.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is EventEmitter?
blocks.text: A class that lets objects publish named events and lets other code subscribe with `on`, `once` and `off`. Many core APIs extend it.

blocks.title: Are listeners called synchronously?
blocks.text: Yes, in the order they were registered, during the `emit` call.

blocks.title: How do emitters cause memory leaks?
blocks.text: Listeners hold references to their closures. Registering them repeatedly on a long-lived emitter without removing them keeps all of that alive.
A **stream** handles data piece by piece instead of loading all of it. A **buffer** is a chunk of raw bytes. Files, HTTP requests and responses, compression and encryption are all streams in Node.
The benefit is constant memory. A 5 GB file can be read, compressed and sent to a client using a few megabytes of RAM.
**Backpressure** is what happens when the receiver is slower than the sender. A correct pipeline makes the sender pause until the receiver catches up. `pipeline()` does that for you.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Water through pipes instead of buckets. With buckets you need one big enough for the whole lake. With pipes the flow matters, not the size. Backpressure is the tap closing when the sink is full.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Readable streams are `AsyncSequence` in Swift and `Stream` in Dart, and you can loop over them with `for await`. A transform stream is a `map` over that sequence. `Buffer` is `Data` / `Uint8List`.
Backpressure in a pipeline

rows: The source produces chunks faster than the disk can write them.
The writable's internal buffer passes its limit (`highWaterMark`). `write()` returns false.
`pipeline` pauses the source. Memory stops growing.
The disk catches up and the writable emits `drain`.
The source resumes. This cycle repeats for the whole transfer.

blocks.text: The four stream types
Pitfalls

items: `readFile` on a large file inside a request handler. Memory spikes by the file size for every concurrent request.
Chaining `.pipe()` without error handling. If one stream fails the others are left open. Use `pipeline`.
Ignoring the return value of `write()` in a manual loop, which removes backpressure and fills memory.
Using `string.length` for byte size. Use `Buffer.byteLength`.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use streams?
blocks.text: To process data larger than memory, to start sending output before all input has arrived, and to compose steps such as read, compress and send.

blocks.title: What is backpressure?
blocks.text: A signal from a slow consumer that tells the producer to pause, so data does not pile up in memory. In Node it is `write()` returning false followed by a `drain` event.

blocks.title: `pipe` versus `pipeline`?
blocks.text: `pipe` connects streams but does not forward errors or clean up. `pipeline` connects them, propagates errors, destroys all streams on failure and returns a promise.

blocks.title: What is a Buffer?
blocks.text: A fixed-length sequence of raw bytes outside the normal string type, used for binary data and for text in a specific encoding.
Backpressure by hand, and writing your own streams

`pipeline` hides the mechanism, so here it is in the open. A writable stream has an internal buffer with a limit called `highWaterMark`. `write()` returns `false` when the buffer is at or over that limit. That is the signal to stop writing and wait for the `drain` event. Ignoring it still works for small data, and for large data it grows the buffer until the process runs out of memory.

You can create your own streams by implementing one method: `read()` for a source, `write()` for a destination, `transform()` for a step in between. A readable created from an async generator is usually the simplest source. Calling `done()` in a writable is what tells Node you are ready for the next chunk, so a slow destination naturally slows the whole chain.
`write()` returning false

rows: The buffer limit is 4. Three rows are waiting to be written to the slow disk.
A fourth row arrives and the buffer reaches its limit.
A careful producer waits for `drain`. A careless one keeps writing and the buffer grows without limit.
The disk catches up, the buffer empties and `drain` is emitted.

blocks.text: Stream events and methods to recognise
Check yourself

blocks.title: What does it mean when `write()` returns false?
blocks.text: The writable's buffer has reached `highWaterMark`. The producer should stop writing and continue after the `drain` event.

blocks.title: What is `highWaterMark`?
blocks.text: The buffer size threshold of a stream: bytes for binary streams (16 KB by default for most) or a number of objects in object mode. It controls when backpressure starts.

blocks.title: What is object mode?
blocks.text: A stream setting where each chunk is any JavaScript value instead of a Buffer or string, used for rows and records.

blocks.title: Flowing versus paused mode in a readable?
blocks.text: In paused mode data is delivered only when the consumer asks with `read()`. Attaching a `data` handler or piping switches to flowing mode, where chunks are pushed as they arrive.
