modules.summary: From a socket to a tested API

lessons.title: An HTTP server with no framework

blocks.text: Node has a web server built in. `createServer` takes one function, and Node calls it for every request with two objects: `req` (what came in) and `res` (what you send back). Both are streams.

You will use a framework for real projects. Writing one server by hand first shows you exactly what a framework does: match the method and path, read and parse the body, set the status and headers, and handle errors.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `req` is the `URLRequest` you used to build on the client, seen from the receiving end. `res.writeHead(status, headers)` and `res.end(body)` build the `HTTPURLResponse` and data your app receives.
One POST request through raw Node

rows: A TCP connection opens. Node parses the request line and headers and calls your function.
The body arrives in chunks. You collect them.
method, path, headers, raw body text
You parse the JSON yourself and handle the failure case.
You write the status line and headers, then the body, then end the response.

diagram.title: What a framework adds on top

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: No limit on body size. A client can send gigabytes and exhaust memory. Frameworks cap it, and you must too.
Forgetting to end the response. The client waits until it times out.
Writing headers after the body has started.
Listening on `localhost` inside a container. Bind to `0.0.0.0` so the port is reachable.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What are `req` and `res`?
blocks.text: `req` is an `IncomingMessage`, a readable stream with the method, URL and headers. `res` is a `ServerResponse`, a writable stream you use to send the status, headers and body.

blocks.title: Why is the request body not just a property?
blocks.text: It arrives over the network in pieces and may be large, so Node exposes it as a stream you read or pipe.

blocks.title: What does a web framework do for you?
blocks.text: Routing, body parsing with limits, middleware, error handling and response helpers, on top of the same `http` module.

Express is the most widely used Node web framework. An Express app is a **chain of middleware**. A middleware is a function `(req, res, next)`. It can read or change the request, send a response, or call `next()` to pass control to the next function in the chain.
Logging, authentication, body parsing, routes and error handling are all middleware. Their **order** is the design of your app.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Airport security lanes. Each station checks one thing and either waves you on to the next or turns you back. The order of stations matters: you show your ticket before the bag scan, not after boarding.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Middleware is a Dio interceptor chain or `URLProtocol` stack on the server side. `requireUser` below is the server half of the auth interceptor you have written on the client.
A request walking the middleware chain

rows: `GET /orders/1` with user 8 arrives. The JSON parser has nothing to parse and calls `next()`.
The logger notes the start time, registers a `finish` listener and calls `next()`.
The path starts with `/orders`, so `requireUser` runs. The header is present. It sets `req.userId = 8`.
The router matches `GET /:id`. The order belongs to user 7, not 8.
The response is sent. Later middleware never runs. The logger's `finish` listener prints the line.

blocks.text: Express, Fastify, NestJS

rows: Small to medium APIs, most tutorials and existing code
Fast, schema-based validation and serialisation built in
Performance matters, you want structure without a full framework
Full framework: modules, dependency injection, decorators, TypeScript first
Large teams and codebases that need enforced structure

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Registering the error handler before the routes. It must come last.
Forgetting `next()` or a response in a middleware. The request hangs.
Sending two responses (`res.json` twice) because of a missing `return`.
Returning 403 for someone else's order. It confirms the order exists. Return 404.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is middleware?
blocks.text: A function with access to the request, the response and `next`. It runs in registration order and either ends the request or passes it on.

blocks.title: How does Express recognise error middleware?
blocks.text: By its four parameters `(err, req, res, next)`. It is called when a handler throws, rejects (Express 5) or calls `next(err)`.

blocks.title: `app.use` versus `app.get`?
blocks.text: `app.use` runs for every method and for any path starting with its prefix. `app.get` runs only for GET requests matching the exact route pattern.

blocks.title: How do you structure routes in a larger app?
blocks.text: One `express.Router()` per resource in its own file, mounted under a prefix, with handlers calling service functions that hold the business rules.
Middleware is a 25-line idea

Express feels like a large framework, but its core is small. An app is an array of functions. Handling a request means calling the first one with a `next` function that calls the second, and so on. Calling `next(err)` skips forward to the first function that takes four arguments. Writing this once removes the mystery from every Node framework, because Koa, Fastify hooks and NestJS interceptors are variations of the same loop.
The onion: code before and after `next()`

rows: The timing middleware runs first and records the start time. It awaits `next()`.
Auth runs, sets the user and calls `next()`.
The route handler sets the response and returns.
Control unwinds. Auth's call to `next()` resolves, then timing's does.
Timing computes the duration after everything inside it has finished.

blocks.text: Request lifecycle in a real Express app

rows: Request id, logging, security headers, CORS, body parsing, rate limit
Calls a service, sends the response

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does `next()` work internally?
blocks.text: The framework keeps an index into its middleware list. `next()` advances the index and calls the next function, passing itself along. `next(err)` skips to the next error handler.

blocks.title: Why is middleware order important?
blocks.text: Each middleware only affects what comes after it. A body parser must precede handlers that read the body, and the error handler must be last.

blocks.title: What is the onion model?
blocks.text: Each middleware can run code before and after the rest of the chain by awaiting `next()`, so the request passes inward through the layers and the response passes back out.

blocks.title: How would you add a request id to every log line?
blocks.text: A first middleware creates or reads the id, stores it in `AsyncLocalStorage` and on the response header. The logger reads it from the store.

TypeScript types vanish at run time, so a request body typed as `Order` could contain anything. **Zod** closes that gap. You write one schema. It validates and converts real data at run time, and TypeScript derives the static type from the same schema, so the two can never disagree.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Zod is to Node what Pydantic is to Python, and what `Codable` with validation would be in Swift: declare the shape once, get parsing, conversion and a typed result or a list of errors.

nodes.label: z.infer gives the TypeScript type (compile time)
Typed, cleaned data reaches the handler

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Validating the body but not `req.params` and `req.query`. They are user input too and always strings.
Writing a TypeScript interface and a separate hand-made validator that drift apart.
Using `.parse` (throws) in a handler without a catch. Use `.safeParse`, or let central error middleware map the error to 422.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is TypeScript not enough to validate requests?
blocks.text: Types are erased when the code is compiled. At run time the body is whatever the client sent.

blocks.title: What does `z.infer` do?
blocks.text: It derives the TypeScript type from a schema, so the static type and the run-time check share one source.

blocks.title: `parse` versus `safeParse`?
blocks.text: `parse` returns the data or throws. `safeParse` returns an object with `success` and either `data` or `error`, with no exception.
Node talks to PostgreSQL through a driver (`pg`) or through a layer on top of it. A **query builder or ORM** such as Prisma or Drizzle gives you typed queries generated from your schema.
Whatever layer you choose, three things stay the same: use a **connection pool**, pass values as **parameters** and wrap multi-step writes in a **transaction**.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The pool is like a shared `URLSession`: created once for the process and reused by every request. A transaction is `performBatchUpdates` for data: all the changes land together or none do.

blocks.caption: The same read with Prisma

blocks.text: Two customers, one last packet of milk

rows: Stock is 1. Customers A and B both try to buy it in the same millisecond.
A runs `UPDATE ... WHERE available >= 1`. The row is locked and set to 0.
A commits. The lock is released.
B's update re-checks the condition. `0 >= 1` is false, so no row changes.
B's code sees `rowCount === 0`, throws and rolls back. Nobody is oversold.

diagram.title: A query from an async handler

blocks.text: Choosing a data layer

rows: Full control, no type safety on rows
SQL-shaped and typed, some learning curve
Schema file, generated typed client, migrations
Very productive, less control over complex SQL

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: "Read stock, check in JavaScript, then write." Two requests can both read 1 and both write. Put the condition in the `UPDATE` itself, as above.
Using `pool.query` for the steps of a transaction. Each call may use a different connection. Use one client.
Forgetting `client.release()` on an error path. The pool runs dry and every request hangs.
Pool size times number of instances exceeding the database's connection limit.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use a connection pool?
blocks.text: Opening a database connection is slow and the database allows a limited number. A pool keeps a few open and lends them to requests.

blocks.title: How do you prevent overselling under concurrency?
blocks.text: Make the check and the change one atomic statement (`UPDATE ... WHERE available >= qty`) or lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction.

blocks.title: What is SQL injection and how do parameters stop it?
blocks.text: Injection is user input being interpreted as SQL. With parameters the SQL text and the values are sent separately, so a value can never change the query's structure.

blocks.title: ORM versus raw SQL in Node?
blocks.text: An ORM gives typed results, migrations and faster development for ordinary queries. Raw SQL gives full control for complex or performance-critical queries. Teams commonly mix them.
Pool exhaustion, pagination and migrations

The most common production failure with a database in Node is not a slow query. It is an **exhausted pool**. Every instance has a fixed number of connections. A code path that takes a connection and does not give it back on an error leaks one per failure. When all are leaked, every new request waits for a connection that never comes, and the service hangs with no CPU load and no errors.

Two more topics come up constantly. **Pagination** with `OFFSET` gets slower as the page number grows, because the database still reads all skipped rows. **Keyset** (cursor) pagination asks for "rows after this id" and stays fast. **Migrations** are versioned files that change the schema step by step, applied in order by a tool and committed with the code.

blocks.caption: Keyset pagination

blocks.text: A leak draining a pool of three

rows: A request fails validation after taking a connection, on a path with no `release()`.
Two more failures of the same kind over the next hour.
Every following request waits for a connection. CPU is idle, the database is idle, and the API times out.
With `try / finally`, each failure returns its connection and the pool never drains.

blocks.text: Sizing the pool

rows: PostgreSQL allows a limited number of connections (often 100 to 500)
Instances times pool size must stay below it
One query uses one connection for its whole duration
A transaction pins one connection until commit
Keep transactions short, no network calls inside them
More connections than CPU cores on the database rarely helps
Start with about 10 per instance and measure
Many small instances or serverless functions
Put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What happens when a connection pool is exhausted?
blocks.text: New requests wait for a free connection, up to a timeout if one is configured. The service appears to hang without CPU load.

blocks.title: How do you guarantee a connection is released?
blocks.text: Acquire it, then do all work inside `try` and call `release()` in `finally`. Or use a helper that takes a callback and releases for you.

blocks.title: Offset versus keyset pagination?
blocks.text: Offset skips N rows, which the database must still read, so deep pages are slow and rows can shift between pages. Keyset filters by the last seen key using an index, so every page is equally fast and stable.

blocks.title: What is a database migration?
blocks.text: A versioned, ordered change to the schema stored with the code and applied by a tool, so every environment reaches the same schema in the same way.

blocks.title: Why avoid long transactions?
blocks.text: They hold a connection, hold locks that block other writers and delay cleanup of old row versions.

The flow is the same in every language. Verify the user's credentials once, hand back a signed token, then verify that token on every request and load the user from it. In Node the token check lives in a middleware that runs before protected routes.
Password hashing must be slow on purpose and must not block the event loop, so use the asynchronous `scrypt` from the built-in `crypto` module (or `argon2` / `bcrypt` packages).

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: You have written the client half: store tokens securely, attach `Authorization: Bearer`, refresh on 401. This lesson is the half that issues and checks them.

nodes.label: Access token 15 min + refresh token 30 days
New access token (and a rotated refresh token)

blocks.text: Where to keep tokens
Pitfalls

items: Not pinning `algorithms` in `verify`. Accepting whatever the token header says has caused real breaches.
Synchronous hashing (`scryptSync`, `bcrypt.hashSync`) in a handler. It blocks every request for about 100 ms per login.
Storing sessions only in one server's memory, so a second instance does not recognise the user.
Authenticating the user but forgetting to check they own the resource.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does JWT verification work?
blocks.text: The server recomputes the signature over the header and payload with its secret (or public key) and compares. It also checks claims such as `exp`. No database lookup is needed.

blocks.title: Sessions versus JWT?
blocks.text: A session stores state on the server and the client holds an opaque id, so it is easy to revoke. A JWT is self-contained and stateless, so it scales easily but stays valid until it expires unless you add a revocation list.

blocks.title: Why short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens?
blocks.text: A stolen access token is useful for minutes only. The refresh token is used rarely, can be stored more securely and can be revoked.

blocks.title: Why must password hashing be asynchronous in Node?
blocks.text: Hashing is deliberately CPU-heavy. Run synchronously, it would block the event loop for every other request.
Server-side sessions, signed cookies, CSRF and roles

JWTs are one way to stay logged in. The older way, **sessions**, is often the better fit for web apps. The server creates a random session id, stores the session data itself (in Redis or a database) and gives the browser only the id in a cookie. Logging out or banning a user means deleting one record, which takes effect at once. That immediate revocation is exactly what plain JWTs lack.

The cookie is **signed** with a server secret so the server can detect tampering, and marked `HttpOnly` (JavaScript cannot read it), `Secure` (HTTPS only) and `SameSite` (not sent on most cross-site requests).

Because browsers attach cookies automatically, another site can trigger requests that carry your cookie. That is **CSRF**. The defence is `SameSite` plus a secret token that the page must send in a header, which a foreign site cannot read. APIs that authenticate with an `Authorization` header are not exposed to CSRF, since nothing attaches that header automatically.
A cross-site request forgery, blocked

rows: The user is logged in to shop.example. The browser holds its session cookie.
The user opens evil.example, which contains a hidden form that posts to shop.example/refund.
The forged request arrives with a valid cookie but no `x-csrf-token`. The evil page cannot read the token.
With `SameSite=Lax` a modern browser would not even attach the cookie to that cross-site POST. Two layers of defence.

blocks.text: Sessions or JWT

rows: Needs a blocklist or short expiry
Any service with the key can verify

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does session authentication work?
blocks.text: After login the server stores session data under a random id and sends the id in a cookie. Each request presents the cookie and the server looks the session up.

blocks.title: What do `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` do on a cookie?
blocks.text: `HttpOnly` hides it from JavaScript, limiting theft through XSS. `Secure` sends it only over HTTPS. `SameSite` stops it being sent on cross-site requests, limiting CSRF.

blocks.title: What is CSRF and how is it prevented?
blocks.text: A malicious site causes the user's browser to send an authenticated request. Prevent it with `SameSite` cookies and a CSRF token the attacker cannot read, checked on state-changing requests.

blocks.title: What is XSS and why does it matter for tokens?
blocks.text: Injected script running in your page. It can read anything JavaScript can, including tokens in `localStorage`, which is why session cookies should be `HttpOnly`.

blocks.title: When would you choose sessions over JWT?
blocks.text: When you need instant revocation and have one backend or a shared store, typically a browser application.

lessons.title: Structure, config, logging and request context

blocks.text: A maintainable Node service separates three layers: **routes** deal with HTTP, **services** hold business rules and **repositories** talk to the database. Configuration is read from environment variables once at startup and validated, so a missing setting fails the deploy instead of the first request.

Logs are JSON lines with a **request id** on every line, so one request can be followed through the system. `AsyncLocalStorage` carries that id through async calls without passing it as a parameter everywhere.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The layering is the same idea as view, view model or bloc, and repository in a mobile app. `AsyncLocalStorage` is like a Swift task-local value or a Dart `Zone` value: data that follows the async call chain.

blocks.code:
src/
  server.ts            # start listening, graceful shutdown
  app.ts               # build the Express app: middleware + routers
  config.ts            # read and validate process.env once
  routes/orders.ts     # HTTP: parse, call service, respond
  services/orders.ts   # rules: pricing, stock, state changes
  repos/orders.ts      # SQL or ORM calls only
  lib/logger.ts  lib/errors.ts
test/
blocks.caption: Folder layout

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Reading `process.env` all over the codebase. Read it once in `config`.
`console.log` of free text. Use a structured logger (`pino`) with levels, and never log tokens or personal data.
Business rules inside route handlers, where a queue worker or a test cannot reuse them.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why validate configuration at startup?
blocks.text: A missing or malformed setting stops the deploy immediately with a clear message, instead of failing some requests later.

blocks.title: What is AsyncLocalStorage?
blocks.text: A store whose value follows an asynchronous call chain. Code anywhere in that chain can read it, which is how request ids reach log lines without being passed explicitly.

blocks.title: What goes in a route, a service and a repository?
blocks.text: Route: HTTP parsing and response codes. Service: business rules and orchestration. Repository: persistence queries only.

Node has a test runner built in: `node:test` with `node:assert`. Vitest and Jest are popular alternatives with the same shape. `describe` groups tests, `it` defines one and `assert` checks the result.
Test pure business functions directly. Test the HTTP layer by starting the app on a random port and calling it with `fetch`, or with the `supertest` package.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: `describe` / `it` map to `XCTestCase` classes and test methods, or `group` / `test` in Dart. `mock.method` is a spy. Starting the app on port 0 is the API equivalent of pumping a widget in a test harness.

blocks.caption: test/orders.test.js

blocks.code:
node --test                          # runs every *.test.js
node --test --watch                  # rerun on change
node --test --experimental-test-coverage

nodes.label: In production: real notifier and database

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A module that creates its database connection on import. Tests cannot replace it. Pass dependencies into a factory function.
A test that forgets `await`. It passes before the assertion runs.
Tests sharing state in a database without cleanup, so they pass alone and fail together.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Unit versus integration test?
blocks.text: A unit test checks one function or module in isolation with fakes around it. An integration test checks several real parts together, such as a route, the service and a test database.

blocks.title: How do you test code that calls an external service?
blocks.text: Inject the client as a dependency and pass a fake or mock in tests. Verify the real integration separately in a small number of tests against a sandbox.

blocks.title: What is `mock.fn`?
blocks.text: A function that records how it was called, so a test can assert on the number of calls and their arguments.

modules.title: Node.js: Stage 4 · Real-time and scale
modules.summary: Many users, slow work, limited CPU

blocks.text: Real-time means the server sends data without the client asking each time. This is what Node is best known for, because each open connection costs almost nothing while it is idle.
**Server-sent events** are a one-way stream over normal HTTP, good for status updates and AI text. A **WebSocket** is a two-way connection, good for chat and live location.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: On the app side you would use `URLSessionWebSocketTask` or `web_socket_channel`. The server keeps a registry of open sockets grouped by a key such as order id (a "room") and writes to every socket in the room when something happens.

blocks.caption: Live rider location over WebSocket
Order status over server-sent events

blocks.text: Scaling WebSockets past one server

rows: One server. Rider and customer are both connected to it. A message goes straight from one socket to the other.
A second server is added behind the load balancer. The customer reconnects and lands on server 2.
The rider sends a position to server 1. Server 1 has no customer socket for this order. The message would be lost.
rider socket, position update (nowhere to send)
Fix: server 1 publishes the update to a Redis channel named after the order.
Every server subscribes. Server 2 receives it and writes to the customer socket it holds.

blocks.text: Real-time checklist

rows: Verify the token during the connection handshake, and check the user may join that room
Ping every 30 seconds, drop sockets that do not answer
Client retries with backoff, server sends current state first
Cap the per-socket send buffer and drop or disconnect

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A room registry that only exists in one process, with more than one instance running.
No authorisation on joining a room. Anyone could subscribe to any order id.
Never removing closed sockets from the registry, which leaks memory.
Sending every GPS tick. Throttle to what the screen can show, for example one update per second.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: WebSocket versus HTTP?
blocks.text: HTTP is one request and one response. A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that is upgraded to a persistent two-way connection where either side can send at any time.

blocks.title: How do you scale WebSockets horizontally?
blocks.text: Each instance keeps its own connections. A shared pub/sub layer broadcasts events to all instances, and each delivers to the sockets it holds. Sticky sessions help with reconnects but do not replace pub/sub.

blocks.title: When would you choose SSE over WebSocket?
blocks.text: When data only flows from server to client: notifications, progress, status, AI text. SSE is plain HTTP, simpler to proxy, authenticate and reconnect.

blocks.title: Why is Node well suited to this?
blocks.text: Idle connections cost a small amount of memory and no thread each, so one process can hold tens of thousands of them.
Heartbeats, reconnects and authentication on connect

A TCP connection can die without either side being told: a phone enters a tunnel, a proxy drops an idle link. The server would keep a dead socket forever. A **heartbeat** fixes that. The server pings every socket on a timer and terminates any that did not answer the previous ping.

The client's half is **reconnecting**: wait a little, try again, and wait longer after each failure, with random jitter so that ten thousand phones do not all reconnect in the same second after a deploy. After reconnecting, the client must ask for the current state, since it missed every event sent while it was away.

**Authentication** happens once, during the HTTP upgrade request that opens the socket. Check the token there and refuse the upgrade if it is invalid. After that, check on every subscription that this user may see that order.

blocks.caption: Heartbeat and authenticated upgrade with `ws`

blocks.text: A phone loses signal and comes back

rows: The phone is connected and has received events 1 and 2.
The phone enters a lift. No close frame is sent. The server still believes the socket is open.
An event is written to the dead socket. The next heartbeat gets no pong, and the round after that terminates it.
The phone regains signal. Its client retries after a jittered delay and reconnects with its token and `lastEventId=2`.
The server replays everything after event 2, then continues with live events.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why do WebSocket servers need heartbeats?
blocks.text: A connection can break without a close frame. Pings detect sockets that no longer respond so the server can free them and stop sending.

blocks.title: How should a client reconnect?
blocks.text: With exponential backoff and random jitter, capped at a maximum delay, and reset after a successful connection. On reconnect it should request missed events or the current state.

blocks.title: How do you authenticate a WebSocket?
blocks.text: Validate a token during the HTTP upgrade request and reject the upgrade if it fails. Then authorise each room or topic subscription.

blocks.title: How do you avoid losing events during a disconnect?
blocks.text: Give events increasing ids, keep a short history per topic, and have the client send the last id it saw so the server can replay the gap. Otherwise send a full snapshot.

blocks.title: What is the thundering herd problem here?
blocks.text: After a server restart every client reconnects at once and overloads it. Jittered backoff and gradual rollout spread the reconnects.

Keep request handlers fast. Anything slow that the user does not have to wait for becomes a **job**: the handler puts a small message on a queue and answers at once, and a separate **worker** process does the work with retries.
A **cache** stores the result of an expensive read for a short time. In Node both usually sit on Redis, with BullMQ as the queue library.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: The queue is a durable `OperationQueue` / `WorkManager`: work survives a crash and runs on another machine. The cache is a shared `NSCache` with expiry times.

blocks.caption: The same with BullMQ and Redis

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Jobs that are not idempotent. A retried "charge card" job charges twice. Use a job id and check "already done" first.
Putting large payloads in the job. Store ids and load the data in the worker.
Running workers inside the API process. A CPU-heavy job then slows every request.
Unbounded in-memory caches. They become the memory leak. Cap the size or use Redis with expiry.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why move work to a queue?
blocks.text: Faster responses, retries with backoff when a dependency fails, control over concurrency, and the ability to scale workers separately from the API.

blocks.title: What does at-least-once delivery imply?
blocks.text: A job may run more than once, so handlers must be idempotent: running twice has the same effect as running once.

blocks.title: What is a dead-letter queue?
blocks.text: Where jobs go after exhausting their retries, so they can be inspected and replayed instead of being lost or retried forever.

blocks.title: Cache invalidation strategies?
blocks.text: Expiry by time, deleting the key when the underlying data changes, and versioned keys. Choose based on how stale the data is allowed to be.
Single-flight, idempotent consumers and a sliding-window limiter
The same three reliability patterns from the Python track, in JavaScript, because you will be asked to write them.

**Single-flight**: when many requests miss the cache for the same key at once, only the first runs the expensive load. The rest await the same promise. In JavaScript this is short, because a promise can be stored in a `Map` and awaited by any number of callers.
**Idempotent consumer**: a queue delivers at least once, so a job can arrive twice. The consumer records each job id it has finished and skips repeats.
**Sliding-window rate limiter**: allow at most N requests per user in the last M milliseconds, by keeping timestamps and dropping the old ones.
One hundred cache misses, one query

rows: The cache entry for `slots:560103` has just expired. Request 1 arrives and finds nothing in flight.
Request 1 starts the load and stores its promise in the map.
Requests 2 to 100 arrive while it runs. Each finds the promise and awaits it. No new query.
The query returns. The one promise resolves, all 100 requests continue, and the map entry is removed.

blocks.text: Rate limiting algorithms

rows: Simple, but allows a double burst at the boundary
Count requests in the last N seconds
Tokens refill steadily, each request spends one
Queue drained at a fixed rate

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How do you implement single-flight in JavaScript?
blocks.text: Keep a map from key to the in-progress promise. Callers for a key that is already loading return that promise, and the entry is deleted when it settles.

blocks.title: How do you make a queue consumer idempotent?
blocks.text: Give every job a unique id and record completed ids atomically, for example with a unique database constraint or Redis `SET NX`. Skip jobs already recorded.

blocks.title: Where should rate-limit counters live when you have several instances?
blocks.text: In a shared store such as Redis, updated atomically. In-memory counters would allow the limit once per instance.

blocks.title: Fixed window versus sliding window?
blocks.text: A fixed window resets at boundaries, so a client can send a full quota just before and just after the boundary. A sliding window always looks at the most recent period and avoids that.

lessons.title: CPU work: worker threads and cluster

blocks.text: The event loop is one thread. A calculation that takes 200 ms freezes the whole server for 200 ms. Node gives you two ways to use more CPU cores.

**Worker threads** run JavaScript on additional threads inside the same process. Use them to move a heavy calculation off the main thread. **Cluster**, or simply running several copies of the process, puts one event loop on each core to serve more requests.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: A worker thread is a Dart isolate: its own memory and event loop, talking to the main thread through messages that are copied. Swift developers can think of an actor that lives on another thread and only accepts sendable values.
Main thread versus worker

rows: A request needs a heavy calculation. Done on the main thread, the event loop cannot run anything else.
With a worker, the main thread posts a message and is immediately free.
The worker finishes and posts the result back. A callback on the main thread resolves the promise.

nodes.label: Short CPU burst (image resize, PDF, hashing)?
More requests than one core can serve?
More processes: cluster, PM2 or more containers
Nothing needed, the event loop already handles it

blocks.text: Worker threads versus cluster versus child process

rows: Serving more traffic on all cores

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Starting a new worker per request. Starting a thread costs milliseconds and megabytes. Keep a pool.
Sending huge objects through `postMessage`. They are copied. Transfer an `ArrayBuffer` or share memory.
Using worker threads for I/O. It adds overhead and no benefit.
Running cluster inside a container that already has several replicas managed by the platform.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Is Node single-threaded?
blocks.text: Your JavaScript runs on one main thread. Node itself uses more: the libuv thread pool for file and crypto work, and any worker threads you create.

blocks.title: Worker threads versus cluster?
blocks.text: Worker threads add threads within one process for CPU-heavy tasks. Cluster starts several processes that share a port, to use every core for handling requests.

blocks.title: How do threads communicate?
blocks.text: By messages with `postMessage`, which copies data using structured clone. Binary data can be transferred without copying or shared through `SharedArrayBuffer`.

blocks.title: When should work go to a queue instead of a worker thread?
blocks.text: When it is long, must survive restarts, needs retries or should scale independently of the API.
A worker pool, and real shared memory

Creating a thread costs time and memory, so production code keeps a fixed **pool** of workers and feeds them jobs through a queue. That is what libraries such as `piscina` do. The version below is small enough to read in a minute.

Workers normally share nothing. Messages are copied. The exception is `SharedArrayBuffer`: a block of memory several threads can read and write at once. That brings back the classic problem of two threads updating the same number. `Atomics` provides operations that complete as a single indivisible step. This is the same race you saw in the Python GIL lesson, now with real parallel threads.
A pool of two workers and five jobs

rows: Five jobs arrive. Two start immediately. Three wait in the pool's queue.
Worker 2 finishes. Its promise resolves and it takes the next job at once.
The last job is taken. No thread was created or destroyed after startup.

blocks.text: Passing data to a worker

rows: Moves ownership, no copy. The sender loses access
No copy, both sides see changes

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why use a worker pool instead of a worker per task?
blocks.text: Starting a worker costs milliseconds and several megabytes. A pool reuses a fixed number of threads and queues extra work, which bounds CPU and memory use.

blocks.title: How many workers should a pool have?
blocks.text: About the number of CPU cores available to the process, minus one for the main thread. More threads than cores adds switching cost without more throughput.

blocks.title: What is `SharedArrayBuffer`?
blocks.text: A fixed block of memory that can be accessed from several threads at once without copying.

blocks.title: What is `Atomics` for?
blocks.text: Reading and modifying shared memory as indivisible operations, and for waiting and notifying between threads, to avoid races on `SharedArrayBuffer` data.

blocks.title: What is a transferable object?
blocks.text: An object such as an `ArrayBuffer` whose ownership can be moved to another thread without copying. It becomes unusable in the sending thread.

Two numbers describe the health of a Node process. **Event loop delay** is how late callbacks run. If it climbs, something is blocking the loop. **Heap used** is how much memory your objects take. If it climbs steadily under constant load and never comes back down, you have a leak.

V8 frees memory automatically with a garbage collector, but only for objects nothing refers to any more. A leak in JavaScript is always a reference you forgot about: a growing `Map`, an array, a listener, a closure.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Leaks are the same idea as retain cycles and undisposed controllers in mobile apps, except the cause is usually an unbounded cache instead of a cycle. The heap snapshot in Chrome DevTools is Instruments' Allocations or the Dart DevTools memory view.

nodes.label: Follow its "retainers" to the Map, array or listener holding it
Make it async, cache it or move to a worker

blocks.text: Usual suspects

rows: Unbounded `Map` cache, arrays of history, per-request listeners
Synchronous work on the event loop
A slow query, N+1 queries, a slow downstream service
Out of memory on large exports

blocks.code:
node --inspect src/server.js          # then open chrome://inspect for CPU and heap tools
node --cpu-prof src/server.js         # writes a .cpuprofile file
node --max-old-space-size=2048 src/server.js   # raise the heap limit (MB)
npx autocannon -c 100 -d 20 http://localhost:3000/health   # load test
blocks.caption: Tools

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: "Caching" in a module-level object keyed by user or request with no limit.
Raising the heap limit instead of finding the leak. It only delays the crash.
Benchmarking on a laptop with debug logging on and drawing conclusions.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What causes memory leaks in Node?
blocks.text: References that are never released: unbounded caches and maps, global arrays, event listeners that are added and not removed, timers never cleared, and closures capturing large objects.

blocks.title: How do you detect that the event loop is blocked?
blocks.text: Measure event loop delay with `monitorEventLoopDelay` or your metrics library, and take a CPU profile to find the synchronous code responsible.

blocks.title: How does garbage collection work in V8?
blocks.text: New objects go in a small young generation that is collected often and quickly. Survivors move to the old generation, which is collected less often with mark-and-sweep. Only unreachable objects are freed.

blocks.title: How would you load test an API?
blocks.text: Use a tool such as autocannon or k6 against a production-like environment, increase concurrency in steps, and watch p95 latency, error rate, event loop delay, CPU and database connections.
Listener leaks, weak references and reading heap numbers

V8 divides the heap by age. New objects are created in the **young generation**, which is small and collected often and quickly. Objects that survive a couple of collections are moved to the **old generation**, which is large and collected less often. A request's temporary objects die young and cost almost nothing. A leak is something that keeps getting promoted to the old generation and is never released.

The leak you will most often meet in Node is a **listener leak**: code that adds a listener to a long-lived emitter for every request and never removes it. Each listener is a closure that holds its request's data.
A `WeakMap` is the right tool for attaching extra data to objects you do not own. Its keys are held weakly, so an entry disappears when the key object is no longer used anywhere else.
An object's life in the V8 heap

rows: A request creates temporary objects in the young generation.
The response is sent. Nothing refers to them. The next fast collection frees them.
Another request's cart is captured by a listener that is never removed. It survives collections.
Survivors are promoted to the old generation.
This repeats for every request. The old generation grows until the process hits its limit and crashes.

blocks.text: Reading `process.memoryUsage()`

rows: The number your container limit applies to
A steady climb under constant load is a leak
Memory of objects outside the heap, such as Buffers
Large with file or network buffering

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: How does V8's garbage collector work?
blocks.text: It is generational. A fast scavenger collects the small young generation often. Survivors are promoted to the old generation, which is collected by mark-and-sweep with compaction, less often and partly concurrently.

blocks.title: What is a listener leak and how do you prevent it?
blocks.text: Listeners added repeatedly to a long-lived emitter and never removed, each retaining its closure. Remove them with `off` when the request ends, or use `once` for one-shot events. Watch `listenerCount` and the MaxListenersExceededWarning.

blocks.title: `Map` versus `WeakMap`?
blocks.text: A `Map` holds its keys strongly and can be iterated. A `WeakMap` holds object keys weakly, cannot be iterated, and lets entries be collected once the key is unreachable elsewhere.

blocks.title: What is the difference between `rss` and `heapUsed`?
blocks.text: `heapUsed` is JavaScript objects on the V8 heap. `rss` is everything the process holds, including the heap, Buffers, code and thread stacks.

blocks.title: What does the "JavaScript heap out of memory" error mean?
blocks.text: The old generation reached V8's size limit and collection could not free enough. It usually indicates a leak or loading too much data at once. Raising `--max-old-space-size` only helps if the workload legitimately needs more.

Most breaches of Node services come from a short list of mistakes: trusting input, missing authorisation checks, leaked secrets and outdated dependencies. Security is mostly doing the ordinary things every time.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Mobile apps are the untrusted side. Anything the app sends can be forged with a proxy tool, so every rule the app enforces in its UI must be enforced again on the server.
The checklist

rows: Change the id in the URL, read someone else's order
Check ownership in every query: `WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`
User input becomes SQL or a shell command
Negative quantity, 10 MB string, extra `isAdmin: true` field
Zod schemas on body, params and query, with size limits
Environment variables or a secret manager, rotate if leaked
A package three levels down has a known hole
`npm audit`, automated update PRs, lock file
Rate limit per user and IP, lock out, alert
Generic message to the client, details in logs
Huge bodies, slow requests, bad regular expressions
Body limits, timeouts, avoid backtracking-heavy regexes

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A wallet endpoint accepts `{ "amount": -500 }` for a "pay" action because the app's UI never allows negative numbers and nobody validated on the server. The balance goes up instead of down. The fix is one line in a schema (`z.number().int().positive()`), and the lesson is that the UI is not a security control.
Pitfalls

items: Trusting any header or field that says who the user is. Identity comes only from the verified token.
CORS set to allow every origin with credentials on a cookie-based API.
Logging request bodies that contain passwords, OTPs or card data.
Running the container as root.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the most common API vulnerability?
blocks.text: Broken object level authorisation: the user is authenticated, but the server does not check that the requested object belongs to them.

blocks.title: What is mass assignment?
blocks.text: Copying a whole request body onto a database record, which lets a client set fields it should not control, such as a role. Pick allowed fields explicitly.

blocks.title: How do you store secrets?
blocks.text: Outside the code and the image: environment variables injected by the platform or a secret manager, with different values per environment and a rotation process.

blocks.title: What does helmet do?
blocks.text: It sets HTTP response headers with safe defaults, such as a content security policy and no MIME sniffing. They matter mainly for browser clients.
Four attacks you can run on your own machine
Reading about vulnerabilities is not the same as seeing one work. Each demo below is safe and local.

**Prototype pollution**: a recursive merge copies a key named `__proto__` from JSON input and ends up writing onto `Object.prototype`. Every object in the process then has the attacker's property. This has turned "update my profile" endpoints into privilege escalation.

**Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS)**: some patterns take exponential time on certain inputs. Since a regex runs on the main thread, one request can freeze the server for seconds or minutes.
**Path traversal**: a file name such as `../../etc/passwd` escapes the folder you meant to serve.
**Command injection**: building a shell command from user input lets the user append their own commands. Pass arguments as an array so they are never interpreted by a shell.
How `__proto__` in JSON reaches every object

rows: The request body is parsed. `JSON.parse` creates an ordinary own property literally named `__proto__`.
The merge loop reaches the key `__proto__`. Reading `target["__proto__"]` returns the real `Object.prototype`.
The loop recurses into it and assigns `isAdmin = true`.
Every object in the process now inherits it. A later check `if (user.isAdmin)` passes for everyone.

blocks.text: Defences

rows: Validate with a schema that drops unknown keys, skip `__proto__` / `constructor` / `prototype`, use `Map` or `Object.create(null)` for dictionaries
Avoid nested quantifiers, limit input length before matching, use a linear-time engine (`re2`) for user-supplied patterns
Resolve the path and verify it stays inside the root, or map ids to stored file names
`execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array, never `exec` with interpolated input
Lock file, `npm audit`, review new dependencies, pin and update on a schedule

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is prototype pollution?
blocks.text: Writing attacker-controlled properties onto `Object.prototype`, usually through an unsafe recursive merge or path-set with keys like `__proto__`. All objects then inherit them.

blocks.title: What is ReDoS?
blocks.text: A regular expression whose matching time grows exponentially on crafted input because of backtracking, blocking the event loop. Nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+` are the classic cause.

blocks.title: How do you serve user-named files safely?
blocks.text: Resolve the requested name against the root directory and confirm the result is still inside it, or avoid user-supplied paths by looking up a stored name by id.

blocks.title: `exec` versus `execFile`?
blocks.text: `exec` runs a string through a shell, so special characters in input are interpreted. `execFile` runs a program with an argument array and no shell, so input stays data.

blocks.title: What is a supply-chain attack?
blocks.text: Malicious code arriving through a dependency: a compromised or typo-squatted package. Mitigate with lock files, audits, minimal dependencies and careful updates.

A Node service is packaged as a Docker image and run as several identical copies behind a load balancer. The platform (Kubernetes, ECS, a PaaS) restarts copies that crash and replaces them during a deploy.

Two behaviours make that safe: a **health endpoint** the platform can poll, and **graceful shutdown**, which means that when told to stop, the process stops accepting new requests, finishes the ones in flight, closes its database connections and then exits.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Think of app lifecycle callbacks. `SIGTERM` is the server's `applicationWillTerminate`: a short window to finish work and clean up before the process is killed.

blocks.code:
FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
blocks.caption: Dockerfile
Graceful shutdown

blocks.text: A rolling deploy with no dropped requests

rows: Three copies of version 1 serve traffic.
The platform starts one copy of version 2 and waits for its health check to pass.
Version 2 is healthy. One v1 copy receives `SIGTERM`. Its health check turns 503 and it finishes in-flight requests.
The drained copy exits. The cycle repeats for the others.
All copies run version 2. No request was cut off.

blocks.text: Observability

rows: pino to stdout, collected by the platform
How many, how fast, how many failing

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: No graceful shutdown. Every deploy drops in-flight requests and users see errors.
`NODE_ENV` not set to `production`. Express then skips optimisations and may expose error details.
Wrapping `node` in `npm start` inside the container. Signals may not reach your process.
One instance. Any deploy or crash is downtime.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is graceful shutdown?
blocks.text: On a termination signal the process stops accepting new work, completes in-flight requests, closes connections and exits within a time limit.

blocks.title: Why run several instances of a single-threaded runtime?
blocks.text: To use all CPU cores, to survive the crash of one instance and to deploy without downtime.

blocks.title: What does PM2 do?
blocks.text: It is a process manager for Node on plain servers: starts several instances, restarts them on crashes and reloads without downtime. Container platforms provide the same things, so PM2 is usually unnecessary there.

blocks.title: What would you alert on?
blocks.text: Error rate, p95 latency, event loop delay, memory growth, restarts and saturation of the database pool.
Draining requests, readiness and using every core

The sample below proves what "graceful" means. A slow request is in flight when shutdown starts. `server.close()` stops the server from accepting new connections but lets the open one finish. A new request is refused, the slow one completes, and only then does the server report closed.

In production the sequence is driven by the platform. It sends `SIGTERM`, your process turns its **readiness** check to "not ready" so the load balancer stops routing to it, drains, and exits before the grace period ends. **Liveness** is a different question: "is this process stuck and in need of a restart". Do not make liveness depend on the database, or a database outage will restart every instance in a loop.
To use all CPU cores, run one process per core. The container platform usually does that with replicas. On a single machine, the `cluster` module forks workers that share one port.

blocks.caption: One process per core with cluster

blocks.text: What the platform and your process do on a deploy

rows: The platform sends `SIGTERM` to an old instance and starts a grace timer, often 30 seconds.
Your handler flips readiness to 503 and calls `server.close()`.
Open requests finish. No new ones arrive.
You close the database pool and queue connections, then exit with code 0.
If the process were still alive when the timer ends, it would be killed with `SIGKILL` and anything in flight would be lost.

blocks.text: Liveness and readiness

rows: Only that the event loop responds
Startup finished, not shutting down, critical dependencies reachable
Stops routing to it, does not restart

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What does `server.close()` do?
blocks.text: It stops the server from accepting new connections and calls back once existing connections have ended. In-flight requests are allowed to finish.

blocks.title: Why separate liveness from readiness?
blocks.text: A dependency outage should take instances out of rotation, not restart them. Liveness failing restarts the process, so it should only detect a stuck process.

blocks.title: What is the cluster module?
blocks.text: A way to fork several Node processes that share a listening port, so one machine uses all cores. The primary can restart workers that die.

blocks.title: Why can long-lived connections break graceful shutdown?
blocks.text: Keep-alive and WebSocket connections stay open, so `close()` may never complete. Close idle connections, tell clients to reconnect, and enforce a deadline.

blocks.title: What exit code should a process use?
blocks.text: 0 for a clean, intended exit and non-zero for failure, so the platform and scripts can tell the difference.

Node is a good front door for AI features: it is strong at streaming and at holding many slow connections open, which is exactly what model calls need. The model providers ship official TypeScript SDKs, so calling a model looks like any other async client.
The architecture is the same as in the Python track. The phone talks to your server, your server holds the API key, adds context and rules, calls the model and streams the answer back.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: This is the server that sits behind the chat screen you would build in SwiftUI or Flutter. The SSE events it writes are what your `AsyncSequence` or Dart `Stream` reads on the client.

No per-user rate limit or token budget on an AI endpoint.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Why is Node a good fit for serving model responses?
blocks.text: Model calls are long, mostly idle network waits with incremental output. The event loop holds many such streams at once with little memory.

blocks.title: How do you stream a model answer to a client?
blocks.text: Open a streaming request to the model, and for each text delta write a server-sent event to the HTTP response. End with a final event carrying usage data, and abort upstream if the client disconnects.

blocks.title: Should AI logic live in Python or Node?
blocks.text: Either can call model APIs. Choose Python when you need its data and ML libraries (pandas, evaluation tools, model training). Choose Node when the AI feature is part of an existing Node or TypeScript product and mostly orchestrates API calls.

blocks.title: How do you protect an AI endpoint?
blocks.text: Authenticate, rate-limit per user, cap input size and `max_tokens`, validate outputs, check permissions inside tools and log usage per user.
The tool loop by hand, typed output and cheaper repeated prompts
Three additions make the earlier examples production-shaped.

**The loop by hand.** The SDK's tool runner is the default, but writing the loop once shows what it does: send messages and tool definitions, run every `tool_use` block the model returns, send back one `tool_result` per block in a single user message, and repeat until the model stops asking.
**Typed output.** A Zod schema describes the object you want. The SDK asks the model to fill it and returns a parsed, validated value, so your code never parses free text.

**Prompt caching.** When every request starts with the same long system prompt or policy document, mark the request for caching. The repeated prefix is then billed at a fraction and answered faster. Keep the stable text first and the changing question last.

blocks.title: What must each `tool_result` contain?
blocks.text: Its type, the `tool_use_id` of the request it answers, and the content. Add `is_error: true` when the tool failed.

blocks.title: Why send all tool results in one message?
blocks.text: The API expects every `tool_use` from an assistant turn to be answered in the next user turn. Splitting them breaks the pairing and discourages the model from calling tools in parallel.

blocks.title: How do you get typed data from a model in TypeScript?
blocks.text: Define a Zod schema and pass it as the output format. The SDK returns a parsed object validated against the schema.

blocks.title: When does prompt caching pay off?
blocks.text: When many requests share a long identical prefix such as a system prompt, tool definitions or a document, and arrive close enough together for the cache to still be warm.

blocks.title: Where do you enforce per-user AI budgets?
blocks.text: On your server: record tokens from each response's usage against the user and refuse or degrade when a limit is reached.

modules.title: Side by side: Big picture
modules.summary: What a backend is, in any language

blocks.text: A backend is a set of programs that run on computers you control and answer requests from apps. Whatever language you pick, the same boxes appear. Learn the boxes once and every architecture diagram becomes readable.

The **API server** runs your code. The **database** remembers things. The **cache** remembers recent answers so they are fast. The **queue** holds work to do later, and **workers** do it. The **load balancer** spreads requests over several copies of the API server. **Object storage** holds files such as images.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant. The waiter is the API: takes orders, never cooks. The kitchen ticket rail is the queue. Cooks are workers. The pantry is the database. The counter of ready-made snacks is the cache. The host at the door, sending guests to free tables, is the load balancer.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: From the app you only ever saw one box: a base URL. Everything in this lesson sits behind that URL. Timeouts, 5xx errors and "works on retry" behaviour you have seen from the client are these boxes being slow, restarting or overloaded.
"Place order", box by box

rows: The app sends `POST /orders` with a token.
The API server verifies the token and validates the body.
Delivery slots for the pincode are needed. They were looked up a minute ago.
The order, its items and the stock change are written together.
The invoice email and push notification are slow and can be retried.
The API answers `201 Created`. Total time about 80 ms.
A moment later a worker sends the email and the push.
Runs the jobs, retries on failure

blocks.text: Which box fixes which problem

rows: Too many requests for one machine
The same expensive read again and again
A slow step the user need not wait for
One part needs to scale differently
Split it into its own service

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Adding boxes before you need them. Start with an API and a database. Add a cache or queue when a measurement asks for it.
Keeping important state inside an API server's memory. Copies come and go, so state belongs in the database or cache.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What is the difference between a web server, an API server and a database?
blocks.text: A web server accepts HTTP connections. An API server runs application code that turns requests into responses. A database stores data durably and answers queries. One program can play the first two roles.

blocks.title: Vertical versus horizontal scaling?
blocks.text: Vertical means a bigger machine. Horizontal means more machines behind a load balancer. Horizontal needs stateless servers and gives redundancy as well as capacity.

blocks.title: What is a load balancer?
blocks.text: A component that distributes incoming requests across healthy server instances and stops sending traffic to ones that fail health checks.

blocks.title: Monolith versus microservices?
blocks.text: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices are several small ones that communicate over the network. Start with a well-structured monolith and split only where teams or scaling needs force it.

blocks.title: What is a CDN?
blocks.text: A network of servers close to users that caches static content such as images, so it is served quickly and your servers do less work.

lessons.title: Python or Node: how to choose

blocks.text: Both can build any backend you are likely to need. The choice is mostly about the **libraries around the job** and the **team around you**, not raw speed. For most APIs the database is the slow part, and it is the same database in both.

A fair summary: Python is the stronger choice when data or AI work is central. Node is the stronger choice when the workload is real-time, or when the team already writes TypeScript for the web. Learning both, in that order, makes you useful on either kind of team.
Head to head

rows: asyncio, threads, processes; GIL limits CPU threads
One event loop; worker threads for CPU
SDKs for model APIs, little beyond that
Shares code with a web front end

blocks.title: Real example
blocks.text: A common production shape uses both. A Node or TypeScript "backend for frontend" serves the apps: auth, aggregation, WebSockets. Python services sit behind it for recommendations, search ranking and AI features. They talk over HTTP or a queue. Knowing both lets you follow a request across that boundary.

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: You have lived this choice already: Swift versus Kotlin for native, Flutter for both. The backend version is similar. Each side can do the other's job, each has a home ground, and many companies run both.
Pitfalls

items: Choosing by benchmark charts. A missing database index costs more than any language difference.
Rewriting a working service in the other language for taste.
Learning both at once from zero. Get one to the "deployed API with tests" level first.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Is Node faster than Python?
blocks.text: For CPU-bound JavaScript versus Python code, usually yes, because V8 compiles to machine code. For typical APIs the time is spent in the database and network, so the practical difference is small.

blocks.title: When would you choose Python over Node?
blocks.text: When the service depends on the data and ML ecosystem: pandas, NumPy, model training, evaluation tooling, or when the team is Python-first.

blocks.title: When would you choose Node over Python?
blocks.text: For real-time, connection-heavy services, for a backend-for-frontend sharing TypeScript types with web clients, or when the team is JavaScript-first.

blocks.title: Can a company use both?
blocks.text: Yes, and many do: each service picks the language that suits it, and they communicate through HTTP, gRPC or a message queue.

lessons.title: The same endpoint in both languages

blocks.text: The fastest way to see how alike the two ecosystems are is to build one endpoint twice. The task: `POST /orders` validates a body, applies a pricing rule and returns the created order, with a 422 for bad input.
Read the two versions next to each other. The shape is identical: declare a schema, register a route, call a plain function with the business rule, return JSON.

blocks.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Item(BaseModel):
    sku: str = Field(min_length=1)
    price: int = Field(gt=0)          # paise
    qty: int = Field(gt=0, le=20)

class OrderIn(BaseModel):
    items: list[Item] = Field(min_length=1)
    member: bool = False

def price_order(order: OrderIn) -> dict:            # the business rule: no web code
    subtotal = sum(i.price * i.qty for i in order.items)
    fee = 0 if order.member or subtotal >= 50_000 else 4_000
    return {"subtotal": subtotal, "delivery_fee": fee, "total": subtotal + fee}

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/orders", status_code=201)
def create_order(order: OrderIn) -> dict:
    return {"id": 1, "status": "placed", **price_order(order)}

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.post("/orders", json={"items": [{"sku": "milk", "price": 6200, "qty": 2}]}).json())
print(client.post("/orders", json={"items": []}).status_code)

Pitfalls

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What does FastAPI do automatically that Express does not?
blocks.text: It reads type hints to parse and validate the body, query and path parameters, returns 422 on failure, and generates OpenAPI documentation. In Express you add a validator and documentation tooling yourself.

blocks.title: Why keep the pricing rule in a plain function in both versions?
blocks.text: It can be unit tested without HTTP and reused from a queue worker, a script or another endpoint.

blocks.title: Pydantic versus Zod?
blocks.text: Both validate and convert untrusted data against a schema and give typed results. Pydantic schemas are classes with type hints. Zod schemas are built with function calls and TypeScript infers the type from them.
Both runtimes handle many requests the same basic way: one thread runs your code, and waiting happens somewhere else. The differences are in the details, and interviewers like those details.

In Node the event loop is always on. Every I/O call is non-blocking by default and you cannot avoid the model. In Python the event loop is opt-in. Normal Python code blocks, and you choose `asyncio` (with async libraries) when you want the same behaviour. Python also has the GIL, which stops threads from running Python code in parallel.
Same question, two answers

rows: Many (`requests`, sync DB drivers), must avoid in async code
Yes, but the GIL lets one run Python at a time
Move to a worker or a queue
Heavy loop on the main thread

blocks.text: Three requests arrive at once. Each needs a 100 ms database query.

rows: Sync Python with one worker: requests are handled one after another.
The first finishes at 100 ms, the second at 200 ms, the third at 300 ms. More workers or threads are needed to do better.
Async Python or Node: all three queries are started immediately. The single thread is free while the database works.
All three results come back at about 100 ms and each handler resumes in turn.
Now each request needs 100 ms of CPU instead. Async does not help: one thread, 300 ms total, in both languages.
300 ms, and everything else is blocked meanwhile

Python: process pool / Node: worker thread pool
Queue + separate worker processes in both
Need every CPU core for request handling?
Run several processes behind a load balancer in both

blocks.title: From the app side
blocks.text: Dart isolates and the single UI thread are the closest mental model for both. "Never block the main thread" from mobile becomes "never block the event loop" here, with the difference that the thread you block is shared by every user.
Pitfalls

items: Saying "Node is single-threaded" or "Python cannot do concurrency" without the qualifications. Both statements are half true and interviewers probe the other half.
Using async for CPU-bound code and expecting a speed-up.

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: Concurrency versus parallelism?
blocks.text: Concurrency is dealing with many tasks by interleaving them, possibly on one core. Parallelism is executing several tasks at the same instant on several cores. An event loop gives concurrency. Processes and worker threads give parallelism.

blocks.title: How does the GIL compare with Node's single thread?
blocks.text: Both mean only one thread executes your language-level code at a time. Python can still have many OS threads that take turns and overlap on I/O. Node has one JavaScript thread by design and offloads I/O to the system and libuv.

blocks.title: Blocking versus non-blocking I/O?
blocks.text: A blocking call makes the thread wait until the operation completes. A non-blocking call returns immediately and reports completion later through a callback, promise or awaitable.

blocks.title: Why does async code handle more connections with less memory than threads?
blocks.text: A waiting coroutine or promise is a small object on the heap. A waiting thread holds a full stack and costs a context switch to resume.

lessons.title: Backend interview questions that apply to both

blocks.text: Language questions are covered inside each lesson. This page holds the questions that are asked whichever language you use: API design, data, reliability and scaling. Answer each aloud in under a minute before opening it.

A good answer has three parts: a one-sentence definition, why it matters, and a concrete example from something you built or used. As a mobile developer, your examples from the client side are valid and often better than textbook ones.

diagram.title: A structure for system design answers

blocks.text: Numbers worth remembering

rows: Redis read on the same network
Call to another service in the same region
Hundreds to a few thousand simple requests per second

blocks.text: Check yourself

blocks.title: What makes an API RESTful?
blocks.text: Resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP methods with their usual meanings, stateless requests, and standard status codes. For example `GET /orders/184`, `POST /orders`, `PATCH /orders/184`.

blocks.title: REST versus GraphQL versus gRPC?
blocks.text: REST is resource URLs over HTTP and JSON, simple and cacheable. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs from one endpoint, useful for varied screens. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 with generated clients, common between internal services.

blocks.title: How do you make a payment endpoint safe to retry?
blocks.text: The client sends a unique idempotency key. The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result if the same key arrives again, instead of charging twice.

blocks.title: How do you version an API when old app versions stay in use for years?
blocks.text: Only make additive changes within a version: new optional fields, new endpoints. Never remove or rename fields. For breaking changes add `/v2` or a version header and keep the old one until usage drops.

blocks.title: How do you paginate a large list?
blocks.text: Cursor pagination: return a cursor pointing at the last item and ask for items after it. It stays correct when rows are inserted and stays fast on large tables, unlike large `OFFSET` values.

blocks.title: SQL versus NoSQL?
blocks.text: SQL databases give relations, joins, transactions and a fixed schema, and suit most business data. NoSQL stores (document, key-value, wide-column) trade some of that for flexible schemas or horizontal scale on specific access patterns.

blocks.title: What is database replication and what is replication lag?
blocks.text: Copies of the primary database receive its changes and serve reads. Lag is the delay before a write appears on a replica, which can make a just-written value seem missing if read from a replica.

blocks.title: What is the CAP theorem in one sentence?
blocks.text: When a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. It cannot guarantee both.

blocks.title: How do you rate-limit an API?
blocks.text: Count requests per key (user or IP) in a shared store such as Redis using a fixed window, sliding window or token bucket, and return 429 with a `Retry-After` header when the limit is passed.

blocks.title: What is a circuit breaker?
blocks.text: A wrapper around calls to a dependency that stops calling it for a while after repeated failures, failing fast instead, then lets a few test calls through to see if it has recovered.

blocks.title: What happens when you type a URL and press enter?
blocks.text: DNS resolves the name to an IP, a TCP connection and TLS handshake are made, the HTTP request is sent, a load balancer forwards it to a server, the server responds, and the client renders the response.

blocks.title: How would you design live order tracking?
blocks.text: Riders send positions over a WebSocket or frequent posts. The API publishes each update to a pub/sub channel per order. API instances holding customer connections subscribe and push updates. Store the latest position in Redis and send it first on reconnect.

blocks.title: How do you deploy a database schema change without downtime?
blocks.text: In steps that keep old and new code working: add the new column as nullable, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column in a later release.

blocks.title: An endpoint became slow. How do you investigate?
blocks.text: Confirm with metrics which route and since when. Check recent deploys. Look at traces or logs for where time is spent. If it is a query, read its plan. If it is CPU, profile. Fix, then add an alert.

blocks.title: What is eventual consistency?
blocks.text: Different parts of a system may briefly show different values after a write, and converge to the same value shortly after. It is the price of replicas, caches and asynchronous messaging.

blocks.title: How do services communicate asynchronously?
blocks.text: Through a message broker. One service publishes an event such as "order placed", and other services consume it when they can. The publisher does not wait and does not need to know the consumers.

questions.q: Why learn Python instead of only Swift or Dart for backend and AI?
questions.a: Most AI libraries, model SDK examples and data tools are Python first, and frameworks like FastAPI make it a quick way to ship a backend. Swift and Dart have small server ecosystems by comparison.

questions.q: What does the interpreter do?
questions.a: It reads your source file, compiles it to bytecode and executes that bytecode one instruction at a time. There is no separate build step that you run yourself.

questions.q: What problem does a virtual environment solve?
questions.a: Two projects that need different versions of the same library. Each environment has its own site-packages folder, so they do not clash.

questions.q: What is the difference between `pip install x` and `pip install -r requirements.txt`?
questions.a: The first installs one named package. The second installs every package listed in a file, usually with pinned versions, so the setup is repeatable.

questions.q: What is PyPI?
questions.a: The public package index that pip downloads from. It is the Python equivalent of pub.dev or CocoaPods trunk.

questions.q: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
questions.a: Both in sequence. Source is compiled to bytecode, then the bytecode is interpreted by the CPython virtual machine. It is not compiled to machine code ahead of time.

questions.q: What is CPython?
questions.a: The standard implementation of Python, written in C. When people say Python they almost always mean CPython.

questions.q: What is the REPL good for?
questions.a: Trying a single expression or library call and seeing the result at once, without creating a file.

questions.q: What is dynamic typing?
questions.a: The type belongs to the value, not to the variable name. A name can refer to an int now and a str later, and type errors appear at run time.

questions.q: What is the difference between `is` and `==`?
questions.a: `==` asks whether two values are equal. `is` asks whether two names point at the very same object. Use `is` for `None`, `True` and `False`.

questions.q: How big can a Python int get?
questions.a: As big as memory allows. There is no overflow at 64 bits.

questions.q: How does Python manage memory?
questions.a: Every object has a reference count and is freed as soon as it reaches zero. A generational cyclic garbage collector additionally finds groups of objects that reference each other and are otherwise unreachable.

questions.q: What is the difference between mutable and immutable objects?
questions.a: A mutable object can be changed in place, so every name bound to it sees the change. An immutable one cannot, so any "change" creates a new object.

questions.q: Why does `a = 256; b = 256; a is b` print True but large numbers may not?
questions.a: CPython pre-creates and reuses small integers from -5 to 256, so both names point at the same object. This is an implementation detail, which is why you compare values with `==`.

questions.q: What is a weak reference?
questions.a: A reference that does not increase the reference count. It is used for caches and observers so they do not keep objects alive.

questions.q: Why are strings immutable?
questions.a: So they can be shared safely and used as dictionary keys. Any change creates a new string object.

questions.q: How do you reverse a string?
questions.a: With a slice that steps backwards: `s[::-1]`.

questions.q: What does `"a,b,,c".split(",")` return?
questions.a: `['a', 'b', '', 'c']`. Empty pieces are kept when you pass a separator.

questions.q: What values are treated as false in an `if`?
questions.a: `False`, `None`, zero, and empty containers such as `""`, `[]`, `{}` and `set()`. Everything else is true.

questions.q: What does `for ... else` do?
questions.a: The `else` block runs only if the loop finished without hitting `break`. It is useful for "searched everything, found nothing".

questions.q: What is the difference between `range(5)` and `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]`?
questions.a: `range` produces numbers one at a time and stores only start, stop and step. The list holds all five numbers in memory.

questions.q: What is the mutable default argument bug?
questions.a: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A default list or dict is shared between calls, so data leaks from one call to the next. Use `None` as the default and build the object inside the function.

questions.q: What are `*args` and `**kwargs`?
questions.a: `*args` gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple. `**kwargs` gathers extra keyword arguments into a dict. They let a function accept any call shape, which wrappers and decorators rely on.

questions.q: Does Python pass arguments by value or by reference?
questions.a: Neither exactly. It passes a reference to the object. Reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller, but mutating the object (appending to a list) does.

questions.q: What is a closure?
questions.a: A function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.

questions.q: What is the LEGB rule?
questions.a: The order in which Python resolves a name: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module), Built-in.

questions.q: Why do closures created in a loop all return the same value?
questions.a: They capture the variable, which is looked up when the function is called. By then the loop has finished and the variable holds its last value. Bind the current value with a default argument or `functools.partial`.

questions.q: What does `nonlocal` do?
questions.a: It tells Python that an assignment refers to a variable in an enclosing function's scope instead of creating a new local one.

questions.q: What is a pure function and why prefer it?
questions.a: A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing outside itself. It is easy to test, cache and run concurrently.

questions.q: List versus tuple: when do you use each?
