questions.a: A regular expression whose matching time grows exponentially on crafted input because of backtracking, blocking the event loop. Nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+` are the classic cause.

questions.q: How do you serve user-named files safely?
questions.a: Resolve the requested name against the root directory and confirm the result is still inside it, or avoid user-supplied paths by looking up a stored name by id.

questions.q: `exec` versus `execFile`?
questions.a: `exec` runs a string through a shell, so special characters in input are interpreted. `execFile` runs a program with an argument array and no shell, so input stays data.

questions.q: What is a supply-chain attack?
questions.a: Malicious code arriving through a dependency: a compromised or typo-squatted package. Mitigate with lock files, audits, minimal dependencies and careful updates.

questions.q: What is graceful shutdown?
questions.a: On a termination signal the process stops accepting new work, completes in-flight requests, closes connections and exits within a time limit.

questions.q: Why run several instances of a single-threaded runtime?
questions.a: To use all CPU cores, to survive the crash of one instance and to deploy without downtime.

questions.q: What does PM2 do?
questions.a: It is a process manager for Node on plain servers: starts several instances, restarts them on crashes and reloads without downtime. Container platforms provide the same things, so PM2 is usually unnecessary there.

questions.q: What would you alert on?
questions.a: Error rate, p95 latency, event loop delay, memory growth, restarts and saturation of the database pool.

questions.q: What does `server.close()` do?
questions.a: It stops the server from accepting new connections and calls back once existing connections have ended. In-flight requests are allowed to finish.

questions.q: Why separate liveness from readiness?
questions.a: A dependency outage should take instances out of rotation, not restart them. Liveness failing restarts the process, so it should only detect a stuck process.

questions.q: What is the cluster module?
questions.a: A way to fork several Node processes that share a listening port, so one machine uses all cores. The primary can restart workers that die.

questions.q: Why can long-lived connections break graceful shutdown?
questions.a: Keep-alive and WebSocket connections stay open, so `close()` may never complete. Close idle connections, tell clients to reconnect, and enforce a deadline.

questions.q: What exit code should a process use?
questions.a: 0 for a clean, intended exit and non-zero for failure, so the platform and scripts can tell the difference.

questions.q: Why is Node a good fit for serving model responses?
questions.a: Model calls are long, mostly idle network waits with incremental output. The event loop holds many such streams at once with little memory.

questions.q: How do you stream a model answer to a client?
questions.a: Open a streaming request to the model, and for each text delta write a server-sent event to the HTTP response. End with a final event carrying usage data, and abort upstream if the client disconnects.

questions.q: Should AI logic live in Python or Node?
questions.a: Either can call model APIs. Choose Python when you need its data and ML libraries (pandas, evaluation tools, model training). Choose Node when the AI feature is part of an existing Node or TypeScript product and mostly orchestrates API calls.

questions.q: How do you protect an AI endpoint?
questions.a: Authenticate, rate-limit per user, cap input size and `max_tokens`, validate outputs, check permissions inside tools and log usage per user.

questions.q: What must each `tool_result` contain?
questions.a: Its type, the `tool_use_id` of the request it answers, and the content. Add `is_error: true` when the tool failed.

questions.q: Why send all tool results in one message?
questions.a: The API expects every `tool_use` from an assistant turn to be answered in the next user turn. Splitting them breaks the pairing and discourages the model from calling tools in parallel.

questions.q: How do you get typed data from a model in TypeScript?
questions.a: Define a Zod schema and pass it as the output format. The SDK returns a parsed object validated against the schema.

questions.q: When does prompt caching pay off?
questions.a: When many requests share a long identical prefix such as a system prompt, tool definitions or a document, and arrive close enough together for the cache to still be warm.

questions.q: Where do you enforce per-user AI budgets?
questions.a: On your server: record tokens from each response's usage against the user and refuse or degrade when a limit is reached.

questions.q: What is the first thing that breaks when this service gets ten times the traffic?
questions.a: Usually the database: connection limits and slow queries. Then in-memory state that assumed one instance. Measure before guessing.

questions.q: How would you split this into services later?
questions.a: Along lines that scale differently: the real-time gateway (many idle connections), the order API (transactional) and workers (CPU and retries), communicating through a queue or event stream.

questions.q: What is the difference between a web server, an API server and a database?
questions.a: A web server accepts HTTP connections. An API server runs application code that turns requests into responses. A database stores data durably and answers queries. One program can play the first two roles.

questions.q: Vertical versus horizontal scaling?
questions.a: Vertical means a bigger machine. Horizontal means more machines behind a load balancer. Horizontal needs stateless servers and gives redundancy as well as capacity.

questions.q: What is a load balancer?
questions.a: A component that distributes incoming requests across healthy server instances and stops sending traffic to ones that fail health checks.

questions.q: Monolith versus microservices?
questions.a: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices are several small ones that communicate over the network. Start with a well-structured monolith and split only where teams or scaling needs force it.

questions.q: What is a CDN?
questions.a: A network of servers close to users that caches static content such as images, so it is served quickly and your servers do less work.

questions.q: Is Node faster than Python?
questions.a: For CPU-bound JavaScript versus Python code, usually yes, because V8 compiles to machine code. For typical APIs the time is spent in the database and network, so the practical difference is small.

questions.q: When would you choose Python over Node?
questions.a: When the service depends on the data and ML ecosystem: pandas, NumPy, model training, evaluation tooling, or when the team is Python-first.

questions.q: When would you choose Node over Python?
questions.a: For real-time, connection-heavy services, for a backend-for-frontend sharing TypeScript types with web clients, or when the team is JavaScript-first.

questions.q: Can a company use both?
questions.a: Yes, and many do: each service picks the language that suits it, and they communicate through HTTP, gRPC or a message queue.

questions.q: What does FastAPI do automatically that Express does not?
questions.a: It reads type hints to parse and validate the body, query and path parameters, returns 422 on failure, and generates OpenAPI documentation. In Express you add a validator and documentation tooling yourself.

questions.q: Why keep the pricing rule in a plain function in both versions?
questions.a: It can be unit tested without HTTP and reused from a queue worker, a script or another endpoint.

questions.q: Pydantic versus Zod?
questions.a: Both validate and convert untrusted data against a schema and give typed results. Pydantic schemas are classes with type hints. Zod schemas are built with function calls and TypeScript infers the type from them.

questions.q: Concurrency versus parallelism?
questions.a: Concurrency is dealing with many tasks by interleaving them, possibly on one core. Parallelism is executing several tasks at the same instant on several cores. An event loop gives concurrency. Processes and worker threads give parallelism.

questions.q: How does the GIL compare with Node's single thread?
questions.a: Both mean only one thread executes your language-level code at a time. Python can still have many OS threads that take turns and overlap on I/O. Node has one JavaScript thread by design and offloads I/O to the system and libuv.

questions.q: Blocking versus non-blocking I/O?
questions.a: A blocking call makes the thread wait until the operation completes. A non-blocking call returns immediately and reports completion later through a callback, promise or awaitable.

questions.q: Why does async code handle more connections with less memory than threads?
questions.a: A waiting coroutine or promise is a small object on the heap. A waiting thread holds a full stack and costs a context switch to resume.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: Why Python before Node in this plan?
questions.a: Python has less syntax to learn, AI material is Python first, and the backend concepts learned once transfer directly to Node.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What should every week produce?
questions.a: Something that runs: a script, an endpoint, a test suite or a deployment. Running code exposes the gaps that reading hides.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What makes an API RESTful?
questions.a: Resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP methods with their usual meanings, stateless requests, and standard status codes. For example `GET /orders/184`, `POST /orders`, `PATCH /orders/184`.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: REST versus GraphQL versus gRPC?
questions.a: REST is resource URLs over HTTP and JSON, simple and cacheable. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs from one endpoint, useful for varied screens. gRPC uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 with generated clients, common between internal services.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do you make a payment endpoint safe to retry?
questions.a: The client sends a unique idempotency key. The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result if the same key arrives again, instead of charging twice.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do you version an API when old app versions stay in use for years?
questions.a: Only make additive changes within a version: new optional fields, new endpoints. Never remove or rename fields. For breaking changes add `/v2` or a version header and keep the old one until usage drops.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do you paginate a large list?
questions.a: Cursor pagination: return a cursor pointing at the last item and ask for items after it. It stays correct when rows are inserted and stays fast on large tables, unlike large `OFFSET` values.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: SQL versus NoSQL?
questions.a: SQL databases give relations, joins, transactions and a fixed schema, and suit most business data. NoSQL stores (document, key-value, wide-column) trade some of that for flexible schemas or horizontal scale on specific access patterns.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What is database replication and what is replication lag?
questions.a: Copies of the primary database receive its changes and serve reads. Lag is the delay before a write appears on a replica, which can make a just-written value seem missing if read from a replica.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What is the CAP theorem in one sentence?
questions.a: When a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. It cannot guarantee both.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do you rate-limit an API?
questions.a: Count requests per key (user or IP) in a shared store such as Redis using a fixed window, sliding window or token bucket, and return 429 with a `Retry-After` header when the limit is passed.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What is a circuit breaker?
questions.a: A wrapper around calls to a dependency that stops calling it for a while after repeated failures, failing fast instead, then lets a few test calls through to see if it has recovered.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What happens when you type a URL and press enter?
questions.a: DNS resolves the name to an IP, a TCP connection and TLS handshake are made, the HTTP request is sent, a load balancer forwards it to a server, the server responds, and the client renders the response.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How would you design live order tracking?
questions.a: Riders send positions over a WebSocket or frequent posts. The API publishes each update to a pub/sub channel per order. API instances holding customer connections subscribe and push updates. Store the latest position in Redis and send it first on reconnect.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do you deploy a database schema change without downtime?
questions.a: In steps that keep old and new code working: add the new column as nullable, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column in a later release.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: An endpoint became slow. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Confirm with metrics which route and since when. Check recent deploys. Look at traces or logs for where time is spent. If it is a query, read its plan. If it is CPU, profile. Fix, then add an alert.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: What is eventual consistency?
questions.a: Different parts of a system may briefly show different values after a write, and converge to the same value shortly after. It is the price of replicas, caches and asynchronous messaging.

questions.topic: Side by side: Plan and practice
questions.q: How do services communicate asynchronously?
questions.a: Through a message broker. One service publishes an event such as "order placed", and other services consume it when they can. The publisher does not wait and does not need to know the consumers.
